You are going to be blind for a time, not even able to see the light of the sun.” Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. 12 When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Practice a glad sending: pray, lay a gentle hand, and go tell about Jesus.
dailies.verse: They placed their hands on them and sent them off.
dailies.enoch: Wave goodbye, walk a few steps, and say: Go tell about Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 13:2–3, what two things did the church do after the Holy Spirit spoke?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They fasted and prayed, then placed their hands on them and sent them off.
dailies.jordyn: How should we play a sending game so that we honor the Holy Spirit’s call, and do not turn Elymas’s blindness, or the later hurting of Paul, into a joke or a fight?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not act out blindness, stones, or hitting. We practice a short prayer, a gentle hand on a shoulder, and a walk to another room to say, Jesus is the living God. The game is about being sent, not about harm.
dailies.action: Play a send-and-tell game: one person prays a short sentence, another gently places a hand on a shoulder, and someone walks to another spot and says, Jesus is the living God. Then switch.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the church prayed and sent Barnabas and Saul. Teach us to pray for people who go, and to be glad to tell about Jesus too. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Holy Spirit set Barnabas and Saul apart for the work to which he had called them. The church fasted and prayed, placed their hands on them, and sent them off, and the Holy Spirit sent them on their way. Today we practice that kind of sending, and that kind of telling.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up pray one short sentence, then let you walk a few steps and say: Jesus is the living God!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 13:4–5, who sent them on their way, and what did they do when they arrived at Salamis?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They were sent on their way by the Holy Spirit. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. John was with them as their helper.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is proclaiming the word of God a better center for a game than the conflict at Paphos?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The reason they were set apart was the work to which the Lord had called them: to tell the word of God. The conflict is part of the story, and we tell it with care. The game should practice the sending and the telling, which is the heart of this week.
dailies.passageText: 2 While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” 3 So after they had fasted and prayed, they placed their hands on them and sent them off. 4 The two of them, sent on their way by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus. 5 When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. John was with them as their helper.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: In Lystra a lame man walks, the crowd is pointed to the living God, and the disciples are strengthened.
dailies.verse: We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.
dailies.enoch: Stand up tall and say: The living God made the world!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 14:8–15, what happened to the man who had never walked, and what did Barnabas and Paul do when the crowd wanted to offer sacrifices?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Paul called out, “Stand up on your feet!” and the man jumped up and began to walk. When the crowd wanted to treat them like gods, Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes, rushed out, and told them they were only human, bringing good news about the living God.
dailies.jordyn: Paul is hurt so badly that people think he is dead, and then he gets up, goes back, and keeps strengthening the disciples (Acts 14:19–22). What does that show you about remaining true to the faith?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The hurting is real, and we say it simply, not as a frightening show. Paul gets up and goes back to the work. He and Barnabas encourage the disciples to remain true to the faith, even through many hardships. Being sent does not mean everything will be easy. It means the good news is still worth telling.
dailies.action: Read Acts 14:8–23 together, then tell someone: Paul and Barnabas pointed people to the living God, and they kept strengthening the disciples.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the lame man stood up, and that Paul and Barnabas would not take honor that belongs only to you. Help us remain true to the faith, even when it is hard. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: In Lystra a man lame from birth listened to Paul, and Paul called out, “Stand up on your feet!” The man walked. The crowd thought the gods had come down and wanted to offer sacrifices, but Barnabas and Paul rushed out and pointed them to the living God who made all things. Later, people hurt Paul so badly they thought he was dead, but he got up, went back into the city, and then preached in Derbe. They returned, strengthening the disciples. “We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said, and they appointed elders, committing them to the Lord with prayer and fasting.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up stand with you, then point upward and say: We tell about the living God, not about us!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 14:21–23, where did they go after Derbe, and what did they do in the churches?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples, encouraging them to remain true to the faith, appointing elders in each church, and, with prayer and fasting, committing them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.
dailies.jordyn2: Why do Paul and Barnabas refuse the sacrifices, and then later appoint elders and commit the churches to the Lord?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They will not let people treat messengers like gods. The living God made the world, and the good news is about him. Then they do not leave the new disciples alone. They strengthen them, appoint elders, and commit them to the Lord with prayer and fasting, because the churches belong to him.
dailies.passageText: 8 In Lystra there sat a man who was lame. He had been that way from birth and had never walked. 9 He listened to Paul as he was speaking. Paul looked directly at him, saw that he had faith to be healed 10 and called out, “Stand up on your feet!” At that, the man jumped up and began to walk. 11 When the crowd saw what Paul had done, they shouted in the Lycaonian language, “The gods have come down to us in human form!” 12 Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes because he was the chief speaker. 13 The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates because he and the crowd wanted to offer sacrifices to them. 14 But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of this, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting: 15 “Friends, why are you doing this? We too are only human, like you. We are bringing you good news, telling you to turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and everything in them. 16 In the past, he let all nations go their own way. 17 Yet he has not left himself without testimony: He has shown kindness by giving you rain from heaven and crops in their seasons; he provides you with plenty of food and fills your hearts with joy.” 18 Even with these words, they had difficulty keeping the crowd from sacrificing to them. 19 Then some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won the crowd over. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead. 20 But after the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. The next day he and Barnabas left for Derbe. 21 They preached the gospel in that city and won a large number of disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, 22 strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain true to the faith. “We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said. 23 Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Pray for someone who tells the good news, or tell one person that Jesus is the living God.
dailies.verse: They proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues.
dailies.enoch: Cup your hands and say: I can tell someone about Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 13:5 and 14:21, what were Paul and Barnabas doing in the towns they visited?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They proclaimed the word of God, and in Derbe they preached the gospel and won a large number of disciples.
dailies.jordyn: The church sent them, and they kept telling the good news even after a hard day in Lystra (Acts 13:3; 14:20–21). What would a right-sized challenge look like for you this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Pray by name for someone who tells the good news, or tell one person, in a simple sentence, that Jesus is the living God. The challenge is not to copy every hardship in the story. It is to take a real part in the sending and the telling.
dailies.action: Choose one: pray this week for someone who tells the good news, or tell one person that Jesus is the living God, and let a parent know which you chose.
dailies.prayer: Father, the church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus. Give us a name to pray for, or a person to tell, and make us glad to share this good news. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The church sent them off, and they proclaimed the word of God. Later, after a hard time in Lystra, they still preached the gospel in Derbe and won a large number of disciples. Sending and telling belong together, and we can take a small, real part in both.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up name one person you can pray for, or one person you can tell about Jesus this week.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 14:23, how did Paul and Barnabas leave the new churches in the Lord’s care?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.
dailies.jordyn2: How can prayer be part of both sending people out and caring for those who already believe?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The church in Antioch prayed before they sent Barnabas and Saul. Paul and Barnabas also prayed and fasted as they committed the new churches to the Lord. Prayer is how we ask God to keep the work, at both ends of the trip.
dailies.passageText: 3 So after they had fasted and prayed, they placed their hands on them and sent them off. 5 When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. John was with them as their helper. 21 They preached the gospel in that city and won a large number of disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, 23 Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that he sent Paul and Barnabas, and ask him to keep his people true to the faith.
dailies.verse: They committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God, for sending Paul and Barnabas!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 13:2–3 and 14:23, how does prayer show up at the beginning and at the end of this story?
dailies.elijahAnswer: At the beginning, the church fasted and prayed, then sent Barnabas and Saul. At the end, Paul and Barnabas appointed elders and, with prayer and fasting, committed the churches to the Lord.
dailies.jordyn: Paul and Barnabas would not take honor that belongs to the living God (Acts 14:14–15), and they committed the churches to the Lord (Acts 14:23). How can thanking God this week keep him at the center, not the messengers?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Thank God that he set them apart, that he made the lame man walk, that the proconsul believed, and that the churches were committed to him. Then ask him to keep you true to the faith, and to keep the honor with him, the living God.
dailies.action: Pray together: thank God that the church sent Paul and Barnabas, and ask him to help you remain true to the faith and to tell others about Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you set apart Barnabas and Saul, and that the church sent them. Thank you that you are the living God who made all things, and that new believers were committed to you. Keep us true to the faith, and keep our praise aimed at you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This story begins with worship, fasting, and prayer in Antioch, and it ends with prayer and fasting as elders are appointed and churches are committed to the Lord. In the middle, the messengers refuse to be treated like gods. Prayer is a fitting way to end the week, because the work belongs to the Lord.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up thank God out loud that he sent Paul and Barnabas to other towns.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 14:15, who did Barnabas and Paul say the people should turn to?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They were bringing good news, telling them to turn from worthless things to the living God, who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and everything in them.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is the living God the right last word of a prayer after a week about sending?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The church did not send Paul and Barnabas so that people would praise the messengers. They were sent so that other towns would hear about the living God, and about Jesus. Our thanks should land in the same place.
dailies.passageText: 2 While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” 3 So after they had fasted and prayed, they placed their hands on them and sent them off. 15 “Friends, why are you doing this? We too are only human, like you. We are bringing you good news, telling you to turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and everything in them. 23 Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: The church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus, and next we will hear about grace in Jerusalem.
dailies.verse: The church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus.
dailies.enoch: Wave goodbye, then cup your hands, and say: The church sent them to tell about Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 13:2–3 and 14:21–22, how did this trip begin, and what did Paul and Barnabas keep doing even after Lystra?
dailies.elijahAnswer: It began with the Holy Spirit setting them apart, and the church praying and sending them off. After Lystra they still preached the gospel in Derbe, then returned, strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain true to the faith.
dailies.jordyn: This week a sending church told other towns about Jesus. How does that get your heart ready for next week, when there will be a meeting in Jerusalem about how people are saved?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The good news they carried is not a list of extra rules. Next week we will hear that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. The same grace is why the sending was worth the hardships.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: The church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus. Then thank God, and look ahead to a meeting in Jerusalem about being saved by grace.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus. Get our hearts ready to hear that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that the church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus. The Holy Spirit set them apart, the church prayed and sent them, the proconsul believed, a lame man walked, and the messengers pointed people to the living God. They went through hardships, then strengthened the churches and committed them to the Lord. Next week we will see a meeting in Jerusalem, and hear that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week we will hear that we are saved by grace!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 14:22, what did they encourage the disciples to do, and what did they say about hardships?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They encouraged them to remain true to the faith. “We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is the church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus a fitting last word before a week about grace?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They were sent with good news, not with a heavier set of rules. Next week’s meeting in Jerusalem will say plainly that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. The sending and the grace belong to the same gospel.
dailies.passageText: 2 While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” 3 So after they had fasted and prayed, they placed their hands on them and sent them off. 21 They preached the gospel in that city and won a large number of disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, 22 strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain true to the faith. “We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said. 23 Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.

weeks.bigIdea: We are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 33 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Acts 15:1–5 out loud, then Acts 15:6–9, then Acts 15:10–11.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 1 Certain people came down from Judea to Antioch and were teaching the believers: “Unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved.” 2 This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dispute and debate with them. So Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question. 3 The church sent them on their way, and as they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, they told how the Gentiles had been converted. This news made all the believers very glad. 4 When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and elders, to whom they reported everything God had done through them. 5 Then some of the believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees stood up and said, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.”

6 The apostles and elders met to consider this question. 7 After much discussion, Peter got up and addressed them: “Brothers, you know that some time ago God made a choice among you that the Gentiles might hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. 8 God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us. 9 He did not discriminate between us and them, for he purified their hearts by faith.

10 Now then, why do you try to test God by putting on the necks of Gentiles a yoke that neither we nor our ancestors have been able to bear? 11 No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

story: Last week the church sent Paul and Barnabas to tell other towns about Jesus, and people believed. Then a hard question came. Certain people came down from Judea to Antioch and were teaching the believers: “Unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved.” They wanted to add an extra rule, as if trusting Jesus were not enough. This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dispute and debate with them. So Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question.

The church sent them on their way. As they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, they told how the Gentiles had been converted, and this news made all the believers very glad. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and elders, and they reported everything God had done through them. Then some of the believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees stood up and said, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.”

The apostles and elders met to consider this question. After much discussion, Peter got up and spoke. He reminded them that God had already chosen that the Gentiles would hear the good news and believe. God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to the Jewish believers. He did not discriminate between them. He purified their hearts by faith. Why, then, try to test God by putting a heavy yoke on their necks, a load neither they nor their ancestors had been able to bear? No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.
That is the heart of the meeting: we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules. Next week we will see God open Lydia’s heart, and a midnight song used to save a jailer.
weeks.enochLine: We are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus!
enochActivities: Activity: Open hands. Hold your hands open and say: Jesus saves us by grace!
Activity: Same welcome. Hold a friend’s hand and say: God welcomes us the same way!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 15:1–2, what were certain people teaching, and what did the church do about the dispute?
In Acts 15:3–5, what news made the believers glad, and what did some of the Pharisee believers say in Jerusalem?
In Acts 15:7–9, how had God already shown that he accepted the Gentile believers?
In Acts 15:10–11, what heavy load did Peter not want put on the Gentiles, and how did he say we are saved?
elijahAnswers: They were teaching, “Unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved.” This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dispute with them, so the church appointed Paul and Barnabas, and some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders (Acts 15:1–2).

As they traveled, they told how the Gentiles had been converted, and this news made all the believers very glad. In Jerusalem some of the believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees said, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.” (Acts 15:3–5).

Peter said God had chosen that the Gentiles would hear the gospel and believe. God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us. He did not discriminate between them, for he purified their hearts by faith (Acts 15:7–9).

He did not want a yoke put on their necks that neither they nor their ancestors had been able to bear. He said, We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are (Acts 15:10–11).
jordynQuestions: The teachers in Antioch said you cannot be saved unless you also keep this custom (Acts 15:1). Peter says God already accepted the Gentiles and purified their hearts by faith (Acts 15:8–9). What is the difference between those two ways of thinking about being saved?

Peter calls the extra requirement a yoke that even their own ancestors could not bear (Acts 15:10), and then he says we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are (Acts 15:11). What does that tell you about grace, and about treating Gentile believers as full members of the family?

This week the meeting in Jerusalem says we are saved by grace, not by extra rules. Next week God will open Lydia’s heart, and a midnight song will be used to save a jailer. What do both stories show you about how God saves people?
jordynAnswers: The first way adds a rule as if faith in Jesus were not enough. Peter points to what God has already done: he gave the Holy Spirit, he did not discriminate, and he purified their hearts by faith. Being saved is God’s accepting work, received by faith, not a prize for finishing extra requirements.

Grace means Jewish and Gentile believers are saved the same way, through the Lord Jesus. No one gets to hang a heavier yoke on someone else’s neck as the price of belonging. If God has accepted them by faith, the church must not treat them as second-class.

God saves by the grace of the Lord Jesus. He opens hearts, and he meets people in unexpected places. Next week we will see that same grace at work in Lydia and in a jailer. The meeting in Jerusalem tells us what that salvation is: grace, not extra rules.
weeks.jordynApplication: We are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules (Acts 15:1–11). This week, thank God out loud that you are saved by grace, and be careful not to add an extra rule when you talk with someone about belonging to Jesus. Next week we will see God open Lydia’s heart, and a midnight song used to save a jailer.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she thanked God for being saved by grace, and whether she noticed a place where it is easy to add extra rules. If it is fitting, thank God together that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you know the heart, and that you accepted the Gentile believers by giving them the Holy Spirit and purifying their hearts by faith. Thank you that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules. Keep us from putting a heavy yoke on anyone’s neck, and teach us to welcome people the way you have welcomed them. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: A sharp dispute arises, and the church sends leaders to Jerusalem to settle a question about being saved.
dailies.verse: Unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved.
dailies.enoch: Shake your head gently and say: Jesus is enough to save us!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 15:1–2, what were certain people teaching in Antioch, and what did the church decide to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They were teaching that unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved. This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dispute and debate with them, so the church appointed them, with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question.
dailies.jordyn: The argument is about what must be added before a person can be saved (Acts 15:1, 5). How should we tell this part with care, especially the custom named in the text, and still be clear about the real issue?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can name what the official text says, without turning a body custom into a joke or a graphic lesson. The real issue is the claim that faith in Jesus is not enough, and that extra rules must be kept in order to be saved. That is why the church sent people to Jerusalem.
dailies.action: Read Acts 15:1–5 together, then tell someone: Some people wanted to add extra rules to being saved, so the church sent Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the church did not ignore this question. Give us wisdom to tell the truth with care, and to remember that being saved is about your grace, not extra rules. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Certain people came down from Judea and taught that you cannot be saved unless you also keep a custom from the law of Moses. Paul and Barnabas disputed this, and the church sent them, with others, to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem. On the way they told how the Gentiles had been converted, and the believers were very glad. In Jerusalem they were welcomed, and they reported everything God had done. Then some of the Pharisee believers said the Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up walk with you a few steps, as if going to ask a question, and say: The church went to find the answer!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 15:3–4, what did they report, and how were they received in Jerusalem?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They told how the Gentiles had been converted, and this news made all the believers very glad. In Jerusalem they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and elders, and they reported everything God had done through them.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it good that the church both argued the issue and also sent it to the apostles and elders, instead of splitting or staying silent?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The question was about how people are saved, so it could not be shrugged off. They debated it, and then they went together to the leaders in Jerusalem. The unity of the church, and the truth of the gospel, both mattered.
dailies.passageText: 1 Certain people came down from Judea to Antioch and were teaching the believers: “Unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved.” 2 This brought Paul and Barnabas into sharp dispute and debate with them. So Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question. 3 The church sent them on their way, and as they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, they told how the Gentiles had been converted. This news made all the believers very glad. 4 When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and elders, to whom they reported everything God had done through them. 5 Then some of the believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees stood up and said, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to keep the law of Moses.”

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Practice a same welcome: we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by extra rules.
dailies.verse: We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.
dailies.enoch: Hold your hands open and say: We are saved by grace!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 15:8–9 and 15:11, how had God already treated the Gentile believers, and how are we saved?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God accepted them, gave them the Holy Spirit, did not discriminate, and purified their hearts by faith. We are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are.
dailies.jordyn: How should we play a grace-and-welcome game so that we honor God’s acceptance, and do not make the law, or anyone’s body, into a joke?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not act out customs, or pretend to load people with shame. We practice the same welcome for everyone: open hands, and the words, We are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. The game is about grace, not about mocking a rule or a group.
dailies.action: Play a same-welcome game: one person stands at a door, and each family member is welcomed in the same way, with open hands, while someone says, We are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. Then switch.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you do not discriminate, and that you save us through the grace of our Lord Jesus. Teach us to welcome people the way you have welcomed them. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to the others. He purified their hearts by faith. Peter would not put a yoke on their necks that even their ancestors could not bear. We are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. Today we practice that same welcome.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up welcome you at a doorway with open hands, and say together: We are saved by grace!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 15:10, what did Peter say they should not put on the necks of the Gentiles?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: A yoke that neither they nor their ancestors have been able to bear.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is a same welcome a better picture for a game than acting out a heavy yoke?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The yoke is a warning in Peter’s speech, and we can say that simply. The good news at the center is that God has already accepted people by faith, and we are saved by the same grace. The game should practice that welcome, not the burden God refuses to lay on them.
dailies.passageText: 8 God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us. 9 He did not discriminate between us and them, for he purified their hearts by faith. 10 Now then, why do you try to test God by putting on the necks of Gentiles a yoke that neither we nor our ancestors have been able to bear? 11 No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Peter stands up: God has accepted the Gentiles by faith, and we are saved by grace.
dailies.verse: We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands and say: God accepted them, and he accepts us too!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 15:6–9, who met to consider the question, and how had God shown that he accepted the Gentiles?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The apostles and elders met. After much discussion, Peter said God had chosen that the Gentiles would hear the gospel and believe. God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us, and he purified their hearts by faith.
dailies.jordyn: Peter’s last word is that Jewish and Gentile believers are saved the same way: through the grace of our Lord Jesus (Acts 15:11). Why does he say just as they are, and not that one group has a harder path?
dailies.jordynAnswer: If God has already given the Spirit and purified their hearts by faith, there is not a second, heavier way of being saved. Grace puts both groups on the same ground. Extra rules would test God, and would make some believers look like they belonged less.
dailies.action: Read Acts 15:6–11 together, then tell someone: We are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you know the heart, that you give the Holy Spirit, and that you save us through the grace of our Lord Jesus. Keep us from adding a yoke you have not required. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The apostles and elders met. After much discussion, Peter stood up. God had already chosen that the Gentiles would hear the good news and believe. God, who knows the heart, accepted them, gave them the Holy Spirit, did not discriminate, and purified their hearts by faith. Peter asked why they would test God by putting a yoke on the Gentiles that even their ancestors could not bear. No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up place a hand over your heart and say: God knows the heart, and he saves by grace!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 15:11, what two-letter word does Peter begin with, and what does he say we believe?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He begins with No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.
dailies.jordyn2: The official story this week stops at verse 11. Why is that last sentence a complete enough word for this meeting, even before we hear the rest of the chapter later in life?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The question was how people are saved. Peter answers it: through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. That is the week’s big idea, and it is already enough to hold onto. The later part of the chapter is not our official reading this week.
dailies.passageText: 6 The apostles and elders met to consider this question. 7 After much discussion, Peter got up and addressed them: “Brothers, you know that some time ago God made a choice among you that the Gentiles might hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. 8 God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us. 9 He did not discriminate between us and them, for he purified their hearts by faith. 10 Now then, why do you try to test God by putting on the necks of Gentiles a yoke that neither we nor our ancestors have been able to bear? 11 No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Thank God that you are saved by grace, and do not add an extra rule to the good news.
dailies.verse: We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.
dailies.enoch: Hold your hands open and say: Thank you, Jesus, for your grace!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 15:1 and 15:11, what did some people say you must add in order to be saved, and what did Peter say instead?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Some said that unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses, you cannot be saved. Peter said we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are.
dailies.jordyn: What would a right-sized challenge look like this week, if the danger is adding extra rules to the good news, not forgetting to be kind or obedient in ordinary life?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Thank God out loud that you are saved by grace. Then notice one place where it is easy to make belonging to Jesus sound like a list of extras, and practice saying the good news simply: we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. The challenge is not to treat obedience as if it does not matter. It is to keep extra rules from becoming the door into salvation.
dailies.action: This week, thank God out loud that you are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, and tell one person the good news without adding an extra rule. Let a parent know you did it.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. Keep us from adding extra rules to your good news, and make us glad to share that grace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Some taught that you cannot be saved unless you also keep an extra custom. Peter said no: we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. A fitting challenge is to thank God for that grace, and to tell the good news without hanging a yoke on anyone’s neck.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up thank God out loud with you that Jesus saves us by grace.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 15:9, what did God do to their hearts, and how?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He purified their hearts by faith.
dailies.jordyn2: How can thanking God for grace, and telling the good news simply, fit together this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: If God has purified hearts by faith, then the right first word is thanks, not a new entrance exam. Telling the good news simply is a way of trusting that same grace for someone else.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that he accepts people by faith, and that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus.
dailies.verse: God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands, then open them, and say: Thank you, God, for accepting us by grace!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 15:8–11, what did God already do, and what does Peter want the church to believe?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God, who knows the heart, accepted them, gave them the Holy Spirit, did not discriminate, and purified their hearts by faith. Peter wants them to believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are.
dailies.jordyn: How can prayer this week thank God both for his welcome, and for a church that would not let extra rules replace grace?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Thank God that he knows the heart and gives the Holy Spirit. Thank him that the church took the question seriously and heard Peter’s word about grace. Then ask him to keep your family from adding a yoke he has not required, and to make you glad that we are saved just as they are.
dailies.action: Pray together: thank God that he accepts people by faith, and that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.
dailies.prayer: Father, you know the heart. Thank you that you accepted the Gentile believers and gave them the Holy Spirit, and that you purify hearts by faith. Thank you that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. Keep us from testing you with extra rules, and teach us to welcome others as you have welcomed us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: God knows the heart. He accepted the Gentiles, gave them the Holy Spirit, and purified their hearts by faith. Peter would not put a yoke on them, because we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. That is a word for thanking God, and for asking him to keep this gospel clear.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up thank God out loud that he knows the heart and saves by grace.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 15:6–7, what happened before Peter spoke, and how did he begin?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The apostles and elders met to consider this question. After much discussion, Peter got up and addressed them, beginning by reminding them that some time ago God made a choice among them that the Gentiles might hear from his lips the message of the gospel and believe.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it fitting to thank God after a meeting that included sharp dispute and much discussion?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The discussion was real, and the church did not pretend the question was small. God used it to make the gospel clear: salvation is by the grace of the Lord Jesus. Thanks belongs at the end of a hard, faithful conversation like that.
dailies.passageText: 6 The apostles and elders met to consider this question. 7 After much discussion, Peter got up and addressed them: “Brothers, you know that some time ago God made a choice among you that the Gentiles might hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. 8 God, who knows the heart, showed that he accepted them by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as he did to us. 9 He did not discriminate between us and them, for he purified their hearts by faith. 10 Now then, why do you try to test God by putting on the necks of Gentiles a yoke that neither we nor our ancestors have been able to bear? 11 No! We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

dailies.elijahAnswer: Some taught that you cannot be saved unless you are circumcised, according to the custom taught by Moses. Peter said we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are.
dailies.jordyn: This week a meeting in Jerusalem made the gospel clear: saved by grace, not by extra rules. How does that get your heart ready for next week, when God will open Lydia’s heart, and a midnight song will be used to save a jailer?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The same grace that the meeting named is the grace that opens hearts and saves people in unexpected places. Next week we will see that grace at work in Lydia and in a jailer. No one is saved by a heavier set of rules. God saves by the grace of the Lord Jesus.

dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus, just as they are. Get our hearts ready to see you open Lydia’s heart, and to see a midnight song used to save a jailer. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

readings.text: 11 From Troas we put out to sea and sailed straight for Samothrace, and the next day we went on to Neapolis. 12 From there we traveled to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of that district of Macedonia. And we stayed there several days. 13 On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer. We sat down and began to speak to the women who had gathered there. 14 One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 15 When she and the members of her household were baptized, she invited us to her home. “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” she said, “come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us.

16 Once when we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a female slave who had a spirit by which she predicted the future. She earned a great deal of money for her owners by fortune-telling. 17 She followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are telling you the way to be saved.” 18 She kept this up for many days. Finally Paul became so annoyed that he turned around and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” At that moment the spirit left her. 19 When her owners realized that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to face the authorities. 20 They brought them before the magistrates and said, “These men are Jews, and are throwing our city into an uproar 21 by advocating customs unlawful for us Romans to accept or practice.” 22 The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the magistrates ordered them to be stripped and beaten with rods. 23 After they had been severely flogged, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was commanded to guard them carefully. 24 When he received these orders, he put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.

25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 26 Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose. 27 The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself because he thought the prisoners had escaped. 28 But Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” 29 The jailer called for lights, rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. 30 He then brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” 32 Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house. 33 At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptized. 34 The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them; he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.

story: Last week we heard that we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by keeping extra rules. Then Paul and his companions sailed to Philippi, a leading city in Macedonia, and stayed there several days. On the Sabbath they went outside the city gate to the river, where they expected to find a place of prayer, and they began to speak to the women who had gathered there. One of those listening was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, and a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and the members of her household were baptized, she invited them to her home. “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” she said, “come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded them.

Once, on the way to the place of prayer, they were met by a female slave who had a spirit by which she predicted the future. Her owners made a great deal of money from that. She followed Paul and the others, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are telling you the way to be saved.” She kept this up for many days. Finally Paul turned to the spirit and said, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” At that moment the spirit left her. We tell this simply, and we honor the girl. She is not a joke in the story. When her owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, dragged them to the authorities, and made an angry charge against them. The magistrates ordered them to be beaten, and they were thrown into prison. The jailer put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks. We say the hurting simply. We do not act it out.

About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose. The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he thought the prisoners had escaped, and he was about to harm himself. But Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. He brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house. At that hour of the night the jailer washed their wounds, and he and all his household were baptized. He brought them into his house, set a meal before them, and was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.
God opened Lydia's heart, and he used a midnight song to save a jailer. Next week Paul will tell the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus.
weeks.enochLine: God opened Lydia’s heart, and a jailer believed in Jesus!
enochActivities: Activity: Open heart. Place a hand over your heart and say: God opened Lydia’s heart!

elijahQuestions: In Acts 16:13–15, who was Lydia, and what did the Lord do so that she responded to Paul’s message?
In Acts 16:16–24, what happened with the slave girl, and how did Paul and Silas end up in prison?
In Acts 16:25–28, what were Paul and Silas doing at midnight, and what did Paul shout to the jailer?
In Acts 16:29–34, what did the jailer ask, what answer was he given, and what happened in his house that night?
elijahAnswers: Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, and a worshiper of God. She was listening by the river, and the Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. She and her household were baptized, and she invited them to stay at her house (Acts 16:14–15).

A female slave who had a spirit followed them, shouting that they were servants of the Most High God, telling the way to be saved. Paul, in the name of Jesus Christ, commanded the spirit to come out of her, and it left. Her owners, angry that their hope of making money was gone, seized Paul and Silas. They were beaten and thrown into prison, with their feet in the stocks (Acts 16:16–24).

About midnight they were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening. An earthquake shook the prison, the doors flew open, and the chains came loose. Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” (Acts 16:25–28).

The jailer asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” They spoke the word of the Lord to his household. He washed their wounds, he and his household were baptized, and he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God (Acts 16:30–34).
jordynQuestions: Lydia is a worshiper of God, and still it is the Lord who opens her heart to respond (Acts 16:14). What does that show you about how people come to believe?

Paul and Silas are beaten and locked up, and at midnight they pray and sing, and the jailer is told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” (Acts 16:25, 31). How is this the same good news Lydia received, even though the setting is so different?

This week God opens Lydia’s heart and saves a jailer through a midnight song. Next week Paul will tell the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. What do both stories show you about the way this good news keeps traveling?
jordynAnswers: Listening and even already worshiping God is not the same as a heart opened to the message. The Lord does that work. We speak the message, and we also ask him to open hearts, because believing is his gift, not only a person’s effort.

The same Lord who opened Lydia’s heart is the one the jailer must believe in. Salvation is not a different door in a prison than it was by the river. It is trust in the Lord Jesus, for him and for his household, after the word of the Lord is spoken.

God opens hearts in a riverside prayer meeting, and he saves a jailer in the middle of the night. Next week the message will be spoken in a new city, to people who do not yet know the God who made the world and raised Jesus. The good news keeps moving, and the way to be saved stays the same.
weeks.jordynApplication: God opened Lydia’s heart, and he used a midnight song to save a jailer (Acts 16:11–34). This week, ask the Lord to open someone’s heart, and tell one person, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” Next week Paul will tell the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she prayed for someone whose heart needs to be opened, or told someone to believe in the Lord Jesus. If it is fitting, thank God together that he opened Lydia’s heart, and that a jailer and his household came to believe.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you opened Lydia’s heart to respond to the message, and that at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang to you. Thank you that Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” and that the jailer heard, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” Open hearts this week, keep us from despair, and fill us with the joy of believing in you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.elijah: In Acts 16:13–15, where did they meet Lydia, and what happened after the Lord opened her heart?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They went outside the city gate to the river, to a place of prayer, and spoke to the women gathered there. Lydia, a worshiper of God, listened, and the Lord opened her heart to respond. She and her household were baptized, and she invited them to stay at her house.
dailies.jordyn: Lydia is already a worshiper of God, and still the Lord must open her heart (Acts 16:14). What does that tell you about the message, and about God’s work in a person who is already listening?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The message must still be spoken, and God must still open the heart. Being near a place of prayer, or already honoring God, is not the same as responding to the good news. The Lord does that inner work, and then Lydia’s house becomes a place of welcome.
dailies.action: Read Acts 16:11–15 together, then tell someone: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart, and she asked the messengers to stay at her house.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you opened Lydia’s heart to respond to the message. Open hearts in our house too, and make us glad to welcome people who tell the good news. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul and his companions came to Philippi. On the Sabbath they went to the river, to a place of prayer, and spoke to the women there. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira and a worshiper of God, was listening. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. She and her household were baptized, and she said, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” and, “come and stay at my house.” She persuaded them.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up welcome you at the door, as Lydia did, and say: Come and stay! God opened Lydia’s heart!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 16:15, what two things did Lydia say when she invited them, and what had already happened in her household?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: She said, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” and, “come and stay at my house.” She and the members of her household had been baptized, and she persuaded them to stay.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it fitting that the first story in Philippi is a heart opened by the Lord, and then an open house?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God begins the work inside, and then the new believer’s home becomes a place of welcome. Lydia does not open her heart by herself, and she does not keep the gift to herself either.

dailies.enoch: Sing a short line to God, then say: Believe in the Lord Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 16:14–15 and 16:25, what did the Lord do for Lydia, and what were Paul and Silas doing at midnight in the prison?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart, and she welcomed them to her house. At midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening.
dailies.jordyn: How should we play a sing-and-welcome game so that we honor Lydia, honor the jailer, and do not turn the slave girl, the beating, or the jailer’s despair into a show?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not act out fortune-telling, hitting, chains as a fight, or anyone harming himself. We practice a short song to God in a quiet room, and a glad welcome at the door, like Lydia. The hard parts of the story we tell simply, with care, when we read them. The game is about singing and welcoming.
dailies.action: Play a sing-and-welcome game: dim a light, sing one short line to God, then go to a door and welcome someone the way Lydia did, saying, Come and stay, and, Believe in the Lord Jesus. Then switch.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Lydia welcomed the messengers, and that Paul and Silas sang to you at midnight. Teach us to sing to you, and to welcome people with glad hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart, and she invited the messengers to stay at her house. Later, in the prison, Paul and Silas prayed and sang hymns to God at midnight, and the other prisoners listened. Today we practice that welcome, and that kind of song, without acting out the hurting in the story.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up sing one short line with you, then welcome you at a doorway and say: Believe in the Lord Jesus!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 16:25, who else heard Paul and Silas praying and singing?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The other prisoners were listening to them.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is a song, and a welcome, a better center for a game than the prison earthquake or the owners’ anger?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The earthquake is God’s work, and we can tell it with wonder when we read it. The anger and the hurting are real, and we tell them simply, not as play. What we can practice is the same as Lydia and the prisoners heard: a welcome, and a song to God, and the call to believe in the Lord Jesus.
dailies.passageText: 14 One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 15 When she and the members of her household were baptized, she invited us to her home. “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” she said, “come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us. 25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: At midnight they sing, the jailer is kept from harm, and he and his household believe in the Lord Jesus.
dailies.verse: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.
dailies.enoch: Sing a short line, then say: Believe in the Lord Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 16:25–31, what happened in the prison at midnight, and what did Paul and Silas tell the jailer he must do to be saved?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They were praying and singing hymns to God when an earthquake shook the prison, the doors opened, and the chains came loose. The jailer thought the prisoners had escaped and was about to harm himself, but Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” The jailer asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”
dailies.jordyn: The jailer’s despair is real, and Paul stops him with a loud, kind word: they are all still there (Acts 16:27–28). How should we tell this part, and what does the jailer’s question show he needs even more than safety?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We tell it simply, not as a frightening show, and we do not act it out. Paul keeps the jailer from harming himself. Then the jailer asks how to be saved. He needs the same Lord Lydia believed in, not only a prison that has stopped shaking.
dailies.action: Read Acts 16:25–34 together, then tell someone: Paul and Silas sang at midnight, and the jailer and his household believed in the Lord Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul and Silas sang to you in prison, that you kept the jailer from harm, and that he and his household believed in the Lord Jesus. Fill us with that same joy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God. An earthquake shook the prison, the doors opened, and the chains came loose. The jailer thought the prisoners had escaped and was about to harm himself. Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” The jailer asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” They spoke the word of the Lord to his house. He washed their wounds, he and his household were baptized, and he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up pretend to wash a sore arm gently, as the jailer washed their wounds, and say: He believed in God, and he was filled with joy!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 16:33–34, what two kind things did the jailer do, and why was he filled with joy?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He washed their wounds, and he set a meal before them in his house. He was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household. He and all his household were also baptized.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it important that the official story includes both “Don’t harm yourself!” and “Believe in the Lord Jesus”?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The Lord cares about the jailer’s life, and about his salvation. Paul first keeps him from harm, then answers the question about being saved. We tell both with dignity: God keeps a man from despair, and he also opens the way to believe and have joy.
dailies.passageText: 25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 26 Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose. 27 The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself because he thought the prisoners had escaped. 28 But Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” 29 The jailer called for lights, rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. 30 He then brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” 32 Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house. 33 At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptized. 34 The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them; he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Ask the Lord to open a heart this week, and tell someone to believe in the Lord Jesus.
dailies.verse: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.
dailies.enoch: Place a hand over your heart and say: God, please open someone’s heart!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 16:14 and 16:31, what did the Lord do for Lydia, and what were the jailer and his household told to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to respond to Paul’s message. The jailer was told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”
dailies.jordyn: What would a right-sized challenge look like this week, if the work of opening a heart belongs to the Lord, and our part is to pray and to speak the same simple word?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Pray by name for one person, asking the Lord to open that person’s heart. Then, if you can do it with a parent’s help, tell someone the same word the jailer heard: Believe in the Lord Jesus. The challenge is not to force a result. It is to ask, and to speak.
dailies.action: This week, pray by name for one person whose heart you want the Lord to open, and tell someone, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” Let a parent know you did it.
dailies.prayer: Father, you opened Lydia’s heart, and you saved a jailer and his household. Please open a heart this week, and help us speak the good news: Believe in the Lord Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart. The jailer was told to believe in the Lord Jesus, and they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house. Prayer and the spoken word belong together in this week’s challenge.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up name one person you can pray for this week, and say together: Lord, please open their heart.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 16:32, after they told the jailer to believe, what did they do next?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is speaking the word of the Lord a fitting next step after the short answer, Believe in the Lord Jesus?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The short answer is true and clear, and the household still needed the word of the Lord explained to them. We can say the simple sentence, and we can also take time to tell more of the good news, as they did that night.
dailies.passageText: 14 One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” 32 Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that he opens hearts, keeps people from harm, and saves those who believe in the Lord Jesus.
dailies.verse: The jailer was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands, then open them, and say: Thank you, God, for saving Lydia and the jailer!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 16:14, 28, and 34, what did God do for Lydia, what did Paul shout, and how did the jailer’s night end?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart. Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” The jailer was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.
dailies.jordyn: How can prayer this week thank God both for an opened heart and for a life kept from despair, without turning the jailer’s crisis into a dramatic story we linger on?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Thank God simply that he opened Lydia’s heart, that Paul could shout that they were all still there, and that the jailer and his household believed and were filled with joy. Then ask him to open hearts, to keep people who are afraid, and to give the joy of believing.
dailies.action: Pray together: thank God that he opened Lydia’s heart, that he used a midnight song, and that the jailer and his household believed in the Lord Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you opened Lydia’s heart, that Paul and Silas sang to you at midnight, and that the jailer heard, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” Thank you that he and his household believed in the Lord Jesus and were filled with joy. Open hearts, keep the afraid, and teach us to sing to you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week’s story gives us many reasons to pray. The Lord opens hearts. His people can sing in a hard place. A man in despair is told not to harm himself, because the prisoners are still there. A household believes and is filled with joy. Prayer can hold all of that, with care and with thanks.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up thank God out loud that the jailer and his household believed and were filled with joy.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 16:25, when did Paul and Silas pray and sing, and who was listening?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: About midnight they were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is a midnight song a fitting picture when we close this week in prayer?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They prayed and sang before the earthquake, not only after the joy at the table. Prayer belongs in the hard hours, and God can use it in ways we cannot plan, as he did with a jailer who came to believe.
dailies.passageText: 14 One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 28 But Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” 34 The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them; he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: God opened Lydia’s heart, he saved a jailer through a midnight song, and next the message will go to Athens.
dailies.verse: The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.
dailies.enoch: Place a hand over your heart, then sing a short line, and say: God opened Lydia’s heart, and a jailer believed!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 16:14 and 16:31–34, how did Lydia come to believe, and how did the jailer’s household come to believe?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to respond to Paul’s message, and she and her household were baptized. The jailer was told to believe in the Lord Jesus, they spoke the word of the Lord to his house, and he and his household were baptized and filled with joy because they had come to believe in God.
dailies.jordyn: This week God opened a heart by the river and saved a jailer at midnight. How does that get you ready for next week, when Paul will tell the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The same good news is about to be spoken in a new city, to people who do not already gather at a Jewish place of prayer. The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart, and who saved a jailer, is the God who made the world and raised Jesus. Next week we will hear Paul say that in Athens.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: God opened Lydia's heart, and he used a midnight song to save a jailer. Then thank God, and look ahead to Paul in Athens.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you opened Lydia’s heart, and that a jailer and his household believed in the Lord Jesus. Get our hearts ready to hear Paul tell the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that God opened Lydia’s heart, and that he used a midnight song to save a jailer. Lydia believed and welcomed the messengers. Paul and Silas were beaten and put in prison, and at midnight they prayed and sang. The jailer was kept from harm and asked how to be saved. He was told to believe in the Lord Jesus, and he and his household believed and were filled with joy. Next week Paul will tell the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week Paul will tell Athens about the God who made the world!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 16:31, what exact word were the jailer and his household given?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”
dailies.jordyn2: Why is God opened Lydia’s heart, and he used a midnight song to save a jailer a fitting last word before a week in Athens?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The message is already traveling from a riverside to a prison, and next it will be spoken in a city full of other gods. The way to be saved will not change: the Lord opens hearts, and people are told to believe in the Lord Jesus, who was raised.
dailies.passageText: 14 One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” 34 The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them; he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.
