readings.text: 22 Paul then stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said: “People of Athens! I see that in every way you are very religious. 23 For as I walked around and looked carefully at your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god. So you are ignorant of the very thing you worship—and this is what I am going to proclaim to you. 24 “The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. 25 And he is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.

26 From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands. 27 God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. 28 ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’

29 “Therefore since we are God’s offspring, we should not think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone—an image made by human design and skill. 30 In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. 31 For he has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

story: Last week God opened Lydia’s heart, and he used a midnight song to save a jailer. Then Paul came to Athens, a city full of objects of worship. He stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said that in every way the people of Athens were very religious. As he walked around and looked carefully at their objects of worship, he even found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god. So they were ignorant of the very thing they worshiped, and this was what he was going to proclaim to them. We say that simply. We do not make fun of the altar, and we do not act out the crowd.

The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. And he is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else. From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands. God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of their own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’

Therefore since we are God’s offspring, we should not think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone—an image made by human design and skill. In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. For he has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead. We tell the judgment day with care, not to frighten little ones. The proof Paul names is this: God raised Jesus.
Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. Next week we will meet Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth.
weeks.enochLine: God made the world, and Jesus was raised!
enochActivities: Activity: Made the world. Point around the room, or to the sky, and say: God made the world!
Activity: Life and breath. Place a hand on your chest, take a quiet breath, and say: God gives us life and breath!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 17:22–23, where did Paul stand up to speak, and what altar had he found?
In Acts 17:24–25, who is the God Paul proclaimed, and what does that God give?
In Acts 17:26–28, why did God make the nations, and what did Paul say about how close God is?
In Acts 17:29–31, what does God now command, and what proof has he given?
elijahAnswers: Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus. He said that in every way the people of Athens were very religious, and he had found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god. That was what he was going to proclaim to them (Acts 17:22–23).

The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. He is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else (Acts 17:24–25).

From one man he made all the nations, and he marked out their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands, so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of their own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’ (Acts 17:26–28).

We should not think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone. In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. He has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed, and he has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:29–31).
jordynQuestions: Paul finds an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god, and then he proclaims the God who made the world and everything in it (Acts 17:23–24). What does that show you about the difference between an unknown god and the Lord of heaven and earth?

God made all the nations from one man, and he did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us (Acts 17:26–27). What does that tell you about God’s heart for people, and about how we look for him?

God now commands all people everywhere to repent, and he has given proof by raising the man he has appointed from the dead (Acts 17:30–31). Next week we will meet Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth. What do both weeks show you about the same good news traveling to new places?
jordynAnswers: An unknown god is a blank the people of Athens could not fill. Paul does not leave them with a guess. He names the God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth, who does not live in temples built by human hands. The true God is not a local image. He is the Maker, and he can be proclaimed.

The nations are not an accident, and their times and lands are marked out so that people would seek God. He is not far. We do not have to invent a way to climb up to him. We reach out for the God who already gives life and breath, and who wants to be found.

The same God who made the world now commands repentance, and he has given proof by raising Jesus. That message is not only for Athens. Next week it will be spoken in Corinth, among friends who work and teach together. The good news keeps traveling, and the proof stays the same: Jesus was raised from the dead.
weeks.jordynApplication: Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus (Acts 17:22–31). This week, thank God that he is not far, and tell one person that the God who made the world has given proof by raising Jesus. Next week we will meet Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she thanked God that he is not far, or told someone that God made the world and raised Jesus. If it is fitting, thank God together that he gives life and breath, and that he has given proof by raising Jesus from the dead.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you are the God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth. Thank you that you give everyone life and breath, and that you are not far from any one of us. ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ Thank you that you have given proof by raising Jesus from the dead. Help us seek you, reach out for you, and tell others about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Paul stands in the Areopagus and begins to proclaim the God the people of Athens do not know.
dailies.verse: I even found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say: Paul told Athens about the one true God!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 17:22–23, what did Paul say about the people of Athens, and what altar had he found?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said that in every way they were very religious. He had found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god, and that was what he was going to proclaim to them.
dailies.jordyn: Paul looks carefully at their objects of worship and then proclaims the God they have not known (Acts 17:23). What is wise about starting there, without making fun of the altar?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He tells the truth about what he has seen, and he does not sneer. Then he uses even an unknown god as a door to name the real God. We can be careful and clear at the same time: we honor people, and we still tell them who God is.
dailies.action: Read Acts 17:22–23 out loud. Then thank God that he can be known, and that he is not an unknown god.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul stood up in Athens and began to proclaim you. Thank you that you are not unknown. Help us listen, and help us speak of you with care. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said that in every way the people of Athens were very religious. As he walked around, he even found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god. He would proclaim to them the very thing they worshiped without knowing. We tell this simply. We do not make fun of the altar.
dailies.enochActivity: Point toward a doorway and say: Paul stood up to tell them about God!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 17:22, where did Paul stand up and speak?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus.
dailies.jordyn2: Why does Paul say he is going to proclaim to them the very thing they worship in ignorance (Acts 17:23)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They have an altar to an unknown god, but God is not meant to stay unknown. Paul will name him and tell them who he is.
dailies.passageText: 22 Paul then stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said: “People of Athens! I see that in every way you are very religious. 23 For as I walked around and looked carefully at your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: to an unknown god. So you are ignorant of the very thing you worship—and this is what I am going to proclaim to you.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: The God who made the world is Lord of heaven and earth, and he himself gives life and breath.
dailies.verse: The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands.
dailies.enoch: Point around the room, or to the sky, and say: God made the world!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 17:24–25, where does the God who made the world not live, and what does he give?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He does not live in temples built by human hands. He is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
dailies.jordyn: The Maker is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything (Acts 17:25). How does that change the way you think about worship, and about who is giving and who is receiving?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God does not need our help to be God. We need him. Worship is not filling up an empty god with gifts. It is receiving life and breath from the Lord of heaven and earth, and then honoring him because he is the Maker.
dailies.action: Play God made it. Look around a room or out a window, name two things God made, and say: The God who made the world is Lord of heaven and earth! Do not pretend to smash an image or make fun of a temple.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you made the world and everything in it, and that you give everyone life and breath. You do not live in temples built by human hands, and you do not need us as if you were empty. Teach us to honor you as the Giver. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. He is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else. This is the God Paul is proclaiming: the Maker, not a local image in a temple.
dailies.enochActivity: Place a hand on your chest, take a quiet breath, and say: God gives us life and breath!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 17:25, what does God himself give everyone?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Life and breath and everything else.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it good news that God is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything (Acts 17:25)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: It means God is not a needy statue we have to keep going. He is already the Giver. We come to him empty, and he gives life and breath.
dailies.passageText: 24 “The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. 25 And he is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: God made all nations so that people would seek him, and he is not far from any one of us.
dailies.verse: God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us.
dailies.enoch: Stretch out your hands and say: God is not far!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 17:26–28, from whom did God make the nations, and what did some of their poets say?
dailies.elijahAnswer: From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth, and he marked out their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands. ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of their own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’
dailies.jordyn: God marked out times and lands so that people would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him (Acts 17:27). What does it mean that he is not far from any one of us?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We are not left to hunt for a distant god who will not be found. The Maker stays near. We live and move in him. So seeking him is not climbing a far mountain so much as reaching out for the God who already holds our life.
dailies.action: Read Acts 17:26–28 out loud. Then thank God that he is not far, and that in him we live and move and have our being.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that from one man you made all the nations, and that you are not far from any one of us. ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ Help us seek you and reach out for you today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: From one man God made all the nations, and he marked out their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands. He did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of their own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’
dailies.enochActivity: Take two small steps as if you were reaching out, and say: God wants us to seek him!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 17:27, how near is God?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He is not far from any one of us.
dailies.jordyn2: Why does Paul quote, ‘We are his offspring.’ after saying that in God we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: If we live in God and are his offspring, then God is not a distant statue. He is the living Maker who holds our life, and we should seek him as his children, not as people trying to keep an image alive.
dailies.passageText: 26 From one man he made all the nations, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands. 27 God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. 28 ‘For in him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: God’s offspring should not think he is like gold or silver or stone, and now he commands all people everywhere to repent.
dailies.verse: In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.
dailies.enoch: Hold up one finger and say: There is one God, and we should turn to him!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 17:29–30, why should we not think the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, and what does God now command?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Since we are God’s offspring, we should not think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone—an image made by human design and skill. In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.
dailies.jordyn: Paul has just said, ‘We are his offspring.’ Then he says we should not think the divine being is like gold or silver or stone (Acts 17:28–29). How does being God’s offspring change what we think God is like?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Offspring belong to a living Father, not to a metal image. If we live and move in God, he cannot be a statue we designed and made. Repentance means turning from that wrong picture, and from the life that fits it, to the living God.
dailies.action: Tell one person, with respect and without a joke about anyone’s shrine, that God is not like gold or silver or stone, and that he now commands people to repent, to turn to him.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that we are your offspring, and that you are not an image made by human design and skill. You now command all people everywhere to repent. Turn our hearts to you, and help us speak this with respect. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Therefore since we are God’s offspring, we should not think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone—an image made by human design and skill. In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent. We say this with dignity. We do not mock an image, and we do not treat repentance as a game.
dailies.enochActivity: Shake your head gently and then nod, and say: God is not a statue. We turn to him!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 17:30, what does God now command all people everywhere to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: To repent.
dailies.jordyn2: What does repent mean here, after Paul has talked about gold, silver, and stone (Acts 17:29–30)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: It means turning from a false picture of God, and from the life that goes with it, to the living God who made the world. God is not overlooking that ignorance now. He calls everyone to turn.
dailies.passageText: 29 “Therefore since we are God’s offspring, we should not think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone—an image made by human design and skill. 30 In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: God has set a day of just judgment, and he has given proof by raising the man he has appointed.
dailies.verse: He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands and say: God raised Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 17:31, what day has God set, and what proof has he given?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.
dailies.jordyn: God will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed, and the proof is that he raised him from the dead (Acts 17:31). Why is the resurrection the right proof for a coming just day?
dailies.jordynAnswer: A just day needs a living appointed man, not only a teaching. God has already raised Jesus, so the world has been given public proof. Judgment is real, and it is just, and it is not a rumor. The same raised Jesus is the proof and the appointed man.
dailies.action: Pray together, with a calm voice, thanking God that the day he has set is just, and that he has given proof by raising Jesus. Do not turn the judgment day into a scare or a skit.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you will judge the world with justice by the man you have appointed, and that you have given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead. Make us ready, and help us trust Jesus, the one you raised. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: God has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead. We tell this with care, especially with little children. The point is not to frighten them. The point is that God is just, and that Jesus was raised.
dailies.enochActivity: Hold both hands open like a gift and say: God has given proof. Jesus was raised!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 17:31, by whom will God judge the world, and how has he given proof?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: By the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.
dailies.jordyn2: How should a family speak about this set day with younger children (Acts 17:31)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: With calm honesty, not with scare tactics. God is just, and the proof he gives is good news: Jesus was raised from the dead. That is the man he has appointed, and that is why we can trust him.
dailies.passageText: 31 For he has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus, and next the message will be at work in Corinth.
dailies.verse: The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands.
dailies.enoch: Tell a grown-up the big idea: God made the world, and Jesus was raised!
dailies.elijah: From Acts 17:22–31, what did Paul tell the people of Athens about God, and what proof did he name at the end?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He told them about the God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth, who gives life and breath and is not far from any one of us. Now God commands all people everywhere to repent, and he has given proof by raising the man he has appointed from the dead.
dailies.jordyn: Why is Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus a fitting last word before a week with Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The message in Athens is already meant to travel. The one God who made the world and raised Jesus will be named in a new city, among friends who work and teach together. The Maker and the raised Jesus do not change from Athens to Corinth.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. Then thank God, and look ahead to Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. Get our hearts ready to meet Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. He stood in the Areopagus and began from an altar to an unknown god. He proclaimed the Maker, who gives life and breath and is not far. He called people to repent, and he named the proof: God has raised the man he appointed. Next week we will meet Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week we will meet friends in Corinth!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 17:31, what exact proof has God given to everyone?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.
dailies.jordyn2: What stays the same when the story moves from Athens to Corinth next week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The one God who made the world and raised Jesus. New friends and a new city will hear the same Maker, and the same proof, the resurrection of Jesus.
dailies.passageText: 24 “The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples built by human hands. 27 God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us. 31 For he has set a day when he will judge the world with justice by the man he has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

weeks.title: Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth
weeks.selectLabel: Week 36 · Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth
weeks.nextUp: Week 37 · God keeps Paul safe in the storm
weeks.bigIdea: Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 36 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Acts 18:1–4 out loud, then Acts 18:5–8, then Acts 18:9–11.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray

readings.text: 1 After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. 2 There he met a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to see them, 3 and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them. 4 Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.

5 When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah. 6 But when they opposed Paul and became abusive, he shook out his clothes in protest and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” 7 Then Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. 8 Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household believed in the Lord; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.

9 One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. 10 For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” 11 So Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.

story: Last week Paul told the people of Athens about the one God who made the world and raised Jesus. After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. There he met a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. We say that simply. Paul went to see them, and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them. Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.

When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah. But when they opposed Paul and became abusive, he shook out his clothes in protest and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” We tell the hard words simply. We do not act out the anger, and we do not make a game of the protest. Paul is saying he has told them the truth, and he will now take the good news to the Gentiles. Then Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household believed in the Lord; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.

One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” We hear the promise of safety with care, not as a fight to act out. So Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God. Friends in Christ worked and taught together so more people could hear about Jesus.
Next week we will hear how God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through a storm.
weeks.enochLine: Friends worked together, and God said: Keep on speaking! I am with you!
enochActivities: Activity: Work together. Sit or stand side by side with someone and say: Friends in Jesus can work together!
Activity: Keep speaking. Cup your hands like a megaphone and say: Keep on speaking! God is with you!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 18:1–3, whom did Paul meet in Corinth, and why did he stay and work with them?
In Acts 18:4–5, what did Paul do every Sabbath, and what did he devote himself to when Silas and Timothy came?
In Acts 18:6–8, what did Paul say when people opposed him, and what happened at the house next door?
In Acts 18:9–11, what did the Lord say to Paul in a vision, and how long did Paul stay in Corinth?
elijahAnswers: He met Aquila, a native of Pontus, and his wife Priscilla, who had come from Italy because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul was a tentmaker as they were, so he stayed and worked with them (Acts 18:1–3).

Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah (Acts 18:4–5).

He shook out his clothes in protest and said, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” He went next door to the house of Titius Justus. Crispus and his household believed in the Lord, and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized (Acts 18:6–8).

The Lord said, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” So Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God (Acts 18:9–11).
jordynQuestions: Paul is a tentmaker, as Priscilla and Aquila are, and he stays and works with them (Acts 18:3). What does that show you about how friends in Christ can help the good news travel?

When some oppose Paul, he says he will go to the Gentiles, and then Crispus and many Corinthians believe and are baptized (Acts 18:6–8). What does that tell you about the door closing in one place, and opening in another?

The Lord tells Paul, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” and Paul stays a year and a half, teaching the word of God (Acts 18:9–11). Next week God will keep Paul safe in a storm. What do both weeks show you about the Lord’s presence with his messengers?
jordynAnswers: The good news does not travel only from a pulpit. Friends share ordinary work, a house, and a trade, and that shared life becomes a place where the message can be spoken. Priscilla, Aquila, and Paul work together, and more people can hear about Jesus.

Opposition does not stop the message. Paul has told the truth, and he takes the same good news next door, to the Gentiles. Even a synagogue leader believes, and many in the city are baptized. A hard no in one room is not the end of the Lord’s work in that city.

The Lord is with Paul when he speaks in Corinth, and he tells him not to be afraid or silent. Next week that same faithful Lord will keep his promise in a storm. The messengers move, the settings change, and the Lord stays with them.
weeks.jordynApplication: Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus (Acts 18:1–11). This week, work with someone in your house to tell one person that Jesus is the Messiah, and remember the Lord’s words: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” Next week we will hear how God kept Paul safe in a storm.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she worked with someone to tell a person about Jesus, or remembered the Lord’s words not to be afraid or silent. If it is fitting, thank God together for friends who work and teach with us, and that the Lord is with his people when they speak.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you for Priscilla and Aquila, and for Paul, who stayed and worked with them. Thank you that many in Corinth believed and were baptized, and that you said, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” Help us work together as friends in Christ so more people can hear about Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Paul meets Priscilla and Aquila in Corinth, and because they share a trade, he stays and works with them.
dailies.verse: and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them.
dailies.enoch: Sit or stand side by side with someone and say: Friends in Jesus can work together!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 18:1–3, where did Paul go after Athens, and whom did he meet there?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He left Athens and went to Corinth. He met Aquila, a native of Pontus, and his wife Priscilla, who had come from Italy. Because Paul was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them.
dailies.jordyn: Priscilla and Aquila have had to leave Rome, and Paul stays and works with them as a tentmaker (Acts 18:2–3). What do you notice about how God uses ordinary work and a shared home?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The Lord does not wait for a perfect, easy setting. A hard move, a shared trade, and a welcome become the start of gospel work in a new city. Friends in Christ can work with their hands and still make a way for people to hear about Jesus.
dailies.action: Read Acts 18:1–3 out loud. Then thank God for friends who work with us, and for a place to stay and speak.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul met Priscilla and Aquila, and that he stayed and worked with them. Teach us to work as friends in Christ so more people can hear about Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. There he met Aquila and his wife Priscilla, who had come from Italy because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. We say that simply. Paul went to see them, and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them.
dailies.enochActivity: Pretend to smooth a piece of cloth or a towel, as if you were helping with tent work, and say: Paul worked with his friends!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 18:3, why did Paul stay and work with Priscilla and Aquila?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Because he was a tentmaker as they were.
dailies.jordyn2: How is a shared trade a kind of friendship in this story (Acts 18:3)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They do the same work, so Paul can stay with them. The friendship is not only talk. It is a shared table and a shared task, and that becomes a base for the message in Corinth.
dailies.passageText: 1 After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. 2 There he met a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to see them, 3 and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Paul works with his friends, and every Sabbath he reasons in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
dailies.verse: Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
dailies.enoch: Cup your hands like a megaphone and say: Jesus is the Messiah!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 18:3–4, what two things is Paul doing in Corinth, one through the week and one on the Sabbath?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He stays and works with Priscilla and Aquila as a tentmaker, and every Sabbath he reasons in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
dailies.jordyn: Paul works with his hands and also reasons in the synagogue (Acts 18:3–4). Why might both matters for a church taking root in a new city?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The message needs a life behind it, and the work needs a message in it. Friends who labor together also open a door for Jews and Greeks to hear. The church in Corinth begins in ordinary days and in Sabbath conversations.
dailies.action: Play Work and speak. Pair up. One person pretends to help with simple work (fold a towel or straighten a chair). The other says: Jesus is the Messiah! Then switch. Do not act out an argument in the synagogue.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul worked with his friends and also reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks. Help our work and our words go together, so more people can hear about Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul was a tentmaker as Priscilla and Aquila were, so he stayed and worked with them. Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks. Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up fold a towel or straighten a chair, then say: We can work and tell about Jesus!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 18:4, whom was Paul trying to persuade?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Jews and Greeks.
dailies.jordyn2: What does it mean that Paul reasoned in the synagogue (Acts 18:4)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: He did not only announce a line and leave. He talked with people, Jews and Greeks, and tried to persuade them. The good news is something to be explained, as well as proclaimed.
dailies.passageText: 3 and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them. 4 Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Paul testifies that Jesus is the Messiah. When some oppose him, he goes to the Gentiles, and many in Corinth believe.
dailies.verse: Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household believed in the Lord; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.
dailies.enoch: Hold up one finger and say: Jesus is the Messiah!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 18:5–8, what did Paul testify, what did he say when people opposed him, and who believed?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He testified to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah. When they opposed him and became abusive, he said, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” He went next door to the house of Titius Justus. Crispus and his household believed, and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.
dailies.jordyn: Paul’s hard sentence, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” is not a taunt to copy (Acts 18:6). What is he saying about his work, and about where the message goes next?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He is saying he has told them the truth, and he is not guilty of hiding it. The same good news will now be spoken to the Gentiles, next door. The opposition is real, but it does not own the story. Crispus believes, and many in the city are baptized.
dailies.action: Read Acts 18:5–8 out loud. Tell the hard words simply. Do not act out the protest or the abuse. Then thank God that many in Corinth believed.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul testified that Jesus was the Messiah, and that when some opposed him, the good news still went next door. Thank you that Crispus and many Corinthians believed and were baptized. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: When Silas and Timothy came, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching, testifying that Jesus was the Messiah. Some opposed him and became abusive. We say that simply, and we do not act it out. Paul said, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” He went next door to Titius Justus. Crispus and his household believed, and many Corinthians believed and were baptized.
dailies.enochActivity: Take one step to the side, as if going next door, and say: The good news kept going!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 18:8, who believed in the Lord, besides many of the Corinthians?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it striking that Crispus, the synagogue leader, believes after Paul has left the synagogue (Acts 18:7–8)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The door Paul left is not empty of faith. The leader of that synagogue and his household believe in the Lord, and many in the city are baptized. God is still at work in the place of opposition, and also in the house next door.
dailies.passageText: 5 When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah. 6 But when they opposed Paul and became abusive, he shook out his clothes in protest and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” 7 Then Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. 8 Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household believed in the Lord; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: The Lord tells Paul not to be afraid and not to be silent, because he is with him and has many people in the city.
dailies.verse: Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent.
dailies.enoch: Cup your hands and say: Keep on speaking! God is with you!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 18:9–10, what did the Lord say to Paul in a vision?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.”
dailies.jordyn: The Lord says, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” (Acts 18:9–10). How do the call to keep speaking, and the promise that the Lord is with him and already has people in the city, belong together?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Paul is not told to be brave in an empty town. The Lord is with him, and the Lord already has people in Corinth. So the call to keep speaking is not a lonely dare. It is work inside a city where God already has a people, even if Paul cannot yet see them all.
dailies.action: Tell one person, with a calm voice, a short line from the vision: the Lord said, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” Do not turn the promise about harm into a scare or a skit.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you spoke to Paul, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” Be with us, and help us keep speaking about Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” We hear the words about attack and harm with care. The point is the Lord’s presence and his people, not a scene to act out.
dailies.enochActivity: Place a hand on your chest and say: God is with you. Keep on speaking!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 18:10, why does the Lord say no one is going to attack and harm Paul?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Because the Lord is with him, and because he has many people in this city.
dailies.jordyn2: The verse in today’s bite stops, in our words, at do not be silent. Why must we also hear the next sentence (Acts 18:9–10)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The official word is one speech. The Lord does not only say keep speaking. He also says he is with Paul, and that no one is going to attack and harm him, because he has many people in this city. The courage has a reason: the Lord is with him.
dailies.passageText: 9 One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. 10 For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.”

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Paul stays in Corinth a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.
dailies.verse: So Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands like a book and say: Paul taught them the word of God!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 18:11, how long did Paul stay in Corinth, and what did he do there?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He stayed for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.
dailies.jordyn: After the vision, Paul stays a year and a half, teaching them the word of God (Acts 18:9–11). What does that long stay show you about the call to keep on speaking?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The Lord’s word is not a short burst of courage and then a quick exit. Paul remains. He teaches the word of God over many months, in a city where the Lord has many people. Keeping on speaking can look like staying, and teaching, for a long time.
dailies.action: Pray together, thanking God that Paul stayed and taught the word of God, and asking the Lord to keep your family speaking about Jesus, even in ordinary weeks.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God. You were with him, and you had many people in that city. Help us keep speaking, and help us stay with the work you give us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Lord told Paul not to be afraid and not to be silent, because he was with him and had many people in the city. So Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God. Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus.
dailies.enochActivity: Hold both hands open and count quietly to three, then say: Paul stayed, and he taught God’s word!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 18:11, what did Paul teach them?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The word of God.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is a year and a half a fitting answer to a night vision (Acts 18:9–11)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The vision is not only comfort for one frightened night. It is a reason to remain. Paul keeps speaking by staying and teaching the word of God until a church can take root in Corinth.
dailies.passageText: 9 One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. 10 For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” 11 So Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, teaching them the word of God.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus, and next we will see the Lord keep Paul through a storm.
dailies.verse: and because he was a tentmaker as they were, he stayed and worked with them.
dailies.enoch: Tell a grown-up the big idea: Friends in Jesus work and teach together!
dailies.elijah: From Acts 18:1–11, whom did Paul work with, what did the Lord tell him, and how long did he stay?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He worked with Priscilla and Aquila as a tentmaker. The Lord told him, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” He stayed a year and a half, teaching them the word of God. Many in Corinth believed and were baptized.
dailies.jordyn: Why is Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus a fitting last word before a week when God keeps Paul safe in a storm?
dailies.jordynAnswer: This week the church takes root in Corinth through shared work, shared teaching, and the Lord’s promise to be with Paul. Next week that same Lord will keep his promise in a storm. The friends and the city matter, and so does the God who stays with his messenger when the road gets rough.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus. Then thank God, and look ahead to the week when God keeps Paul safe in the storm.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for Priscilla, Aquila, and the church in Corinth, and that you told Paul to keep on speaking because you were with him. Get our hearts ready to hear how you kept Paul safe in the storm. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that friends in Christ work and teach together so more people can hear about Jesus. Paul stayed and worked with Priscilla and Aquila. He testified that Jesus was the Messiah. Many in Corinth believed. The Lord said, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” and Paul stayed a year and a half, teaching the word of God. Next week God will keep Paul safe in a storm.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week God keeps Paul safe in the storm!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 18:9–10, what exact words did the Lord say to Paul in the vision?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.”
dailies.jordyn2: What stays the same when the story moves from a workshop in Corinth to a storm at sea next week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The Lord who told Paul, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking, do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one is going to attack and harm you, because I have many people in this city.” is the same Lord who keeps his promises. Friends help the message take root, and God himself keeps his messenger.
