readings.text: 13 When a gentle south wind began to blow, they saw their opportunity; so they weighed anchor and sailed along the shore of Crete. 14 Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island. 15 The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind; so we gave way to it and were driven along. 16 As we passed to the lee of a small island called Cauda, we were hardly able to make the lifeboat secure, 17 so the men hoisted it aboard. Then they passed ropes under the ship itself to hold it together. Because they were afraid they would run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and let the ship be driven along. 18 We took such a violent battering from the storm that the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard. 19 On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. 20 When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved.

21 After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up before them and said: “Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete; then you would have spared yourselves this damage and loss. 22 But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. 23 Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me 24 and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ 25 So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me. 26 Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island.”

39 When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could. 40 Cutting loose the anchors, they left them in the sea and at the same time untied the ropes that held the rudders. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach. 41 But the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was broken to pieces by the pounding of the surf. 42 The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping. 43 But the centurion wanted to spare Paul’s life and kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. 44 The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.

story: Last week Paul stayed in Corinth with Priscilla and Aquila, and the Lord told him to keep on speaking because he was with him. Later Paul is on a ship, being taken toward Rome. When a gentle south wind began to blow, they saw their opportunity; so they weighed anchor and sailed along the shore of Crete. Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island. The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind; so they gave way to it and were driven along. They passed ropes under the ship to hold it together, and they began to throw the cargo overboard. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, they finally gave up all hope of being saved. We tell the storm simply. We do not act it out, and we do not make a game of being afraid.

After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up before them and said, “Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete; then you would have spared yourselves this damage and loss. But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me. Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island.” We hear the angel’s words with care: ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Paul has faith in God that it will happen just as he was told. God has given him the lives of all who sail with him.

After more days at sea, they came near land. When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could. They made for the beach, but the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast, and the stern was broken to pieces by the pounding of the surf. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping. We say this simply, with care. We do not act it out, and we do not make a game of it. But the centurion wanted to spare Paul’s life and kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely. God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm.
Next week we will hear how Paul reached Rome, and the good news kept going.
weeks.enochLine: God kept his promise! Everyone reached land safely!
enochActivities: Activity: Keep up your courage. Hold a grown-up’s hand and say: Keep up your courage! God keeps his promise!
Activity: Safe on land. Step from a rug onto the floor, as if stepping onto the beach, and say: Everyone reached land safely!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 27:13–20, what happened after the gentle south wind, and how did the people on the ship feel after many days?
In Acts 27:21–26, what did Paul urge the men to do, and what did the angel say to him?
In Acts 27:39–41, what did they try to do when daylight came, and what happened to the ship?
In Acts 27:42–44, what did the centurion do, and how did everyone reach land?
elijahAnswers: Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island. The ship was caught by the storm and driven along. They threw cargo and tackle overboard. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, they finally gave up all hope of being saved (Acts 27:13–20).

Paul urged them to keep up their courage, because not one of them would be lost; only the ship would be destroyed. An angel of the God to whom Paul belongs and whom he serves stood beside him and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Paul had faith in God that it would happen just as he was told, and they must run aground on some island (Acts 27:21–26).

They saw a bay with a sandy beach and decided to run the ship aground if they could. They made for the beach, but the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was broken to pieces by the pounding of the surf (Acts 27:39–41).

The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, but we say that simply and do not act it out. The centurion wanted to spare Paul’s life and kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. The rest got there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely (Acts 27:42–44).
jordynQuestions: The people on the ship give up all hope of being saved (Acts 27:20), and then Paul says they should keep up their courage, because not one of them will be lost (Acts 27:22). What does that show you about hope that comes from God’s promise, not from the weather?

The angel says, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ (Acts 27:24). How does that promise hold together Paul’s own journey and the lives of the others on the ship?

The ship is destroyed, and still everyone reaches land safely (Acts 27:41–44). Next week Paul will be in Rome, and the good news will keep going. What do you learn about the kind of safety God promised here?
jordynAnswers: The storm can take away every sign they trust: sun, stars, and hope of being saved. Paul does not pretend the storm is small. He points them to what God has said. Courage here is not a feeling they work up. It is trust that God’s word will stand when the sea will not.

Paul must stand trial before Caesar, so the Lord is still taking him toward Rome. And God has graciously given him the lives of all who sail with him. The promise is not only for the messenger. It is wide enough for the whole ship, even people who did not yet trust Paul’s God.

God did not promise that the ship would stay together. He promised that the people would not be lost. The ship runs aground, the stern breaks, and still everyone reaches land safely. Safety here is God’s kept word, not an easy trip. That same faithful God will take the good news on to Rome.
weeks.jordynApplication: God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm (Acts 27:13–26, 39–44). This week, when something feels too big, remember the angel’s words, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ and say out loud: Keep up your courage. God keeps his promise. Next week we will hear how Paul reached Rome, and the good news kept going.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she remembered to keep up her courage because God keeps his promises, or told someone that everyone on the ship reached land safely. If it is fitting, thank God together that he kept his word to Paul, and that his promises still hold.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that when the storm was strong and hope was gone, you sent your word to Paul. Thank you for the angel’s words, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Thank you that everyone reached land safely. Help us keep up our courage, because you keep your promises. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: A gentle wind turns into a storm, and after many days the people on the ship give up all hope of being saved.
dailies.verse: When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved.
dailies.enoch: Hold a grown-up’s hand and say: The storm was strong, but God still had a promise!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 27:13–15, what happened after the gentle south wind began to blow?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They weighed anchor and sailed along the shore of Crete. Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island. The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind, so they gave way to it and were driven along.
dailies.jordyn: In Acts 27:18–20, what do the people throw overboard, and what happens to their hope?
dailies.jordynAnswer: They take such a violent battering that they throw the cargo overboard, and on the third day they throw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. When neither sun nor stars appear for many days and the storm continues raging, they finally give up all hope of being saved.
dailies.action: Read Acts 27:13–20 out loud. Then thank God that this story does not end with lost hope, because he still has a promise for Paul.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that even when the storm was strong and hope was gone, you still had a promise for Paul. Help us trust you when we cannot see a way through. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: When a gentle south wind began to blow, they sailed along the shore of Crete. Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island. The ship was caught by the storm and driven along. They threw cargo and tackle overboard. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, they finally gave up all hope of being saved. We tell the storm simply. We do not act it out, and we do not make a game of being afraid.
dailies.enochActivity: Look out a window, then come back and hold a grown-up’s hand and say: We cannot always see the way, but God still keeps his promise!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 27:20, why did they finally give up all hope of being saved?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Because neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging.
dailies.jordyn2: The storm takes away the signs sailors use to find their way (Acts 27:20). What does that help you notice before Paul speaks God’s promise?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They are not only wet and tired. They have lost the ordinary helps they trust: sun, stars, and hope of being saved. The next word will have to come from God, not from the sky.
dailies.passageText: 13 When a gentle south wind began to blow, they saw their opportunity; so they weighed anchor and sailed along the shore of Crete. 14 Before very long, a wind of hurricane force, called the Northeaster, swept down from the island. 15 The ship was caught by the storm and could not head into the wind; so we gave way to it and were driven along. 16 As we passed to the lee of a small island called Cauda, we were hardly able to make the lifeboat secure, 17 so the men hoisted it aboard. Then they passed ropes under the ship itself to hold it together. Because they were afraid they would run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and let the ship be driven along. 18 We took such a violent battering from the storm that the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard. 19 On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. 20 When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Paul urges the men to keep up their courage, because God has promised that not one of them will be lost.
dailies.verse: But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed.
dailies.enoch: Hold a grown-up’s hand and say: Keep up your courage! God keeps his promise!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 27:21–22, what does Paul urge the men to do, and what does he say will happen to the people and to the ship?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He urges them to keep up their courage, because not one of them will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed.
dailies.jordyn: Paul says not one of them will be lost, and only the ship will be destroyed (Acts 27:22). Why is it important that the promise is about the people, not about the boat staying together?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God can keep a promise even when the thing they are standing on does not last. The storm may break the ship, and still the people are not lost. Courage here is trust in God’s word, not trust in the ship.
dailies.action: Play Keep up your courage. Hold a grown-up’s hand, or hold a rolled towel like a shared rope, and say: Keep up your courage! God keeps his promise! Then switch. Do not act out the storm, the ship breaking, or anyone sinking.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul urged the men to keep up their courage, because not one of them would be lost. Teach us to trust your promise more than what we can see. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up and told them they should have taken his advice not to sail from Crete. But now he urges them to keep up their courage, because not one of them will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. We do not typographically close Paul’s words early. We hear the first part of his speech and wait for the rest of God’s promise.
dailies.enochActivity: Hold both of a grown-up’s hands and say, slowly: Keep up your courage!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 27:22, what two things does Paul say about the people and the ship?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Not one of them will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed.
dailies.jordyn2: Why might it have been hard to believe Paul’s words in Acts 27:22 after so many days of storm?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: They have already given up all hope of being saved. The sea still looks stronger than the promise. Paul is asking them to trust God’s word before they can see land.
dailies.passageText: 21 After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up before them and said: “Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete; then you would have spared yourselves this damage and loss. 22 But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: An angel of God tells Paul not to be afraid, and Paul says he has faith that it will happen just as God told him.
dailies.verse: ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’
dailies.enoch: Place a hand over your heart and say: Do not be afraid, Paul. God keeps his promise!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 27:23–24, who stood beside Paul, and what did he say?
dailies.elijahAnswer: An angel of the God to whom Paul belongs and whom he serves stood beside him and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’
dailies.jordyn: In Acts 27:25–26, why does Paul tell the men to keep up their courage, and what does he say must still happen?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He has faith in God that it will happen just as he told him. Nevertheless, they must run aground on some island.
dailies.action: Read Acts 27:21–26 out loud. Then thank God that he spoke to Paul in the storm, and that Paul believed it would happen just as God said.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for the angel’s words, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Help us keep up our courage, because we have faith in you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul stood up and said, “Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete; then you would have spared yourselves this damage and loss. But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me. Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island.” The angel’s words are God’s care for Paul and for everyone sailing with him. Paul has faith in God that it will happen just as he was told, even though they must run aground on some island.
dailies.enochActivity: Stand still, then take one brave step forward and say: I have faith in God!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 27:25, what reason does Paul give for keeping up courage?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He has faith in God that it will happen just as he told him.
dailies.jordyn2: The angel says Paul must stand trial before Caesar, and God has graciously given him the lives of all who sail with him (Acts 27:24). What two promises are held together here?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God is still taking Paul where he said he would go, and he is also keeping the other people on the ship. The promise is personal to Paul, and it is wide enough for everyone sailing with him.
dailies.passageText: 21 After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up before them and said: “Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete; then you would have spared yourselves this damage and loss. 22 But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. 23 Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me 24 and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ 25 So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me. 26 Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island.”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: The ship runs aground, and everyone reaches land safely, just as God had said.
dailies.verse: The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.enoch: Step from a rug onto the floor and say: Everyone reached land safely!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 27:39–41, what did they see when daylight came, and what happened when they made for the beach?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They did not recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach and decided to run the ship aground if they could. They made for the beach, but the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast, and the stern was broken to pieces by the pounding of the surf.
dailies.jordyn: In Acts 27:42–44, what hard plan do we tell simply, what did the centurion do, and how did everyone reach land?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping. We say this simply, with care, and we do not act it out. The centurion wanted to spare Paul’s life and kept them from carrying out their plan. Those who could swim jumped overboard first, and the rest got there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.action: Today’s challenge: Tell someone, In this way everyone reached land safely. Then thank God that he kept his promise, even after the ship broke. Do not act out the wreck, the swimming, or the soldiers’ plan.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the ship ran aground and still everyone reached land safely. Thank you for keeping your promise to Paul. Help us tell this part of the story with care and with thanks. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After more days at sea, they came near land. When daylight came, they saw a bay with a sandy beach and tried to run the ship aground. The ship struck a sandbar. The bow stuck fast, and the stern was broken to pieces. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners. We say this simply, with care. We do not act it out, and we do not make a game of it. The centurion wanted to spare Paul’s life and kept them from carrying out their plan. Those who could swim jumped first, and the rest got there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.enochActivity: Step from a rug onto the floor, as if stepping onto a beach, and say: God kept his promise!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 27:43–44, why did the centurion stop the soldiers’ plan, and how did everyone get to land?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He wanted to spare Paul’s life. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land, and the rest got there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.jordyn2: The ship is destroyed, and still everyone reaches land safely (Acts 27:41–44). How does that match what Paul had already said in Acts 27:22?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Paul had said not one of them would be lost; only the ship would be destroyed. That is exactly what happens. God’s promise did not fail when the stern broke. It was kept, down to the last person on board.
dailies.passageText: 39 When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could. 40 Cutting loose the anchors, they left them in the sea and at the same time untied the ropes that held the rudders. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach. 41 But the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was broken to pieces by the pounding of the surf. 42 The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent any of them from swimming away and escaping. 43 But the centurion wanted to spare Paul’s life and kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. 44 The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: We thank God that he kept his promise and brought everyone to land safely.
dailies.verse: So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God, for keeping your promise!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 27:24–25, what did the angel promise, and how did Paul answer that promise in prayer-like faith?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The angel said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Paul told the men to keep up their courage, for he had faith in God that it would happen just as he told him.
dailies.jordyn: Paul has faith in God that it will happen just as he was told (Acts 27:25). How can that shape the way your family prays when a hard day is not over yet?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Prayer can tell the truth about the storm and still hold onto what God has said. Paul does not wait until they are already on the beach to trust God. He prays and speaks courage while they still have to run aground.
dailies.action: Pray today’s prayer out loud as a family. Then each person can thank God for one way he has kept a promise.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for the angel’s words, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Thank you that Paul had faith in you, and that everyone reached land safely. Help us keep up our courage and trust that you keep your word. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: An angel of the God to whom Paul belongs stood beside him and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ Paul had faith in God that it would happen just as he was told. They had to run aground on some island, and later everyone reached land safely. Today we thank God that he kept his promise.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands, then open them like a thank-you, and say: Thank you, God! You kept your promise!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 27:44, what short sentence tells you that God kept the promise Paul believed in Acts 27:25?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: In this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it good to pray about a promise after God has already kept it, not only while you are waiting (Acts 27:25, 44)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Waiting prayer trusts God before you see the end. Thankful prayer remembers that he really did what he said. Both kinds of prayer teach our hearts that God’s word stands.
dailies.passageText: 23 Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me 24 and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ 25 So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me. 26 Nevertheless, we must run aground on some island.” 44 The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm, and next the good news will keep going in Rome.
dailies.verse: In this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week Paul is in Rome, and the good news keeps going!
dailies.elijah: What is this week’s big idea, and what happened at the end of the storm?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm. The ship ran aground, and in this way everyone reached land safely.
dailies.jordyn: Paul heard, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ and later everyone reached land safely (Acts 27:24, 44). Next week Paul will be in Rome, and the good news will keep going. What stays the same from the storm to the next city?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God’s promise does not end on the beach. He said Paul must stand trial before Caesar, and he also kept the people on the ship. The same faithful God who brought them safely through the storm will keep the good news moving toward Rome.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm. Then thank God, and look ahead to Paul in Rome, where the good news keeps going.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you kept your promise and brought Paul safely through the storm, and that everyone reached land safely. Get our hearts ready to hear how the good news keeps going in Rome. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm. The people on the ship gave up all hope of being saved. Paul urged them to keep up their courage, because not one of them would be lost. The angel said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ The ship ran aground, and in this way everyone reached land safely. Next week Paul will be in Rome, and the good news will keep going.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week the good news keeps going!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 27:22 and 27:44, how can you tell that God did what he said?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Paul said not one of them would be lost, and only the ship would be destroyed. At the end, the ship has broken, and everyone reached land safely.
dailies.jordyn2: What stays the same when the story moves from a storm at sea to Paul in Rome next week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The God who kept his promise in the storm is the same God who is taking Paul where he said he would go. The ship does not last, and the good news still does.
dailies.passageText: 20 When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved. 22 But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. 24 and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.’ 44 The rest were to get there on planks or on other pieces of the ship. In this way everyone reached land safely.

readings.text: 11 After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered in the island—it was an Alexandrian ship with the figurehead of the twin gods Castor and Pollux. 12 We put in at Syracuse and stayed there three days. 13 From there we set sail and arrived at Rhegium. The next day the south wind came up, and on the following day we reached Puteoli. 14 There we found some brothers and sisters who invited us to spend a week with them. And so we came to Rome.

15 The brothers and sisters there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged. 16 When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

30 For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. 31 He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!

story: Last week God kept his promise and brought Paul safely through the storm, and everyone reached land safely. After some time they sailed on again. After three months they put out to sea in a ship that had wintered in the island—it was an Alexandrian ship with the figurehead of the twin gods Castor and Pollux. We say the figurehead simply. It is the carving on the ship, and we do not make a game of those names. They put in at Syracuse and stayed there three days. From there they set sail and arrived at Rhegium. The next day the south wind came up, and on the following day they reached Puteoli. There they found some brothers and sisters who invited them to spend a week with them. And so they came to Rome.

The brothers and sisters there had heard that they were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged. When they got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. We say the guard simply, with care. We do not act out being under guard, and we do not make a game of it. After he arrived, Paul spoke with the Jewish leaders about Jesus. Some believed, and some did not. We tell that meeting only as a short bridge. Then the story shows us how the good news kept going.

For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance! Even in Rome, with a soldier nearby, Paul kept telling people about Jesus. The good news was not shut up in that house. It kept going.
Next week we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, and more good fruit the Holy Spirit grows in us.
weeks.enochLine: Even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus!
enochActivities: Activity: Welcome. Pretend to open a door and say: Welcome! Come and hear about Jesus!
Activity: The good news keeps going. Take three steps across the room and say: The good news keeps going!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 28:11–14, how did Paul and his friends travel after three months, and whom did they find at Puteoli?
In Acts 28:15–16, who came out to meet Paul, and what was his life like when he got to Rome?
In Acts 28:30–31, how long did Paul stay in his rented house, and what did he do there?
What is this week’s big idea, and how do Acts 28:16 and 28:31 fit together?
elijahAnswers: After three months they put out to sea in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island. They put in at Syracuse, then sailed to Rhegium, and reached Puteoli. There they found some brothers and sisters who invited them to spend a week with them. And so they came to Rome (Acts 28:11–14).

The brothers and sisters in Rome had heard they were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged. When they got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him (Acts 28:15–16).

For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:30–31).

Even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus. He lived in a house with a soldier to guard him, and still, for two whole years, he welcomed people and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:16, 30–31).
jordynQuestions: Friends travel out as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet Paul, and at the sight of them he thanked God and was encouraged (Acts 28:15). What does that show you about how the good news travels, and how God uses people to strengthen his messengers?

Paul is allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him (Acts 28:16), and yet for two whole years he welcomes all who come and teaches about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:30–31). What do you notice about a guarded house and an unhindered message?

The book of Acts ends with the good news still going in Rome, not with Paul being finished (Acts 28:30–31). Next week we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit. What does an unhindered message in Rome help you expect about the life God grows in his people?
jordynAnswers: The message is already ahead of Paul. Brothers and sisters hear that he is coming, and they walk a long way to meet him. God does not only keep Paul safe on the sea. He also encourages him with the faces of his people. The good news makes a family, and that family can put courage back into a tired servant.

The soldier is real, and we say that simply. Paul is not free to go wherever he wants. But the word is not chained. In a rented house he can welcome people, proclaim the kingdom of God, and teach about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness. A guard at the door does not have to mean a closed gospel.

Acts does not close the story as if the work were over. For two whole years the message keeps being spoken. Next week the fruit of the Spirit will show what the Spirit grows in people who belong to Jesus. The same Lord who kept the word going in Rome is the Lord who grows love, joy, and peace in his people.
weeks.jordynApplication: Even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus (Acts 28:11–16, 30–31). This week, welcome one person with kind words, or tell someone that Paul taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. Next week we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she welcomed someone, or remembered that the good news kept going even when Paul was under guard. If it is fitting, thank God together that Jesus is still being taught with boldness, and that his people can still encourage one another.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you brought Paul to Rome, and that brothers and sisters met him and encouraged him. Thank you that for two whole years he welcomed all who came, and proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance. Help us keep telling people about Jesus, even when the way is not easy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: After three months they sail on, find brothers and sisters at Puteoli, and come to Rome.
dailies.verse: There we found some brothers and sisters who invited us to spend a week with them. And so we came to Rome.
dailies.enoch: Take three small steps and say: And so we came to Rome!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 28:11–13, what kind of ship did they sail on, and which places did they reach before Puteoli?
dailies.elijahAnswer: It was an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island, with the figurehead of the twin gods Castor and Pollux. We say that simply. They put in at Syracuse, set sail and arrived at Rhegium, and then the south wind came up and they reached Puteoli.
dailies.jordyn: In Acts 28:14, whom did they find at Puteoli, and where did the journey finally bring them?
dailies.jordynAnswer: They found some brothers and sisters who invited them to spend a week with them. And so they came to Rome.
dailies.action: Read Acts 28:11–14 out loud. Then thank God that he brought Paul all the way to Rome, and that brothers and sisters were already there to welcome him.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that after three months they sailed on, found brothers and sisters at Puteoli, and came to Rome. Thank you for friends in Jesus who welcome us on the way. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After three months they put out to sea in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island, with the figurehead of the twin gods Castor and Pollux. We say the figurehead simply, and we do not make a game of those names. They stayed three days at Syracuse, reached Rhegium, and then Puteoli. There they found some brothers and sisters who invited them to spend a week with them. And so they came to Rome.
dailies.enochActivity: Point down an imaginary road and say: This way to Rome! God is still taking Paul there!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 28:14, what did the brothers and sisters at Puteoli do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They invited them to spend a week with them. And so they came to Rome.
dailies.jordyn2: The journey has many stops, and then the text says, And so we came to Rome (Acts 28:11–14). Why might those last words matter after last week’s storm?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God had said Paul must stand trial before Caesar, and last week he kept the people on the ship safe. Now the story names Rome itself. The promise is not only that they would live through the storm. It is that Paul would arrive.
dailies.passageText: 11 After three months we put out to sea in a ship that had wintered in the island—it was an Alexandrian ship with the figurehead of the twin gods Castor and Pollux. 12 We put in at Syracuse and stayed there three days. 13 From there we set sail and arrived at Rhegium. The next day the south wind came up, and on the following day we reached Puteoli. 14 There we found some brothers and sisters who invited us to spend a week with them. And so we came to Rome.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Friends travel a long way to meet Paul, and at the sight of them he thanks God and is encouraged.
dailies.verse: At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged.
dailies.enoch: Wave as if you see a friend coming and say: Paul thanked God and was encouraged!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 28:15, how far did the brothers and sisters travel, and what did Paul do when he saw them?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged.
dailies.jordyn: Paul has already been through a storm, and now the sight of brothers and sisters encourages him (Acts 28:15). What does that tell you about the kind of help God often uses?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God can encourage his people through other people. The friends walk out to meet Paul, and their coming makes him thank God. The good news makes a family, and that family can give a tired servant new courage.
dailies.action: Play Come to meet him. One person stands a few steps away. The others walk toward that person, as if meeting a friend on the road, and all say: Thank you, God! Then switch. Do not act out a crowded rush, and do not turn the meeting into a chase.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that brothers and sisters traveled out to meet Paul, and that at the sight of them he thanked you and was encouraged. Make us the kind of friends who put courage into one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The brothers and sisters in Rome had heard that they were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged. Friends in Jesus can walk toward someone and help that person’s heart be strong again.
dailies.enochActivity: Walk a few steps toward a grown-up, wave, and say: I thank God for you!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 28:15, what two things did Paul do when he saw the brothers and sisters?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He thanked God and was encouraged.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it fitting that Paul thanks God, and not only the friends, when they meet him (Acts 28:15)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The friends really did walk out to meet him, and God is the one who gave him that gift. Thanks to God keeps the encouragement in the right place: the Lord used his people.
dailies.passageText: 15 The brothers and sisters there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: When they get to Rome, Paul is allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.
dailies.verse: When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.
dailies.enoch: Sit in a chair and say: Paul lived in a house in Rome, and he still told people about Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 28:16, what was Paul allowed to do in Rome, and who was with him?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.
dailies.jordyn: Paul lives by himself, yet a soldier guards him (Acts 28:16). How should we talk about that part of the story with care?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We say it simply. Paul is under guard, and we do not act that out or make a game of catching him. The next verses will show that even in that house the good news can still be spoken.
dailies.action: Read Acts 28:15–16 out loud. Then thank God that Paul reached Rome, and ask the Lord to help you tell this part of the story with care.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul reached Rome and was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. Help us tell this simply, and to trust that you can still use him there. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Friends met Paul on the way, and he thanked God and was encouraged. When they got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. We say the guard simply, with care. We do not act out being under guard, and we do not make a game of it.
dailies.enochActivity: Sit down beside a grown-up and say: Paul was in a house in Rome, and God was still with him!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 28:16, did Paul go into a prison cell, or was he allowed to live by himself?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.
dailies.jordyn2: Why might it matter that the text says he was allowed to live by himself, and also that a soldier guarded him (Acts 28:16)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Both are true at once. He has a house, and he is not wholly free. Tomorrow we will hear what he does in that house for two whole years. The guard does not get the last word.
dailies.passageText: 15 The brothers and sisters there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged. 16 When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: For two whole years Paul stays in his rented house and welcomes all who come to see him.
dailies.verse: For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him.
dailies.enoch: Pretend to open a door and say: Welcome! Come and hear about Jesus!
dailies.elijah: After Paul arrived, he spoke with the Jewish leaders about Jesus, and some believed and some did not. Then, in Acts 28:30, where did Paul stay, and for how long?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He stayed in his own rented house for two whole years, and welcomed all who came to see him.
dailies.jordyn: Paul welcomes all who come to see him (Acts 28:30). What does that show you about how the good news keeps going when Paul cannot travel freely?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The house becomes a place where people can come. Paul cannot go to every city now, but the people can come to him. Welcome becomes a way the message keeps moving.
dailies.action: Today’s challenge: Welcome someone in your house with kind words, or tell someone that Paul welcomed all who came to see him. Do not act out the soldier or the guard.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that for two whole years Paul stayed in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. Teach us to welcome people so they can hear about Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After Paul arrived, he spoke with the Jewish leaders about Jesus. Some believed, and some did not. We tell that only as a short bridge. Then, for two whole years, Paul stayed in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. Even under guard, he opened the door.
dailies.enochActivity: Stand at a doorway, open your hand, and say: Welcome!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 28:30, what did Paul do for the people who came to see him?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He welcomed all who came to see him.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is all a weighty word in Acts 28:30?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The welcome is not only for one kind of visitor. All who came were received. The good news in that house was not a private club. It was open to the people God sent to the door.
dailies.passageText: 30 For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: We thank God that Paul proclaimed the kingdom and taught about Jesus with all boldness and without hindrance.
dailies.verse: He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God, that the good news kept going!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 28:31, what two things did Paul do, and how does the verse say he did them?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance.
dailies.jordyn: The last words we hear about Paul in Acts are that he taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:31). How can that shape the way your family prays today?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can thank God that the message was not stopped in Rome, and we can ask him to give us boldness to speak about Jesus too. Prayer here is not only a wish for an easier road. It is thanks that God’s word kept going.
dailies.action: Pray today’s prayer out loud as a family. Then each person can thank God that the good news kept going in Rome, or ask him for boldness to speak about Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Paul proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance. Give us thankful hearts, and make us bold to tell people about Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: For two whole years Paul stayed in his rented house and welcomed all who came. He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance. Today we thank God that the good news kept going.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands, then open them like a thank-you, and say: Thank you, God! The good news keeps going!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 28:31, what is the last short phrase that tells you the message was not shut up in that house?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: With all boldness and without hindrance.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it good to pray about an unhindered message, not only about an easy life (Acts 28:16, 31)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Paul still has a soldier to guard him, and still the word is spoken without hindrance. We can ask God for that same kind of courage: not that every hard thing would disappear, but that Jesus would still be taught clearly.
dailies.passageText: 30 For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. 31 He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus, and next we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit.
dailies.verse: He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit!
dailies.elijah: What is this week’s big idea, and what did Paul do for two whole years in Rome?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus. For two whole years he stayed in his rented house, welcomed all who came, proclaimed the kingdom of God, and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
dailies.jordyn: Friends encouraged Paul on the road, a soldier guarded him in the house, and still the message kept going (Acts 28:15–16, 30–31). Next week we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit. What stays the same when the story moves from a house in Rome to the life the Spirit grows in us?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The same Lord who brought Paul to Rome, and who kept the word going there, is the Lord who gives his Spirit to his people. The good news does not stop at the end of Acts. It keeps going, and it grows good fruit in the people who belong to Jesus.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus. Then thank God, and look ahead to the fruit of the Spirit.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that even in Rome Paul kept telling people about Jesus, and that he taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. Get our hearts ready to hear about the fruit of the Spirit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus. Brothers and sisters met him on the way, and he thanked God and was encouraged. He was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. For two whole years he welcomed all who came, proclaimed the kingdom of God, and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance. Next week we will hear about the fruit of the Spirit.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week, the fruit of the Spirit!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 28:16 and 28:31, what two true things stand side by side at the end of the story?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Paul has a soldier to guard him, and he still teaches about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
dailies.jordyn2: What stays the same when the story moves from Paul in Rome to next week’s fruit of the Spirit?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The good news that kept going in that house is the same good news the Spirit plants in us. Jesus is still Lord, and he still grows his people.
dailies.passageText: 15 The brothers and sisters there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged. 16 When we got to Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him. 30 For two whole years Paul stayed there in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to see him. 31 He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!

readings.text: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

story: Last week we heard that even in Rome, Paul kept telling people about Jesus. He also wrote letters to churches, so they would know how to live as people who belong to Jesus. In a letter to the churches in Galatia, Paul names the good life the Holy Spirit grows in us. He calls it fruit, because it is grown, not glued on. We do not make a game of pretending to stick fruit on a tree. The Spirit grows this fruit in people who belong to Jesus.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Love, joy, and peace come first in the list, and then more good fruit: forbearance, which is a patient, steady way of treating people; kindness; goodness; faithfulness; gentleness; and self-control. The Holy Spirit grows all of this in us.

Against such things there is no law means this fruit is not a bad thing God has to stop. It is the good life he wants to grow. We cannot grow it only by trying hard and frowning. We ask the Spirit to grow it, and we practice love, joy, and peace in ordinary days at home.
Next week we will hear that God gives us his armor so we can stand strong in him.
weeks.enochLine: The Holy Spirit grows love, joy, and peace in us!
enochActivities: Activity: Name the fruit. Hold up one finger at a time and say: Love! Joy! Peace!
Activity: Growing, not glued. Open both hands like a growing plant and say: The Spirit grows good fruit in us!
elijahQuestions: In Galatians 5:22, what does Paul call this good life, and which fruit does he name first?
In Galatians 5:22–23, can you name all the fruit of the Spirit in the order the verses give them?
In Galatians 5:23, what two fruit come at the end of the list, and what does Paul say about such things?
What is this week’s big idea, and what does it mean that the Spirit grows fruit in us?
elijahAnswers: He calls it the fruit of the Spirit. He names love, joy, and peace first, and then forbearance, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness (Galatians 5:22).
The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).
Gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law (Galatians 5:23).
The Holy Spirit grows love, joy, peace, and more good fruit in us. Fruit is grown, not glued on. The Spirit grows this good life in people who belong to Jesus (Galatians 5:22–23).
jordynQuestions: Paul calls this the fruit of the Spirit, not the fruit of our willpower (Galatians 5:22). What does that change about how you try to be more loving, joyful, or peaceful?
The list ends with gentleness and self-control, and then says, Against such things there is no law (Galatians 5:23). What do you think Paul wants you to notice about this kind of life?

The same Lord who kept the good news going in Rome last week now names the fruit the Spirit grows in us (Galatians 5:22–23). Next week we will hear about the armor of God. How might grown fruit and God-given armor belong together in a life that belongs to Jesus?
jordynAnswers: Trying hard still matters, but it is not the root. The Spirit grows the fruit. We ask him to work in us, and we practice love and peace as people who are being grown, not as people who can manufacture the fruit alone.
This fruit is not a lawless life, and it is not a life God has to restrain. There is no law against love, joy, peace, and the rest. God is not trying to hold this fruit back. He wants it to grow.

The good news that kept going in Rome is the same good news that brings the Spirit into our ordinary days. Fruit is the life he grows in us. Armor, next week, is how he helps us stand. Both come from God, not from showing off.
weeks.jordynApplication: The Holy Spirit grows love, joy, peace, and more good fruit in us (Galatians 5:22–23). This week, choose one fruit from the list and practice it at home in a real moment—love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, or self-control. Next week we will hear about the armor of God.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week which fruit she practiced, or whether she remembered that the Spirit grows this fruit in us. If it is fitting, thank God together for one fruit you have seen in your house, and ask him to keep growing it.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Thank you that against such things there is no law. Holy Spirit, grow this good fruit in us, at home and everywhere we go. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: The fruit of the Spirit begins with love, joy, and peace.
dailies.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
dailies.enoch: Hold up three fingers and say: Love! Joy! Peace!
dailies.elijah: In Galatians 5:22, what does Paul call this good life, and which three fruit does he name first?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He calls it the fruit of the Spirit, and he names love, joy, and peace first.
dailies.jordyn: Why might it matter that love, joy, and peace come first in the list (Galatians 5:22)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The Spirit’s work in us starts with a heart that loves, a joy that is real, and a peace that can settle a house. The other fruit grows with these, not instead of them.
dailies.action: Read Galatians 5:22 out loud. Then thank God for love, joy, and peace, and ask the Spirit to grow them in your house.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness. Grow love, joy, and peace in us today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul writes, But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness. Today we listen first to love, joy, and peace. This fruit is grown by the Holy Spirit, not glued on by us.
dailies.enochActivity: Smile, take a slow breath, and say: Love, joy, peace—the Spirit grows these in me!
dailies.elijah2: In Galatians 5:22, what word does Paul use for this whole list, fruit or works?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Fruit. He calls it the fruit of the Spirit.
dailies.jordyn2: What is the difference between fruit that is grown and good behavior that is only acted out (Galatians 5:22)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Fruit comes from life inside the tree. The Spirit grows love, joy, and peace in us. We still practice them, but we do not pretend they started with us alone.
dailies.passageText: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: We name the fruit of the Spirit, because the Spirit grows this good life in us.
dailies.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
dailies.enoch: Hold up one finger at a time and try to name love, joy, and peace, then as many more as you can!
dailies.elijah: In Galatians 5:22–23, how many fruit does Paul name, and can you say them in order?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He names nine: love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
dailies.jordyn: The list is called fruit, not fruits (Galatians 5:22). What might that tell you about the life the Spirit grows?
dailies.jordynAnswer: It is one life with many signs, not nine separate projects. The same Spirit grows love and self-control, joy and gentleness, together.
dailies.action: Play Name the fruit. Take turns saying one name from the list. A grown-up can help with forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Do not throw food, and do not make a joke of the names. This is a glad way to learn the Spirit’s fruit.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for every fruit you name: love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Help us remember them, and grow them in us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Today we name them with gladness, because the Spirit grows this fruit in us.
dailies.enochActivity: Open your hands like a growing plant and say each name you remember: Love, joy, peace!
dailies.elijah2: In Galatians 5:23, what does Paul say against such things?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Against such things there is no law.
dailies.jordyn2: How can naming the fruit be a kind of practice, not only a memory game (Galatians 5:22–23)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: When we name love or gentleness, we remember what the Spirit is growing, and we can watch for a real chance to live it at home.
dailies.passageText: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: The same fruit includes forbearance, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness.
dailies.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
dailies.enoch: Hold up four fingers and say: Forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness!
dailies.elijah: In Galatians 5:22, after love, joy, and peace, which four fruit does Paul name?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Forbearance, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness.
dailies.jordyn: Forbearance is a patient, steady way of treating people, and faithfulness keeps going (Galatians 5:22). Why might a family need both?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Kindness and goodness show care in the moment. Forbearance and faithfulness keep that care from giving up when a day is long. The Spirit grows all of them.
dailies.action: Read Galatians 5:22 out loud again, and listen for forbearance, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness. Then thank God for one of those four you want him to grow in you.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the fruit of the Spirit also includes forbearance, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness. Grow a patient, kind, good, and faithful heart in us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The fruit of the Spirit is not only love, joy, and peace. Paul also names forbearance, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness. Forbearance means we do not quickly give up on people. Faithfulness means we keep our word. Kindness and goodness make a house gentle and safe.
dailies.enochActivity: Sit still for a count of three, then say: Forbearance! The Spirit can help me be patient!
dailies.elijah2: In Galatians 5:22, which fruit sounds most like keeping your word?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Faithfulness.
dailies.jordyn2: How is kindness different from only being nice when it is easy (Galatians 5:22)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Kindness and goodness are fruit the Spirit grows, even on a hard day. They are not a thin politeness we put on and take off.
dailies.passageText: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: The list ends with gentleness and self-control, and against such things there is no law.
dailies.verse: gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
dailies.enoch: Place a hand over your heart and say: Gentleness and self-control!
dailies.elijah: In Galatians 5:23, which two fruit end the list, and what does Paul say about such things?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
dailies.jordyn: Self-control is not only about food or toys; it is a Spirit-grown way of holding yourself (Galatians 5:23). What is one ordinary moment at home where gentleness or self-control would be good fruit?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Answers may name a sharp word, a snatched turn, or a quick temper. The point is that the Spirit grows a different way: gentle, and able to wait or stop.
dailies.action: Today’s challenge: Practice gentleness or self-control in one real moment—let someone else go first, use a quiet voice, or stop when a grown-up says stop. Then thank God that against such things there is no law.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for gentleness and self-control, and that against such things there is no law. Grow these fruit in us today, in a real moment at home. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The list ends, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. God is not against this fruit. He wants it to grow. Today we practice one of these in a real moment, and we remember that the Spirit is the one who grows it.
dailies.enochActivity: Use a quiet voice to say: Gentle words. The Spirit can help me!
dailies.elijah2: In Galatians 5:23, what short sentence comes right after gentleness and self-control?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Against such things there is no law.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it good news that there is no law against this fruit (Galatians 5:23)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God is not trying to hold back love, gentleness, or self-control. This is the life he is glad to grow in his people.
dailies.passageText: 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: We thank God for the fruit of the Spirit, and we ask him to grow it in us.
dailies.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Holy Spirit, grow your fruit in me!
dailies.elijah: In Galatians 5:22–23, what do we thank God for when we pray about this fruit?
dailies.elijahAnswer: We thank him that the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, and that against such things there is no law.
dailies.jordyn: If the Spirit grows the fruit, why do we still pray, and not only wait (Galatians 5:22–23)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Prayer is how we ask the Spirit to do what we cannot do alone. We thank him for the fruit he names, and we ask him to grow it in ordinary days.
dailies.action: Pray today’s prayer out loud as a family. Then each person can thank God for one fruit from the list, or ask him to grow that fruit in them.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Holy Spirit, grow this fruit in our home. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we pray the list itself. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. We thank God, and we ask the Spirit to grow this fruit in us.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands, then open them like a thank-you, and say: Thank you, God, for love, joy, and peace!
dailies.elijah2: In Galatians 5:22, what three fruit can even the youngest child thank God for by name?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Love, joy, and peace.
dailies.jordyn2: How can a family prayer over this list keep us from treating the fruit as a score we have to earn (Galatians 5:22–23)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We ask, and we thank. That is the language of gift. The Spirit grows the fruit; we receive it and practice it.
dailies.passageText: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: The Holy Spirit grows good fruit in us, and next we will hear about the armor of God.
dailies.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week, the armor of God!
dailies.elijah: What is this week’s big idea, and can you name the fruit of the Spirit?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Holy Spirit grows love, joy, peace, and more good fruit in us. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
dailies.jordyn: The Spirit grows fruit in us this week, and next week God gives us his armor so we can stand strong in him (Galatians 5:22–23). What stays the same in both weeks?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Both the fruit and the armor come from God. He grows a good life in us, and he also helps us stand. We do not have to invent either one by ourselves.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: The Holy Spirit grows love, joy, peace, and more good fruit in us. Then thank God, and look ahead to the armor of God.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Get our hearts ready to hear that you also give us your armor so we can stand strong in you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that the Holy Spirit grows love, joy, peace, and more good fruit in us. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Next week we will hear that God gives us his armor so we can stand strong in him.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week God gives us his armor!
dailies.elijah2: In Galatians 5:22–23, what short last line should we remember with the whole list?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Against such things there is no law.
dailies.jordyn2: What stays the same when the story moves from the fruit of the Spirit to the armor of God next week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The Lord who grows good fruit in us is the same Lord who gives us what we need to stand. The life and the armor both come from him.
dailies.passageText: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
