readings.text: 12 Now his brothers had gone to graze their father’s flocks near Shechem, 13 and Israel said to Joseph, “As you know, your brothers are grazing the flocks near Shechem. Come, I am going to send you to them.” “Very well,” he replied. 14 So he said to him, “Go and see if all is well with your brothers and with the flocks, and bring word back to me.” Then he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. When Joseph arrived at Shechem, 15 a man found him wandering around in the fields and asked him, “What are you looking for?” 16 He replied, “I’m looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?” 17 “They have moved on from here,” the man answered. “I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them near Dothan. 18 But they saw him in the distance, and before he reached them, they plotted to kill him. 19 “Here comes that dreamer!” they said to each other. 20 “Come now, let’s kill him and throw him into one of these cisterns and say that a ferocious animal devoured him. Then we’ll see what comes of his dreams.” 21 When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue him from their hands. “Let’s not take his life,” he said. 22 “Don’t shed any blood. Throw him into this cistern here in the wilderness, but don’t lay a hand on him.” Reuben said this to rescue him from them and take him back to his father. 23 So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe—the ornate robe he was wearing— 24 and they took him and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty; there was no water in it.

25 As they sat down to eat their meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with spices, balm and myrrh, and they were on their way to take them down to Egypt. 26 Judah said to his brothers, “What will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood? 27 Come, let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay our hands on him; after all, he is our brother, our own flesh and blood.” His brothers agreed. 28 So when the Midianite merchants came by, his brothers pulled Joseph up out of the cistern and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.

15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?” 16 So they sent word to Joseph, saying, “Your father left these instructions before he died: 17 ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: I ask you to forgive your brothers the sins and the wrongs they committed in treating you so badly.’ Now please forgive the sins of the servants of the God of your father.” When their message came to him, Joseph wept. 18 His brothers then came and threw themselves down before him. “We are your slaves,” they said. 19 But Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. 21 So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.

story: Last week we learned that God promised Abraham a family, and God kept his word. Today we hear about Joseph, one of Abraham’s family many years later, and how God was with him and used even hard things for good.

Joseph’s brothers had gone to graze their father’s flocks near Shechem, and Israel said to Joseph, “As you know, your brothers are grazing the flocks near Shechem. Come, I am going to send you to them.” Joseph said, “Very well,” and Israel sent him to see if all was well with his brothers and with the flocks, and to bring word back. A man found him wandering around in the fields and asked him, “What are you looking for?” He replied, “I’m looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?” The man answered, “They have moved on from here,” and, “I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them near Dothan.

But they saw him in the distance, and before he reached them, they plotted to kill him. They said, “Here comes that dreamer!” We say that simply, and we do not stop to invent the dreams. This is a hard part of the story, and we will not make a game of it. Reuben heard this and tried to rescue him from their hands. “Let’s not take his life,” he said. And he said, “Don’t shed any blood. Throw him into this cistern here in the wilderness, but don’t lay a hand on him.” Reuben said this to rescue him from them and take him back to his father. When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe—the ornate robe he was wearing—and they took him and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty; there was no water in it.

As they sat down to eat their meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, on their way down to Egypt. Judah said to his brothers that they should not kill their brother, but sell him to the Ishmaelites; after all, he is our brother, our own flesh and blood. His brothers agreed. When the Midianite merchants came by, his brothers pulled Joseph up out of the cistern and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.

Many years passed. We do not leave today’s readings to tell those middle chapters as official text. In our words, God was with Joseph in Egypt, and in time Joseph was able to help many people when food was scarce, and his brothers came to him. Then, when Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?” They sent word asking him to forgive them. When their message came to him, Joseph wept. His brothers then came and threw themselves down before him. “We are your slaves,” they said. But Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them. God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good.
Next week we will hear that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
weeks.enochLine: God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good!
enochActivities: Activity: Put a hand on your heart and say: God was with Joseph!
Activity: Speak one kind word, the way Joseph spoke kindly to his brothers.
elijahQuestions: In Genesis 37:13–14, what did Israel ask Joseph to do, and what did Joseph say?
In Genesis 37:21–24, what did Reuben try to do, and what happened when Joseph came to his brothers?
In Genesis 37:26–28, what did Judah say they should do, and where was Joseph taken?
In Genesis 50:15–21, what were Joseph’s brothers afraid of, what did Joseph say God intended, and how did Joseph treat them?
elijahAnswers: Israel asked him to go and see if all was well with his brothers and with the flocks, and bring word back. Joseph said, “Very well,” (Genesis 37:13–14).

Reuben tried to rescue him from their hands. “Let’s not take his life,” he said, and he told them not to shed any blood, but to throw him into the cistern and not lay a hand on him, so he could take him back to his father. They stripped Joseph of his ornate robe and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty; there was no water in it (Genesis 37:21–24).

Judah said they should sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay their hands on him, because he was their brother, their own flesh and blood. His brothers agreed, and they sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt (Genesis 37:26–28).

They were afraid Joseph would hold a grudge and pay them back for all the wrongs they did to him. Joseph said, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:15–21).
jordynQuestions: Reuben heard the brothers’ plan and tried to rescue Joseph from their hands, so he could take him back to his father (Genesis 37:21–22). What does it look like to try to protect someone when others are being unkind?

Joseph’s brothers were afraid he would pay them back. Joseph said, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” (Genesis 50:19–21). What is the difference between what they intended and what God intended?
God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good. Next week we will hear that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. What stays the same about God in both stories?
jordynAnswers: Reuben did not join the plan to take Joseph’s life. He spoke up, and he looked for a way to bring Joseph home. Protecting someone can start with words that refuse harm, and with a plan to help, even when it is hard.

They intended to harm him. God intended it for good, to accomplish what was then being done, the saving of many lives. Joseph would not put himself in the place of God. He told them not to be afraid, and he promised to provide for them and their children, and he spoke kindly to them.

God does not leave his people. He was with Joseph in hard things, and he used them for good, even the saving of many lives. Next week we will hear that he heard his people and set them free from Egypt. The same God stays with his people and saves.
weeks.jordynApplication: God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good (Genesis 37:12–28; 50:15–21). This week, when something is hard, remember that God intended Joseph’s hard road for good, for the saving of many lives. Speak kindly to someone, the way Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them. Next week we will hear that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week where she remembered that God can use hard things for good, or whom she spoke kindly to. If it is fitting, thank God together that he was with Joseph, and that he used even hard things for good.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Israel sent Joseph, and that Joseph said, “Very well,” and went. Thank you that Reuben tried to rescue him, and said, “Let’s not take his life,” Thank you that even after Joseph was sold and taken to Egypt, you were with him. Thank you that Joseph said, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” You were with Joseph, and you used even hard things for good. Help us trust you, and help us speak kindly. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Israel sent Joseph to his brothers, and Reuben tried to rescue him when the brothers meant him harm.
dailies.verse: When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue him from their hands. “Let’s not take his life,” he said.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say: Reuben tried to help Joseph!
dailies.elijah: What did Israel ask Joseph to do, and what did Joseph say?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Israel asked him to go and see if all was well with his brothers and with the flocks, and bring word back. Joseph said, “Very well,” (Genesis 37:13–14).
dailies.jordyn: The brothers saw Joseph in the distance and plotted to kill him, but Reuben tried to rescue him and take him back to his father (Genesis 37:18–22). How does Reuben’s word, “Let’s not take his life,” help us think about protecting someone?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Reuben would not join the plan to take Joseph’s life. He looked for a way to keep him safe and bring him home. Protecting someone can start with words that refuse harm.
dailies.action: Read Genesis 37:12–24 together. Then name one way you can look out for a brother, a sister, or a friend this week.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Israel sent Joseph, and that Joseph said, “Very well,” and went. Thank you that Reuben tried to rescue him, and said, “Let’s not take his life,” Help us look out for one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Israel sent Joseph to see if all was well with his brothers and with the flocks. Joseph said, “Very well,” and went. His brothers saw him and plotted to harm him. This is a hard part of the story, and we will not make a game of it. Reuben tried to rescue him. “Let’s not take his life,” he said. They stripped Joseph of his ornate robe and threw him into the empty cistern.
dailies.enochActivity: Put a hand on your heart and say: Reuben tried to help!
dailies.elijah2: What happened when Joseph came to his brothers, and what was the cistern like?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They stripped him of his robe—the ornate robe he was wearing—and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty; there was no water in it (Genesis 37:23–24).
dailies.jordyn2: Reuben said, “Don’t shed any blood. Throw him into this cistern here in the wilderness, but don’t lay a hand on him.” He said this to rescue Joseph and take him back to his father (Genesis 37:22). What was Reuben hoping to do?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: He was trying to rescue Joseph from their hands and take him back to his father, not to leave him in harm’s way.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Joseph walked a long way to find his brothers. Even when the road became hard, God was still with him.
dailies.verse: He replied, “I’m looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?”
dailies.enoch: Take three soft steps and say: God was with Joseph!
dailies.elijah: A man found Joseph wandering around in the fields. What did the man ask, and what did Joseph say he was looking for?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The man asked, “What are you looking for?” Joseph replied, “I’m looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?” (Genesis 37:15–16).
dailies.jordyn: Joseph had to keep looking until he found his brothers near Dothan (Genesis 37:17). What does his long search show us, even before the hard part of the story comes?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Joseph kept going where his father had sent him. He asked for help and went on to Dothan. Faithfulness can look like taking the next step, even when the way is long.
dailies.action: Play a gentle looking game: hide a small soft object in the room, and take turns looking for it. When you find it, say together: God was with Joseph, even when things were hard. Do not act out the cistern or the selling. Keep the game kind.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Joseph went to look for his brothers, and that he said, “I’m looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?” Thank you that you were with him, even when the road became hard. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Joseph was sent, and he went looking for his brothers. A man found him wandering around in the fields and helped him on his way to Dothan. Today’s game is a gentle search, not a play of harm. When the road later became hard, God was still with Joseph.
dailies.enochActivity: Take three soft steps and say: God was with Joseph!
dailies.elijah2: Where did the man say the brothers had gone, and what had he heard them say?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The man answered, “They have moved on from here,” and, “I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them near Dothan (Genesis 37:17).
dailies.jordyn2: How can a simple search game help us remember Joseph, without turning the hard parts of the story into play?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The game can remind us that Joseph kept looking, and that God was with him. We do not act out harm. We remember that God stayed with Joseph even when things were hard.
dailies.passageText: 15 a man found him wandering around in the fields and asked him, “What are you looking for?” 16 He replied, “I’m looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?” 17 “They have moved on from here,” the man answered. “I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” So Joseph went after his brothers and found them near Dothan.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Joseph was sold and taken to Egypt. Years later, he said God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives.
dailies.verse: You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say: God intended it for good!
dailies.elijah: What did Judah say they should do, and where was Joseph taken?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Judah said they should sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay their hands on him, because he was their brother, their own flesh and blood. They sold him for twenty shekels of silver, and the Ishmaelites took him to Egypt (Genesis 37:26–28).
dailies.jordyn: Many years later, after their father had died, the brothers were afraid. What did they worry Joseph would do, and what did Joseph say God had intended?
dailies.jordynAnswer: They said, “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?” Joseph said God intended it for good, to accomplish what was then being done, the saving of many lives. He told them not to be afraid, and he promised to provide for them and their children (Genesis 50:15, 19–21).
dailies.action: Read Genesis 37:25–28, then Genesis 50:15–21. In between, say in your own words that many years passed, and that God was with Joseph in Egypt. Do not treat the skipped chapters as today’s official reading.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that even after Joseph was sold and taken to Egypt, you were with him. Thank you that he said you intended it for good, for the saving of many lives. Help us trust you with hard things. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Judah said they should not kill their brother, but sell him, because he was their own flesh and blood. Joseph was sold for twenty shekels of silver and taken to Egypt. Many years passed. In our words, God was with Joseph in Egypt, and he was able to help many people when food was scarce. Then, when their father was dead, the brothers were afraid, but Joseph wept, spoke kindly, and said God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives.
dailies.enochActivity: Open your hands and say: God intended it for good!
dailies.elijah2: When the brothers’ message came to Joseph, what did he do, and what did they say when they came to him?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Joseph wept. His brothers then came and threw themselves down before him. “We are your slaves,” they said (Genesis 50:17–18).
dailies.jordyn2: Joseph said, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” (Genesis 50:19–21). How does this show both honesty about harm and trust in God?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Joseph did not pretend the brothers had meant well. He said they had intended to harm him. He also trusted that God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives, and he would not put himself in the place of God. Then he promised to provide for them and spoke kindly to them.
dailies.passageText: 25 As they sat down to eat their meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with spices, balm and myrrh, and they were on their way to take them down to Egypt. 26 Judah said to his brothers, “What will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood? 27 Come, let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay our hands on him; after all, he is our brother, our own flesh and blood.” His brothers agreed. 28 So when the Midianite merchants came by, his brothers pulled Joseph up out of the cistern and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt. 15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?” 16 So they sent word to Joseph, saying, “Your father left these instructions before he died: 17 ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: I ask you to forgive your brothers the sins and the wrongs they committed in treating you so badly.’ Now please forgive the sins of the servants of the God of your father.” When their message came to him, Joseph wept. 18 His brothers then came and threw themselves down before him. “We are your slaves,” they said. 19 But Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. 21 So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Joseph wept, reassured his brothers, and spoke kindly to them. God intended the hard road for good.
dailies.verse: And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.
dailies.enoch: Speak one kind word to someone today.
dailies.elijah: After the brothers asked Joseph to forgive them, what did Joseph do, and how did he treat them?
dailies.elijahAnswer: When their message came to him, Joseph wept. He told them not to be afraid, said God intended it for good, promised to provide for them and their children, and reassured them and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:17–21).
dailies.jordyn: Joseph could have paid his brothers back, and they were afraid he would. Instead he spoke kindly and promised to provide for them (Genesis 50:15, 21). What does that kind of forgiveness look like in a family?
dailies.jordynAnswer: It tells the truth about the wrong, and it does not take God’s place. Then it speaks kindly and looks after people, the way Joseph provided for his brothers and their children.
dailies.action: Choose one kind word or one small kindness for someone in your house today, and do it on purpose, the way Joseph spoke kindly and reassured his brothers.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Joseph wept, and that he reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them. Thank you that he would not put himself in your place. Help us tell the truth, and help us be kind. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The brothers were afraid Joseph would pay them back. They asked him to forgive them, and Joseph wept. He told them not to be afraid. God had intended the harm for good, for the saving of many lives. Then Joseph promised to provide for them and their children, and he spoke kindly to them. Today’s challenge is a real kindness, not a skit about harm.
dailies.enochActivity: Speak one kind word and say: Joseph was kind!
dailies.elijah2: What did Joseph promise to do for his brothers, and for whom else?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He said, So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children. And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:21).
dailies.jordyn2: Why does it matter that Joseph asked, Am I in the place of God, before he spoke about good coming from harm (Genesis 50:19–20)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Joseph would not take God’s place. He could be honest about the harm, and still trust God with what God intended. Forgiveness does not pretend we are God. It leaves room for God to work good, and then it speaks kindly.
dailies.passageText: 15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?” 16 So they sent word to Joseph, saying, “Your father left these instructions before he died: 17 ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: I ask you to forgive your brothers the sins and the wrongs they committed in treating you so badly.’ Now please forgive the sins of the servants of the God of your father.” When their message came to him, Joseph wept. 18 His brothers then came and threw themselves down before him. “We are your slaves,” they said. 19 But Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. 21 So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that he was with Joseph, and that he used even hard things for good, for the saving of many lives.
dailies.verse: You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God, for being with Joseph!
dailies.elijah: What did Joseph say God intended, and what was being accomplished?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God intended it for good, to accomplish what was then being done, the saving of many lives (Genesis 50:20).
dailies.jordyn: Joseph told his brothers not to be afraid, and he promised to provide for them and their children (Genesis 50:21). How can that shape the way we pray for our family?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can thank God that he stays with his people in hard things, and ask him to make us people who speak kindly and look after one another, the way Joseph provided and reassured his brothers.
dailies.action: Pray the family prayer slowly. When you hear that God intended it for good, pause and thank him that he was with Joseph.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Joseph said, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” Thank you that you were with him, and that you used even hard things for good, for the saving of many lives. Help us trust you, and help us speak kindly. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we pray with Joseph’s words in our ears. He told his brothers not to be afraid. He would not put himself in the place of God. He said they had intended to harm him, but God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives. Then he promised to provide for them and their children, and he spoke kindly to them.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah2: After Joseph spoke, what two things did he do for his brothers?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He reassured them and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:21).
dailies.jordyn2: How can Joseph’s words, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.”, become a prayer without turning hard things into something we pretend were not hard?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We tell the truth, as Joseph did: the brothers intended harm. We also trust God, as Joseph did: God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives. Then we ask God to help us not be afraid, and to make us kind providers, not people who take his place.
dailies.passageText: 19 But Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. 21 So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good. Next, God heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
dailies.verse: You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week, God sets his people free!
dailies.elijah: What is this week’s big idea, and can you tell how the story moved from the cistern to Joseph’s kind words?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good. Joseph was sent to his brothers, thrown into an empty cistern, and sold and taken to Egypt. Many years later, his brothers were afraid, but Joseph wept and said God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives. He reassured them and spoke kindly to them.
dailies.jordyn: We have seen that God was with Joseph, and that he used even hard things for good. Next week we will hear that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. What stays the same about God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God does not leave his people. He was with Joseph in hard things, and he used them for good, even the saving of many lives. Next week we will hear that he heard his people and set them free from Egypt. The same God stays with his people and saves.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: God was with Joseph, and he used even hard things for good. Then look ahead to Moses, and to the God who heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you were with Joseph, and that you used even hard things for good, for the saving of many lives. Thank you that Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them. Get our hearts ready to hear that you heard your people and set them free from Egypt. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we heard that Israel sent Joseph, that Reuben tried to rescue him, and that Joseph was sold and taken to Egypt. Many years later Joseph told his brothers that they had intended to harm him, but God intended it for good, for the saving of many lives. He spoke kindly, and he promised to provide. God was with Joseph. Next week we will hear that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
dailies.enochActivity: Wave a small hello toward tomorrow and say: God sets his people free!
dailies.elijah2: What did Joseph say God intended, and how did he treat his brothers at the end of the story?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: God intended it for good, to accomplish what was then being done, the saving of many lives. Joseph told them not to be afraid, promised to provide for them and their children, and reassured them and spoke kindly to them (Genesis 50:20–21).
dailies.jordyn2: Joseph’s family ended up in Egypt, and next week we will hear that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. What should we remember as the story moves forward?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should remember that God was with Joseph, and that he used even hard things for good. The same God hears his people. We do not have to be afraid that he has forgotten them when the next hard chapter begins.
dailies.passageText: 13 and Israel said to Joseph, “As you know, your brothers are grazing the flocks near Shechem. Come, I am going to send you to them.” “Very well,” he replied. 14 So he said to him, “Go and see if all is well with your brothers and with the flocks, and bring word back to me.” Then he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. readings.text: 1 Now Moses was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. 2 There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in flames of fire from within a bush. Moses saw that though the bush was on fire it did not burn up. 3 So Moses thought, “I will go over and see this strange sight—why the bush does not burn up.” 4 When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called to him from within the bush, “Moses! Moses!” And Moses said, “Here I am.” 5 “Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” 6 Then he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God. 7 The LORD said, “I have indeed seen the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and I am concerned about their suffering. 8 So I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey—the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. 9 And now the cry of the Israelites has reached me, and I have seen the way the Egyptians are oppressing them. 10 So now, go. I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people the Israelites out of Egypt.” 11 But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” 12 And God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.”

29 At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner, who was in the dungeon, and the firstborn of all the livestock as well. 30 Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night, and there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead. 31 During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. 32 Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” 33 The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and leave the country. “For otherwise,” they said, “we will all die!” 34 So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and carried it on their shoulders in kneading troughs wrapped in clothing. 35 The Israelites did as Moses instructed and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. 36 The LORD had made the Egyptians favorably disposed toward the people, and they gave them what they asked for; so they plundered the Egyptians. 37 The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Sukkoth. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. 38 Many other people went up with them, and also large droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. 39 With the dough the Israelites had brought from Egypt, they baked loaves of unleavened bread. The dough was without yeast because they had been driven out of Egypt and did not have time to prepare food for themselves. 40 Now the length of time the Israelite people lived in Egypt was 430 years. 41 At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions left Egypt. 42 Because the LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, on this night all the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD for the generations to come.

21 Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, 22 and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. 23 The Egyptians pursued them, and all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots and horsemen followed them into the sea. 24 During the last watch of the night the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud at the Egyptian army and threw it into confusion. 25 He jammed the wheels of their chariots so that they had difficulty driving. And the Egyptians said, “Let’s get away from the Israelites! The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt.” 26 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” 27 Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea went back to its place. The Egyptians were fleeing toward it, and the LORD swept them into the sea. 28 The water flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen—the entire army of Pharaoh that had followed the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived. 29 But the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. 30 That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. 31 And when the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the LORD displayed against the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant.

story: Last week we learned that God was with Joseph, and that he used even hard things for good. Joseph’s family was in Egypt. Many years later, the people of Israel were still there, and their life was hard. We do not leave today’s readings to tell those earlier chapters as official text. In our words, they were suffering, and God heard them.

Now Moses was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, and he led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in flames of fire from within a bush. Moses saw that though the bush was on fire it did not burn up. So Moses thought, “I will go over and see this strange sight—why the bush does not burn up.” When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called to him from within the bush, “Moses! Moses!” And Moses said, “Here I am.” “Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” Then he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God.

The LORD said, “I have indeed seen the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and I am concerned about their suffering. So I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey—the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. And now the cry of the Israelites has reached me, and I have seen the way the Egyptians are oppressing them. So now, go. I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people the Israelites out of Egypt.” But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” And God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.”

We do not leave today’s readings to tell every sign that came before this night as official text. In our words, God kept his word, and the night of leaving came. At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in Egypt. Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night, and there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead. We say this simply, and with care. It is not a scene to describe, and we will not make a game of it. During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and leave the country. “For otherwise,” they said, “we will all die!” So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Sukkoth. Now the length of time the Israelite people lived in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions left Egypt. Because the LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, on this night all the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD for the generations to come.

Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. The Egyptians pursued them into the sea. The Egyptians said, “Let’s get away from the Israelites! The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt.” Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD swept them into the sea. The water flowed back and covered the entire army of Pharaoh that had followed the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived. But the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground. That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. We say that simply. The LORD saved his people. We will not make a game of it. And when the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the LORD displayed against the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant. God heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
Next week we will hear that Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family.

elijahQuestions: In Exodus 3:4–6, what did God call to Moses from the bush, what did Moses say, and what did God tell him about the ground?

In Exodus 3:7–12, what had the LORD seen and heard, what did he send Moses to do, and what did God promise when Moses asked, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?”
In Exodus 12:31–42, what did Pharaoh tell Moses and Aaron to do, and what had the LORD done that night after the people had lived in Egypt 430 years?
In Exodus 14:21–31, how did the Israelites go through the sea, what did the LORD do that day, and what did the people do when they saw his mighty hand?
elijahAnswers: God called, “Moses! Moses!” And Moses said, “Here I am.” God said, “Do not come any closer,” and, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” Then he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” (Exodus 3:4–6).

The LORD said he had indeed seen the misery of his people in Egypt, heard them crying out, and was concerned about their suffering. He had come down to rescue them, and he was sending Moses to Pharaoh to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:7–12).

Pharaoh said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” The LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, and at the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions left Egypt (Exodus 12:31–42).

The LORD drove the sea back and turned it into dry land, and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. The people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant (Exodus 14:21–31).
jordynQuestions: Moses asked, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” And God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:11–12). What is the difference between looking at yourself and trusting that God will be with you?
The night of leaving was heavy, and then the LORD made a dry path through the sea (Exodus 12:29–42; 14:21–31). What do these two parts of the story show us about the God who sets his people free?
God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. Next week we will hear that Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family. What stays the same about God in both stories?
jordynAnswers: Moses looked at himself and felt too small for the work. God did not first make Moses feel big. He promised, I will be with you, and he gave a sign that Moses would worship God on that mountain after the people were brought out. The point is God’s presence, not Moses’ size.

God had seen the misery of his people and come down to rescue them. The leaving was real and costly, and we say the hard night simply. Then the LORD made a way through the sea on dry ground and saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. God hears, God comes down, and God saves.
God does not forget his people. He heard them in Egypt and set them free. Next week we will hear that he kindly provided for Ruth’s family. The same God hears, stays with his people, and provides.
weeks.jordynApplication: God heard his people and set them free from Egypt (Exodus 3:1–12; 12:29–42; 14:21–31). This week, when you feel small like Moses, remember that God said he would be with him. Thank God that he hears his people and makes a way. Next week we will hear that Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week where she remembered that God hears and is with his people, or how she thanked him for making a way. If it is fitting, thank God together that he heard his people and set them free from Egypt.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you called Moses from the bush, and that he said, “Here I am.” Thank you that you said, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” Thank you that you had seen the misery of your people, and that you said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” Thank you that you kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, and that you saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. You heard your people and set them free. Help us trust you, and help us put our trust in you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.action: Read Exodus 3:1–12 together. Then take off your shoes for a moment and say God’s words about holy ground.

dailies.teach: Moses saw a bush on fire that did not burn up. God called, “Moses! Moses!” and Moses said, “Here I am.” God told him not to come any closer, and to take off his sandals, for the place was holy ground. God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Moses stood on holy ground, and later God made a dry path through the sea. Both are about God’s presence and God’s way.
dailies.verse: “Here I am.”
dailies.enoch: Take three careful steps and say: God made a way!
dailies.elijah: What did God tell Moses to do with his sandals, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God said, “Do not come any closer,” and, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5).
dailies.jordyn: Later the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left (Exodus 14:22, 29). How can a careful walk help us remember that, without turning the hard parts into play?
dailies.jordynAnswer: A slow, careful walk can remind us that God made a path and that his people went through on dry ground. We do not act out the army or the waters flowing back. We remember that the LORD made a way and saved his people.
dailies.action: Play a gentle two-part game. First, take off your shoes and say, “Here I am.” then, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” Then lay a towel or a few papers as a dry path and walk it slowly, saying: God made a way. Do not act out the firstborn night or the army in the sea. Keep the game quiet and kind.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Moses said, “Here I am.” and that you said, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” Thank you that you made a dry path through the sea. Help us remember that you are with your people, and that you make a way. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: God called Moses by name, and Moses said, “Here I am.” The place was holy ground. Later the LORD drove the sea back and turned it into dry land, and the Israelites went through on dry ground. Today’s game is a holy-ground pause and a careful walk, not a play of harm.
dailies.enochActivity: Take off your shoes, then take three careful steps and say: God made a way!
dailies.elijah2: How did the LORD turn the sea into dry land, and how did the Israelites go through?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: All that night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left (Exodus 14:21–22).
dailies.jordyn2: Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God (Exodus 3:6), and later the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him (Exodus 14:31). What kind of fear is this, and how is it different from panic in a game?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: It is the fear of knowing that God is holy and mighty, and then trusting him. Moses hid his face, and the people put their trust in the LORD. It is not a scare we act out. It is reverence, and it leads to trust.
dailies.passageText: 4 When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called to him from within the bush, “Moses! Moses!” And Moses said, “Here I am.” 5 “Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” 6 Then he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God. 21 Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, 22 and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: The LORD kept vigil that night and brought his people out of Egypt. Then he made a way through the sea and saved them.
dailies.verse: That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say: God set his people free!
dailies.elijah: What did Pharaoh tell Moses and Aaron to do during the night?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” (Exodus 12:31–32).
dailies.jordyn: How long had the Israelite people lived in Egypt, and what had the LORD done that night?
dailies.jordynAnswer: They had lived in Egypt 430 years. At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions left Egypt. Because the LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD for the generations to come (Exodus 12:40–42).
dailies.action: Read Exodus 12:29–42, then Exodus 14:21–31. Say the hard parts simply, and do not turn them into a game. Then thank God that he kept vigil and saved Israel.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you kept vigil that night to bring your people out of Egypt. Thank you that Pharaoh said they should leave and worship you. Thank you that you made a dry path through the sea, and that you saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The night of leaving was heavy, and we say it simply, with care. Pharaoh told Moses and Aaron to leave and worship the LORD. The people left in a hurry, and at the end of 430 years, to the very day, the LORD’s divisions left Egypt. The LORD kept vigil to bring them out. Then Moses stretched out his hand, the LORD made dry land, and his people went through the sea. The LORD saved Israel that day.
dailies.enochActivity: Open your hands and say: God set his people free!
dailies.elijah2: What did the Egyptians say when the LORD jammed the wheels of their chariots, and what did the LORD tell Moses to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The Egyptians said, “Let’s get away from the Israelites! The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt.” Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” (Exodus 14:25–26).
dailies.jordyn2: The reading says there was loud wailing in Egypt, and later that the LORD saved Israel (Exodus 12:30; 14:30). How should we talk about this part of the story at home?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We tell the truth, and we tell it simply. We do not describe it as a spectacle, and we do not make a game of it. We remember that God heard his people, that the night was heavy and real, and that the LORD saved Israel and set them free.
dailies.passageText: 29 At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner, who was in the dungeon, and the firstborn of all the livestock as well. 30 Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night, and there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead. 31 During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. 32 Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” 33 The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and leave the country. “For otherwise,” they said, “we will all die!” 34 So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and carried it on their shoulders in kneading troughs wrapped in clothing. 35 The Israelites did as Moses instructed and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. 36 The LORD had made the Egyptians favorably disposed toward the people, and they gave them what they asked for; so they plundered the Egyptians. 37 The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Sukkoth. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. 38 Many other people went up with them, and also large droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. 39 With the dough the Israelites had brought from Egypt, they baked loaves of unleavened bread. The dough was without yeast because they had been driven out of Egypt and did not have time to prepare food for themselves. 40 Now the length of time the Israelite people lived in Egypt was 430 years. 41 At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions left Egypt. 42 Because the LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, on this night all the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD for the generations to come. 21 Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, 22 and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. 23 The Egyptians pursued them, and all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots and horsemen followed them into the sea. 24 During the last watch of the night the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud at the Egyptian army and threw it into confusion. 25 He jammed the wheels of their chariots so that they had difficulty driving. And the Egyptians said, “Let’s get away from the Israelites! The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt.” 26 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” 27 Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea went back to its place. The Egyptians were fleeing toward it, and the LORD swept them into the sea. 28 The water flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen—the entire army of Pharaoh that had followed the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived. 29 But the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. 30 That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. 31 And when the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the LORD displayed against the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: God promised to be with Moses, and the people put their trust in the LORD. Trust him when you feel small.
dailies.verse: I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.
dailies.enoch: When you feel small, say: God is with his people!
dailies.elijah: What did Moses ask, and what did God promise?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Moses asked, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:11–12).
dailies.jordyn: When the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the LORD, what two things did they do?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant (Exodus 14:31).
dailies.action: Choose one moment today when you feel small or unsure. Pause and say, God said to Moses that he would be with him. Then take the next ordinary step in front of you.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that when Moses asked who he was to go, you said you would be with him. Thank you that the people feared you and put their trust in you. Help us trust you when we feel small, and help us take the next step. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Moses felt too small to go to Pharaoh. God promised to be with him, and gave a sign that the people would worship on that mountain after they were brought out. At the end of the story the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him. Today’s challenge is a real trust, not a skit of the sea.
dailies.enochActivity: Put a hand on your heart and say: God is with his people!
dailies.elijah2: What would be the sign that it was God who had sent Moses?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: God said, When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain (Exodus 3:12).
dailies.jordyn2: How can fearing the LORD and putting your trust in him shape an ordinary hard moment this week, the way it shaped Israel after the sea?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Fear of the LORD is reverence, not panic. The people saw his mighty hand and trusted him. In a hard moment we can remember that God hears, that he is with his people, and that we can take the next step without having to be large enough on our own.
dailies.passageText: 11 But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” 12 And God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” 31 And when the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the LORD displayed against the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that he heard his people, kept vigil to bring them out, and saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians.
dailies.verse: Because the LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, on this night all the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD for the generations to come.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God, for hearing your people!
dailies.elijah: What had the LORD seen and heard, and what did he say he had come down to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He had seen the misery of his people in Egypt, heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and was concerned about their suffering. He had come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians (Exodus 3:7–8).
dailies.jordyn: The LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt (Exodus 12:42), and that day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians (Exodus 14:30). How can those two lines shape the way we pray?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We thank God that he watches over his people and that he saves them. We honor him for the rescue, and we ask him to help us trust him the way Israel put their trust in the LORD.
dailies.action: Pray the family prayer slowly. When you hear that the LORD kept vigil, pause and thank him that he heard his people and set them free.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you had seen the misery of your people, and that you kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt. Thank you that you said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” Thank you that you saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. You heard your people and set them free. Help us honor you, and help us trust you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we pray with the story in our ears. God had seen the misery of his people and come down to rescue them. He kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt. He made a way through the sea, and that day the LORD saved Israel. We thank him simply, and we do not turn the hard parts into a show.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah2: After the LORD saved Israel, what did the people do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant (Exodus 14:31).
dailies.jordyn2: How can keeping vigil, in this passage, help a family pray without pretending the rescue was easy?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD, because the LORD kept vigil to bring them out. Remembering is how we honor him. We tell the truth about the heavy night and the dry path, and we thank God that he heard his people and set them free.
dailies.passageText: 7 The LORD said, “I have indeed seen the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and I am concerned about their suffering. 8 So I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey—the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. 42 Because the LORD kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, on this night all the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the LORD for the generations to come. 30 That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. 31 And when the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the LORD displayed against the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant.

dailies.focus: God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. Next, Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family.
dailies.verse: That day the LORD saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week, God kindly provided!
dailies.elijah: What is this week’s big idea, and can you tell the story from the bush to the dry path through the sea?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. God called Moses from the bush, saw the misery of his people, and promised to be with him. The LORD kept vigil that night and brought them out of Egypt after 430 years. Then the LORD made a dry path through the sea, and that day he saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. The people feared the LORD and put their trust in him.
dailies.jordyn: We have seen that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. Next week we will hear that Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family. What stays the same about God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God does not forget his people. He heard them in Egypt and set them free. Next week we will hear that he kindly provided for Ruth’s family. The same God hears, stays with his people, and provides.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. Then look ahead to Ruth, and to the God who kindly provides.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you heard your people and set them free from Egypt. Thank you that you were with Moses, that you kept vigil, and that you saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. Get our hearts ready to hear that Ruth stayed faithful, and that you kindly provided for her family. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we heard God call Moses, see his people’s misery, and promise to be with him. The LORD kept vigil and brought them out of Egypt. He made a way through the sea and saved Israel. God heard his people and set them free. Next week we will hear that Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family.
dailies.enochActivity: Wave a small hello toward tomorrow and say: God kindly provides!
dailies.elijah2: What did God promise Moses, and what did the people do when they saw the LORD’s mighty hand?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: God said he would be with Moses, and that when he had brought the people out of Egypt, they would worship God on that mountain. The people feared the LORD and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant (Exodus 3:12; 14:31).
dailies.jordyn2: The story began with misery in Egypt and ends with a people set free, trusting the LORD. What should we remember as the story moves toward Ruth?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should remember that God heard his people and set them free. He is with those he sends, and he makes a way. The same God can kindly provide in the next chapter, as we will hear with Ruth.
