readings.text: 16 But Ruth replied, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. 17 Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” 18 When Naomi realized that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.

1 Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a man of standing from the clan of Elimelek, whose name was Boaz. 2 And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said to her, “Go ahead, my daughter.” 3 So she went out, entered a field and began to glean behind the harvesters. As it turned out, she was working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelek. 4 Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and greeted the harvesters, “The LORD be with you!” “The LORD bless you!” they answered. 5 Boaz asked the overseer of his harvesters, “Who does that young woman belong to?” 6 The overseer replied, “She is the Moabite who came back from Moab with Naomi. 7 She said, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the harvesters.’ She came into the field and has remained here from morning till now, except for a short rest in the shelter.” 8 So Boaz said to Ruth, “My daughter, listen to me. Don’t go and glean in another field and don’t go away from here. Stay here with the women who work for me. 9 Watch the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after the women. I have told the men not to lay a hand on you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.” 10 At this, she bowed down with her face to the ground. She asked him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me—a foreigner?” 11 Boaz replied, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. 12 May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

13 So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife. When he made love to her, the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. 14 The women said to Naomi: “Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel! 15 He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” 16 Then Naomi took the child in her arms and cared for him. 17 The women living there said, “Naomi has a son!” And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.

story: Last week we learned that God heard his people and set them free from Egypt. Today we hear about Ruth, who stayed faithful, and about the God who kindly provided for her family.

We do not leave today’s readings to tell the earlier verses as official text. In our words, Naomi was going home, and her life had been very sad. She had lost her husband and her sons, and she urged Ruth to turn back. We say that simply, and with care. It is not a scene to linger on. But Ruth replied, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” When Naomi realized that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.

Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a man of standing from the clan of Elimelek, whose name was Boaz. And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said to her, “Go ahead, my daughter.” So she went out, entered a field and began to glean behind the harvesters. As it turned out, she was working in a field belonging to Boaz. Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and greeted the harvesters, “The LORD be with you!” “The LORD bless you!” they answered. Boaz asked who she was, and the overseer told him she was the Moabite who came back from Moab with Naomi, and that she had asked, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the harvesters.’ She had remained there from morning till now, except for a short rest.

So Boaz said to Ruth, “My daughter, listen to me. Don’t go and glean in another field and don’t go away from here. Stay here with the women who work for me. Watch the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after the women. I have told the men not to lay a hand on you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.” We hear his care simply: he made a way for her to be safe and to have what she needed. At this, she bowed down with her face to the ground. She asked him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me—a foreigner?” Boaz replied, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

We do not leave today’s readings to tell the middle chapters as official text. In our words, God kept being kind, and Boaz took Ruth into his care. So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife. The LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. We say that simply, with honor. The women said to Naomi, “Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel! He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” Then Naomi took the child in her arms and cared for him. The women living there said, “Naomi has a son!” And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family.
Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.
weeks.enochLine: Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided!
enochActivities: Activity: Walk beside someone and say: I will go with you!
Activity: Pick up one small thing and share it, the way Ruth gathered leftover grain.
elijahQuestions: In Ruth 1:16–18, what did Ruth say to Naomi, and what did Naomi do when she realized Ruth was determined to go with her?
In Ruth 2:2–3, what did Ruth ask to do, and whose field did she end up in?
In Ruth 2:8–12, how did Boaz care for Ruth, and what did he ask the LORD to do for her?
In Ruth 4:13–17, what did the LORD do for Ruth, what did the women say to Naomi, and who was Obed in the family line?
elijahAnswers: Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” When Naomi realized that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her (Ruth 1:16–18).

Ruth said, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said, “Go ahead, my daughter.” She entered a field and began to glean, and as it turned out, she was working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelek (Ruth 2:2–3).

Boaz told her to stay with the women who worked for him, not to glean in another field, and that he had told the men not to lay a hand on her. He told her to get a drink from the water jars when she was thirsty. He said, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” (Ruth 2:8–12).

Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife. The LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. The women said, “Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel! He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” They named the child Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:13–17).
jordynQuestions: Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:16–17). What does this kind of loyalty look like, and what does it cost?

Boaz said Ruth had come to take refuge under the wings of the LORD, the God of Israel (Ruth 2:12), and later the women praised the LORD, who had not left Naomi without a guardian-redeemer (Ruth 4:14). How do Ruth’s faithfulness and God’s kindness belong together in this story?

Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family. The story ends with David in the family line. Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. What stays the same about God?
jordynAnswers: Ruth would not turn back. She bound her life to Naomi’s road, her people, and her God, even as far as death and burial. Loyalty like this is not a light feeling. It stays, and it costs leaving what is familiar, as Boaz later said she had left father, mother, and homeland.

Ruth stayed faithful, and she took refuge under the LORD’s wings. God kindly provided through Boaz’s favor, through a son, and through a future for Naomi. The kindness is the LORD’s, and he often shows it through people who notice, protect, and provide.

God is kind, and he does not leave his people without help. He provided for Ruth and Naomi, and he was already at work in the family line that leads to David. Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. The same God can be trusted, and he kindly provides.
weeks.jordynApplication: Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family (Ruth 1:16–18; 2:1–12; 4:13–17). This week, stay faithful to someone you can walk with, the way Ruth would not turn back from Naomi, and look for one kind way to notice and help, the way Boaz did. Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whom she stayed faithful to, or what kindness she showed. If it is fitting, thank God together that Ruth stayed faithful, and that God kindly provided for her family.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” Thank you that Boaz said, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” Thank you that you enabled Ruth to conceive, and that you did not leave Naomi without a guardian-redeemer. Ruth stayed faithful, and you kindly provided for her family. Help us stay faithful, and help us take refuge under your wings. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Ruth would not turn back from Naomi. She stayed faithful, and bound her life to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God.
dailies.verse: Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up walk beside you and say: I will go with you!
dailies.elijah: What did Ruth tell Naomi not to do, and what did she say about going, staying, people, and God?
dailies.elijahAnswer: She said, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:16–17).
dailies.jordyn: When Naomi realized that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her (Ruth 1:18). What does Ruth’s determination show us about loyalty?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Loyalty is more than a kind feeling. Ruth had made up her mind to go, and she would not turn back, even though Naomi had urged her to.
dailies.action: Read Ruth 1:16–18 together. Then walk across the room beside someone and say, in your own words, that you will go with them and not turn back.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” Thank you that she was determined to go with Naomi, and that she would not turn back. Help us stay faithful to you and to the people you have given us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Naomi had urged Ruth to turn back. In our words, Naomi’s life had been very sad, and we say that simply. Ruth would not leave her. She said that where Naomi went, she would go, and that Naomi’s people would be her people, and Naomi’s God her God. When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined, she stopped urging her.
dailies.enochActivity: Walk beside someone and say: I will go with you!
dailies.elijah2: What did Ruth say about death and burial, and about the LORD dealing with her?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: She said, Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me (Ruth 1:17).
dailies.jordyn2: Ruth’s words go all the way to death and burial (Ruth 1:17). How should we hear a vow like this, without making it a game or a light promise?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We hear it as a solemn, faithful yes. Ruth was binding her life to Naomi’s, under the LORD. We do not play at vows. We can practice a smaller faithfulness: staying with someone, and not turning back when it would be easier to leave.
dailies.passageText: 16 But Ruth replied, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. 17 Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” 18 When Naomi realized that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Ruth stayed close to Naomi, and later she gleaned leftover grain in Boaz’s field. Loyalty and kindness can be practiced in small steps.
dailies.verse: “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.”
dailies.enoch: Pick up one small thing and share it!
dailies.elijah: What did Ruth ask Naomi, and what did Naomi say?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Ruth said, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said to her, “Go ahead, my daughter.” (Ruth 2:2).
dailies.jordyn: As it turned out, Ruth was working in a field belonging to Boaz (Ruth 2:3). How can gathering leftovers in this story help us think about kindness, without turning hard parts of the story into play?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Ruth went out to work and to gather what was left, so her family could have food. Kindness later meets her there. A simple gathering game can remind us of her work and of God’s care. We do not act out sadness or marriage. We practice noticing and sharing.
dailies.action: Play a gentle two-part game. First, walk side by side across the room and say, I will go with you. Then scatter a few soft items, pick them up, and share them, the way Ruth gleaned leftover grain. Keep the game kind. Do not act out loss, and do not play at being married.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Ruth said, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Thank you that she stayed close to Naomi, and that you were already providing. Help us stay close, and help us share. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Ruth would not turn back from Naomi. Then she asked to go and pick up leftover grain, and she happened to work in Boaz’s field. Today’s game is a loyal walk and a kind gather, not a play of harm or of grown-up romance.
dailies.enochActivity: Walk beside someone, then pick up one item and share it!
dailies.elijah2: Whose field was Ruth in, and how is Boaz described at the start of the chapter?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: As it turned out, she was working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelek. Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a man of standing from that clan, whose name was Boaz (Ruth 2:1, 3).
dailies.jordyn2: Ruth went out to glean, and as it turned out, she was in Boaz’s field (Ruth 2:3). What does as it turned out help us notice about God’s kindness, without adding official words from later chapters?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The reading does not yet explain every step. It simply says that as it turned out, she was in the field of a relative who could help. We can thank God that he was already kindly providing, even while Ruth was just going out to work.
dailies.passageText: 16 But Ruth replied, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. 17 Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” 18 When Naomi realized that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her. 1 Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a man of standing from the clan of Elimelek, whose name was Boaz. 2 And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said to her, “Go ahead, my daughter.” 3 So she went out, entered a field and began to glean behind the harvesters. As it turned out, she was working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelek.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Boaz noticed Ruth, kept her safe, and asked the LORD to repay her. She had taken refuge under the LORD’s wings.
dailies.verse: May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say: The LORD be with you!
dailies.elijah: How did Boaz greet the harvesters, and how did they answer?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Boaz greeted them, “The LORD be with you!” “The LORD bless you!” they answered (Ruth 2:4).
dailies.jordyn: What did Boaz tell Ruth to do, and what had he told the men? What did he say the LORD could do for her?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He said, “My daughter, listen to me. Don’t go and glean in another field and don’t go away from here. Stay here with the women who work for me. Watch the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after the women. I have told the men not to lay a hand on you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.” And he said, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” (Ruth 2:8–12).
dailies.action: Read Ruth 2:1–12 together. Then greet someone in the house with Boaz’s words, “The LORD be with you!” and let them answer, “The LORD bless you!”
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Boaz said, “The LORD be with you!” and that the harvesters answered, “The LORD bless you!” Thank you that he cared for Ruth, and that he said she had come to take refuge under your wings. Help us notice people, and help us be kind. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Ruth gleaned in Boaz’s field. Boaz asked who she was, and he spoke to her with care. He told her to stay with the women who worked for him, and he made a way for her to be safe and to have water. Ruth asked why she had found favor, since she was a foreigner. Boaz had heard how she had stayed with Naomi since the death of her husband, and he asked the LORD to repay her. She had come to take refuge under the LORD’s wings.
dailies.enochActivity: Wave a small hello and say: The LORD be with you!
dailies.elijah2: What did Ruth ask Boaz after she bowed with her face to the ground?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: She asked him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me—a foreigner?” (Ruth 2:10).
dailies.jordyn2: Boaz had been told what Ruth had done for her mother-in-law since the death of her husband, and he said she had come to take refuge under the LORD’s wings (Ruth 2:11–12). How does noticing someone’s faithfulness become a way of showing God’s kindness?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Boaz did not ignore her. He had heard the truth about her loyalty, and he answered with favor, protection, and a blessing in the LORD’s name. God’s kindness often comes through someone who notices and then acts.
dailies.passageText: 1 Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a man of standing from the clan of Elimelek, whose name was Boaz. 2 And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said to her, “Go ahead, my daughter.” 3 So she went out, entered a field and began to glean behind the harvesters. As it turned out, she was working in a field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelek. 4 Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and greeted the harvesters, “The LORD be with you!” “The LORD bless you!” they answered. 5 Boaz asked the overseer of his harvesters, “Who does that young woman belong to?” 6 The overseer replied, “She is the Moabite who came back from Moab with Naomi. 7 She said, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the harvesters.’ She came into the field and has remained here from morning till now, except for a short rest in the shelter.” 8 So Boaz said to Ruth, “My daughter, listen to me. Don’t go and glean in another field and don’t go away from here. Stay here with the women who work for me. 9 Watch the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after the women. I have told the men not to lay a hand on you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.” 10 At this, she bowed down with her face to the ground. She asked him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me—a foreigner?” 11 Boaz replied, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. 12 May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Ruth stayed faithful, and Boaz showed kindness. Practice one loyal step and one kind notice this week.
dailies.verse: “Go ahead, my daughter.”
dailies.enoch: Do one kind thing for someone in your house.
dailies.elijah: What had Boaz been told about Ruth, and what blessing did he speak?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He said, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” (Ruth 2:11–12).
dailies.jordyn: Ruth left her father and mother and her homeland and came to live with a people she did not know before (Ruth 2:11). What is one loyal step you can take this week that costs you something small, the way her faithfulness cost her the familiar?
dailies.jordynAnswer: It could be staying close to someone who needs you, finishing a hard helpful job, or not turning back from a promise. Loyalty is shown in what we keep doing, not only in what we feel.
dailies.action: Choose one person to stay close to today, and one kind thing to notice and do for them, the way Ruth stayed with Naomi and Boaz noticed Ruth.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Ruth stayed faithful, and that Boaz noticed what she had done. Thank you that she took refuge under your wings. Help us stay faithful, and help us show kindness on purpose. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Ruth had stayed with Naomi. Boaz noticed, protected, and blessed her in the LORD’s name. Today’s challenge is a real loyalty and a real kindness, not a skit of the later wedding or of anyone’s loss.
dailies.enochActivity: Do one kind thing and say: God is kind!
dailies.elijah2: What did Boaz tell Ruth about water, and about staying in his field?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He told her not to glean in another field and not to go away, but to stay with the women who worked for him. And whenever she was thirsty, she could get a drink from the water jars the men had filled (Ruth 2:8–9).
dailies.jordyn2: Ruth asked why she, a foreigner, had found favor (Ruth 2:10). How can a family practice that kind of favor toward someone who might feel left out, without pretending we can do all that God did in this story?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can notice, make room, and speak kindly, as Boaz did. We cannot make ourselves the LORD. We can take refuge under his wings, and we can be one way his kindness is seen.
dailies.passageText: 8 So Boaz said to Ruth, “My daughter, listen to me. Don’t go and glean in another field and don’t go away from here. Stay here with the women who work for me. 9 Watch the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after the women. I have told the men not to lay a hand on you. And whenever you are thirsty, go and get a drink from the water jars the men have filled.” 10 At this, she bowed down with her face to the ground. She asked him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you notice me—a foreigner?” 11 Boaz replied, “I’ve been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband—how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. 12 May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that Ruth stayed faithful, that she took refuge under his wings, and that he kindly provided a son and a future.
dailies.verse: May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God, for your kindness!
dailies.elijah: What did the women say to Naomi after the son was born, and what did they call Ruth?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They said, “Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel! He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” (Ruth 4:14–15).
dailies.jordyn: Naomi took the child in her arms and cared for him, and the women said, “Naomi has a son!” They named him Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:16–17). How can this ending shape the way we pray?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We thank God that he did not leave Naomi without help, and that his kindness reached into the future, even to David. We can ask him to help us stay faithful and to take refuge under his wings.
dailies.action: Pray the family prayer slowly. When you hear under whose wings you have come to take refuge, pause and thank God that he kindly provides.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” Thank you that you did not leave Naomi without a guardian-redeemer, and that Ruth, who loved her, was better to her than seven sons. Thank you that Naomi took the child in her arms, and that Obed was the father of Jesse, the father of David. You kindly provided. Help us take refuge under your wings. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we pray with Ruth’s loyalty and God’s kindness in our ears. Ruth would not turn back. She took refuge under the LORD’s wings. Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. The LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. We say that simply. The women praised the LORD, Naomi cared for the child, and they named him Obed, in the line of David.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah2: What did the women living there say, and whom did they name?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They said, “Naomi has a son!” And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17).
dailies.jordyn2: The women praised the LORD, who had not left Naomi without a guardian-redeemer (Ruth 4:14). How can we pray that praise without skipping the sad beginning of the story?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We remember, simply, that Naomi had known great loss, and we do not make a game of it. Then we praise the LORD because he did not leave her, and because Ruth’s love and God’s kindness met in the gift of this child and this future.
dailies.passageText: 12 May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” 13 So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife. When he made love to her, the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. 14 The women said to Naomi: “Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel! 15 He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” 16 Then Naomi took the child in her arms and cared for him. 17 The women living there said, “Naomi has a son!” And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family. Next, David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.
dailies.verse: And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward the next room and say: Next week, David trusted the Lord!
dailies.elijah: What is this week’s big idea, and can you tell the story from Ruth’s vow to the birth of Obed?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family. Ruth would not turn back from Naomi. She gleaned in Boaz’s field, and Boaz showed her kindness and said she had taken refuge under the LORD’s wings. Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. The LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. They named him Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David.
dailies.jordyn: We have seen that Ruth stayed faithful, and that God kindly provided for her family. The story ends with David in the family line. Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. What stays the same about God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God is kind, and he can be trusted. He provided for Ruth and Naomi, and he was already at work in the family line that leads to David. Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. The same God kindly provides, and he is worthy of trust.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Ruth stayed faithful, and God kindly provided for her family. Then look ahead to David, who trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Ruth stayed faithful, and that you kindly provided for her family. Thank you that Obed was the father of Jesse, the father of David. Get our hearts ready to hear that David trusted you, not his own size or strength. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we heard Ruth refuse to turn back from Naomi, glean in Boaz’s field, and take refuge under the LORD’s wings. God kindly provided a family and a future, all the way to David. Next week we will hear that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.
dailies.enochActivity: Wave a small hello toward tomorrow and say: David trusted the Lord!
dailies.elijah2: What blessing did Boaz speak, and how does the story reach David?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Boaz said, May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge. They named the son Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 2:12; 4:17).
dailies.jordyn2: The book of Ruth ends with David’s name, and next week David will trust the Lord instead of his own size or strength. What should we carry from Ruth into that story?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should remember that God kindly provides, and that people can take refuge under his wings. Loyalty and kindness belong in his work. The same God who provided for Ruth’s family is the Lord David will trust.

Your people will be my people and your God my God. 17 Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.” 2 And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Let me go to the fields and pick up the leftover grain behind anyone in whose eyes I find favor.” Naomi said to her, “Go ahead, my daughter.” 12 May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.” 13 So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife. When he made love to her, the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. 14 The women said to Naomi: “Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. readings.text: 32 David said to Saul, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” 33 Saul replied, “You are not able to go out against this Philistine and fight him; you are only a young man, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” 34 But David said to Saul, “Your servant has been keeping his father’s sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a sheep from the flock, 35 I went after it, struck it and rescued the sheep from its mouth. When it turned on me, I seized it by its hair, struck it and killed it. 36 Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has defied the armies of the living God. 37 The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go, and the LORD be with you.”

38 Then Saul dressed David in his own tunic. He put a coat of armor on him and a bronze helmet on his head. 39 David fastened on his sword over the tunic and tried walking around, because he was not used to them. “I cannot go in these,” he said to Saul, “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off. 40 Then he took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the stream, put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag and, with his sling in his hand, approached the Philistine. 41 Meanwhile, the Philistine, with his shield bearer in front of him, kept coming closer to David. 42 He looked David over and saw that he was little more than a boy, glowing with health and handsome, and he despised him. 43 He said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. 44 “Come here,” he said, “and I’ll give your flesh to the birds and the wild animals!” 45 David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. 46 This day the LORD will deliver you into my hands, and I’ll strike you down and cut off your head. This very day I will give the carcasses of the Philistine army to the birds and the wild animals, and the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel. 47 All those gathered here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give all of you into our hands.”

48 As the Philistine moved closer to attack him, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him. 49 Reaching into his bag and taking out a stone, he slung it and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground. 50 So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him.

story: Last week we learned that Ruth stayed faithful, and that God kindly provided for her family. The story ended with Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David. Today we hear about that David, who trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.

We do not leave today’s reading to tell the earlier verses as official text. In our words, a great Philistine warrior had been challenging Israel, and many people were afraid. We say that simply. Then David said to Saul, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” Saul replied, “You are not able to go out against this Philistine and fight him; you are only a young man, and he has been a warrior from his youth.”

David told Saul that he had been keeping his father’s sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a sheep, he went after it and rescued the sheep. We say the danger simply, and with care. It is not a scene to act out or to linger on. David said that the LORD who rescued him from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear would rescue him from the hand of this Philistine. Saul said to David, “Go, and the LORD be with you.”

Then Saul dressed David in his own tunic, with a coat of armor and a bronze helmet. David tried walking around, because he was not used to them. “I cannot go in these,” he said to Saul, “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off. Then he took his staff, chose five smooth stones from the stream, put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag and, with his sling in his hand, approached the Philistine.

The Philistine came closer, looked David over, and despised him, because he saw that he was little more than a boy. He spoke proudly and threatened David. We hear the boast simply, and we do not make a game of it. David did not trust his own size or strength. He came in the name of the LORD Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel. He said the whole world would know that there is a God in Israel, and that all those gathered there would know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s.

As the Philistine moved closer, David ran quickly toward the battle line. He took a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The Philistine fell facedown on the ground. So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him. We say the fight simply, and with care. We do not make a game of hurting anyone. David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.
Next week we will hear that God used Esther’s courage to save her people.
weeks.enochLine: David trusted the Lord, not his own size!
enochActivities: Activity: Take off a too-big coat, if you have one, and say: I trust the Lord!

elijahQuestions: In 1 Samuel 17:32–33, what did David say to Saul about losing heart, and what did Saul say about David?
In 1 Samuel 17:37, what did David say the LORD who rescued him would do, and what did Saul then say to David?
In 1 Samuel 17:38–40, what happened when David tried Saul’s armor, and what did David take instead?
In 1 Samuel 17:47–50, what did David want all those gathered to know, and how did he triumph over the Philistine?
elijahAnswers: David said, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” Saul replied, “You are not able to go out against this Philistine and fight him; you are only a young man, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” (1 Samuel 17:32–33).

David said that the LORD who rescued him from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear would rescue him from the hand of this Philistine. Saul said to David, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” (1 Samuel 17:37).

Saul dressed David in his own tunic, armor, and a bronze helmet. David tried walking around, because he was not used to them. “I cannot go in these,” he said to Saul, “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off. Then he took his staff, chose five smooth stones from the stream, and, with his sling in his hand, approached the Philistine (1 Samuel 17:38–40).

David said that all those gathered would know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give all of you into our hands. David ran toward the battle line, slung a stone, and struck the Philistine on the forehead, and he fell facedown. So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him. We say that simply (1 Samuel 17:47–50).
jordynQuestions: Saul said, “You are not able to go out against this Philistine and fight him; you are only a young man, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” (1 Samuel 17:33). David answered that the LORD who had rescued him from the lion and the bear would rescue him from this Philistine (1 Samuel 17:37). What does this show about trusting the Lord instead of your own size or strength?

David would not go in Saul’s armor. He said it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s (1 Samuel 17:39, 47). How should we hear the fight that follows, without turning it into a game?
David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. Next week we will hear that God used Esther’s courage to save her people. What stays the same about God?
jordynAnswers: Saul looked at David’s youth and at the Philistine’s long years as a warrior. David looked at the LORD who had already rescued him. Trust is not pretending you are big. It is depending on the living God, who saves his people, even when you feel small.

We tell the truth: David ran to meet the Philistine, a stone struck him, he fell, and David triumphed. We say that simply, and with care. We do not act out the blows, or make a game of killing. The point is not how strong David’s arm was. The point is that the battle is the LORD’s, and David trusted him.

God can be trusted, and he saves his people. He helped David when size and armor were not the point, and next week we will hear that he used Esther’s courage to save her people. The same Lord is worthy of trust.
weeks.jordynApplication: David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength (1 Samuel 17:32–50). This week, when something feels too big, tell the Lord that the battle is his, and take one small faithful step without trying to look stronger than you are. Next week we will hear that God used Esther’s courage to save her people.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week where she chose to trust the Lord instead of her own size or strength. If it is fitting, thank God together that the battle is the LORD’s, and that David trusted him.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that David said, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” Thank you that Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” Thank you that David would not go in armor he was not used to, and that he trusted you, not his own size or strength. You save, not by sword or spear; the battle is yours. Help us trust you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: David was willing to go and fight, because he trusted the LORD who had already rescued him, not his own size.
dailies.verse: Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say with you: Let no one lose heart!
dailies.elijah: What did David say to Saul about losing heart, and what did he say he would do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He said, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” (1 Samuel 17:32).
dailies.jordyn: Saul said David was only a young man, and that the Philistine had been a warrior from his youth (1 Samuel 17:33). How does David’s answer in 1 Samuel 17:37 meet that fear?
dailies.jordynAnswer: David did not argue that he was bigger than he looked. He said that the LORD who rescued him from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear would rescue him from the hand of this Philistine. Then Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.”
dailies.action: Read 1 Samuel 17:32–37 together. Then say, in your own words, that you can trust the Lord even when you feel small.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that David said, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” Thank you that he trusted you to rescue him, and that Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” Help us trust you, not our own size. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: In our words, a great Philistine warrior had been challenging Israel, and many people were afraid. We do not leave today’s reading to tell those earlier verses as official text. David said, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” Saul thought David was too young. David told him about keeping sheep, and about the Lord who had already rescued him from a lion and a bear. We say that simply. The LORD who rescued him would rescue him again. Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.”
dailies.enochActivity: Say with a grown-up: I trust the Lord!
dailies.elijah2: What had David been doing for his father, and what did he say the LORD had done and would do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He had been keeping his father’s sheep. He said that the LORD who rescued him from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear would rescue him from the hand of this Philistine (1 Samuel 17:34–37).
dailies.jordyn2: David had already seen the LORD rescue him while he kept sheep (1 Samuel 17:34–37). Why does that matter when Saul looks only at David’s youth?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Past rescue teaches present trust. David did not trust his own size. He trusted the same LORD who had already helped him. We can remember how the Lord has helped us, and trust him again, without pretending we are strong in ourselves.
dailies.passageText: 32 David said to Saul, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” 33 Saul replied, “You are not able to go out against this Philistine and fight him; you are only a young man, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” 34 But David said to Saul, “Your servant has been keeping his father’s sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a sheep from the flock, 35 I went after it, struck it and rescued the sheep from its mouth. When it turned on me, I seized it by its hair, struck it and killed it. 36 Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has defied the armies of the living God. 37 The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go, and the LORD be with you.”

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Saul’s armor did not fit David. David took it off and went with a staff, five smooth stones, and a sling, trusting the Lord.
dailies.verse: I cannot go in these, because I am not used to them.
dailies.enoch: If a grown-up has a too-big coat, try it on, take it off, and say: I cannot go in these!
dailies.elijah: What did David say when he tried Saul’s armor, and what did he do next?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “I cannot go in these,” he said to Saul, “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off (1 Samuel 17:39).
dailies.jordyn: David chose five smooth stones from the stream and approached the Philistine with his sling (1 Samuel 17:40). What does this show about trusting the Lord instead of borrowed armor?
dailies.jordynAnswer: David did not pretend the armor made him ready. He could not go in what he was not used to. He went as a shepherd who trusted the LORD, not as someone trying to look like Saul.
dailies.action: If it is safe and kind, try on a coat that is too big, walk a few steps, take it off, and say, “I cannot go in these,” Then pick up five small safe objects and set them down again. Do not swing them, and do not aim at anyone.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that David said, “I cannot go in these,” “because I am not used to them.” Thank you that he took the armor off and trusted you. Help us not to put on a false strength. Help us trust you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Saul dressed David in his own tunic, a coat of armor, and a bronze helmet. David tried walking around, because he was not used to them. He said, “I cannot go in these,” “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off. Then he took his staff, chose five smooth stones from the stream, and approached the Philistine with his sling. We practice the too-big coat and the five stones as a remembering game, not as a fight.
dailies.enochActivity: Take off a too-big coat, if you have one, and say: I trust the Lord!
dailies.elijah2: What did Saul put on David, and why did David take it off?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Saul put his own tunic on David, a coat of armor, and a bronze helmet. David fastened on the sword and tried walking around, because he was not used to them. He said, “I cannot go in these,” “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off (1 Samuel 17:38–39).
dailies.jordyn2: This game is about taking off armor that does not belong to you. How do we keep it from becoming a pretend battle?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We do not aim stones, swing a staff at anyone, or act out a fight. We remember that David could not go in Saul’s armor, and that he trusted the Lord. The five stones help us count and remember, not to practice harm.
dailies.passageText: 38 Then Saul dressed David in his own tunic. He put a coat of armor on him and a bronze helmet on his head. 39 David fastened on his sword over the tunic and tried walking around, because he was not used to them. “I cannot go in these,” he said to Saul, “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off. 40 Then he took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the stream, put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag and, with his sling in his hand, approached the Philistine.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: The Philistine despised David for looking small, but David came in the name of the LORD, because the battle is the LORD’s.
dailies.verse: It is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give all of you into our hands.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say with you: The battle is the Lord’s!
dailies.elijah: What did the Philistine think when he looked David over, and whose name did David come in?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He saw that David was little more than a boy, glowing with health and handsome, and he despised him. David came against him in the name of the LORD Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel, whom the Philistine had defied (1 Samuel 17:42, 45).
dailies.jordyn: David said the whole world would know that there is a God in Israel, and that all those gathered would know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s (1 Samuel 17:46–47). What is David trusting, if not sword, spear, or his own size?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He is trusting the LORD Almighty. Size, armor, sword, and spear are not what save. The battle is the LORD’s, and David wanted everyone to know that there is a God in Israel.
dailies.action: Read 1 Samuel 17:38–47 together. Then say, in your own words, that the battle is the Lord’s, and that we do not trust our own size.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that David came in the name of the LORD Almighty, and that he said it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s. Help us trust you when we feel small. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: David took off Saul’s armor and approached the Philistine with a staff, five stones, and a sling. The Philistine came closer, looked at David, and despised him for looking like little more than a boy. He spoke proudly and threatened him. We hear that simply, and we do not repeat the threat as a game. David answered that he came in the name of the LORD Almighty, that the whole world would know there is a God in Israel, and that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s.
dailies.enochActivity: Say: The battle is the Lord’s!
dailies.elijah2: What did David say all those gathered would know?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He said that all those gathered here would know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give all of you into our hands (1 Samuel 17:47).
dailies.jordyn2: The Philistine cursed David by his gods and spoke a cruel threat (1 Samuel 17:43–44). How should we hear those words, and David’s answer, with dignity?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We do not make a game of curses or of harm. We notice the pride that despises a young person, and we notice David’s trust: he came in the name of the LORD Almighty, so that people would know there is a God in Israel, and that the battle is the LORD’s.
dailies.passageText: 38 Then Saul dressed David in his own tunic. He put a coat of armor on him and a bronze helmet on his head. 39 David fastened on his sword over the tunic and tried walking around, because he was not used to them. “I cannot go in these,” he said to Saul, “because I am not used to them.” So he took them off. 40 Then he took his staff in his hand, chose five smooth stones from the stream, put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag and, with his sling in his hand, approached the Philistine. 41 Meanwhile, the Philistine, with his shield bearer in front of him, kept coming closer to David. 42 He looked David over and saw that he was little more than a boy, glowing with health and handsome, and he despised him. 43 He said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. 44 “Come here,” he said, “and I’ll give your flesh to the birds and the wild animals!” 45 David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. 46 This day the LORD will deliver you into my hands, and I’ll strike you down and cut off your head. This very day I will give the carcasses of the Philistine army to the birds and the wild animals, and the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel. 47 All those gathered here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give all of you into our hands.”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: David ran toward the battle line and trusted the Lord. He triumphed, not because he was the biggest, but because the battle was the LORD’s.
dailies.verse: So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up take one brave step forward and say: I trust the Lord!
dailies.elijah: What did David do as the Philistine moved closer, and what happened when he slung the stone?
dailies.elijahAnswer: David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him. He took a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The Philistine fell facedown on the ground (1 Samuel 17:48–49).
dailies.jordyn: The writer says David triumphed with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him (1 Samuel 17:50). How do we tell this truth without turning it into a violent game?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We tell it simply, and with care. David trusted the Lord, ran to meet the danger, and the Lord saved Israel that day. We do not act out the blow or celebrate harm. We thank God that the battle is the LORD’s, and we practice trust in the small hard things in front of us.
dailies.action: Name one thing that feels bigger than you this week. Tell the Lord that the battle is his, then take one small faithful step—a chore, a kind word, or a hard thing you have been putting off. Do not pretend to fight a person.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that David ran toward the battle line and trusted you. Thank you that he triumphed with a sling and a stone, and that the battle is yours. Help us trust you in the thing that feels too big, without making a game of harm. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: As the Philistine moved closer to attack, David ran quickly toward the battle line. He took a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead, and he fell facedown. So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him. We say this simply. Today’s challenge is to trust the Lord in one real thing, not to act out a fight.
dailies.enochActivity: Take one step forward and say: I trust the Lord!
dailies.elijah2: How does 1 Samuel 17:50 describe David’s triumph?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him (1 Samuel 17:50).
dailies.jordyn2: David had said it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves (1 Samuel 17:47), and then he triumphed without a sword in his hand (1 Samuel 17:50). What should we carry from that into a hard thing this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should not put our trust in looking strong, or in tools that make us feel big. We should trust the Lord, tell the truth about the hard thing, and take a faithful step. The victory in this story belongs to the LORD, not to a boast in our own strength.
dailies.passageText: 48 As the Philistine moved closer to attack him, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him. 49 Reaching into his bag and taking out a stone, he slung it and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground. 50 So David triumphed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: We thank God that David trusted him, and we ask for the same trust when we feel small.
dailies.verse: Go, and the LORD be with you.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God. Help us trust you!
dailies.elijah: What did Saul say to David after David trusted the LORD to rescue him?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Saul said to David, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” (1 Samuel 17:37).
dailies.jordyn: David wanted all those gathered to know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s (1 Samuel 17:47). How can that shape a family prayer?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can thank God that he saves, and we can hand him the things that feel too big. We ask him to help us trust him, not our own size or strength, and we do not turn the fight into a game in our prayers.
dailies.action: Pray the family prayer slowly. When you hear, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” pause and ask the Lord to go with you into one thing that feels too big.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that David said, “Let no one lose heart on account of this Philistine; your servant will go and fight him.” Thank you that Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” Thank you that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is yours. Help us trust you, not our own size or strength. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we pray with David’s trust in our ears. He was willing to go, because the LORD had already rescued him. Saul said, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” David later said that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s. We thank God, and we ask for that same trust.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands and say: Help us trust you!
dailies.elijah2: What did David say the LORD who rescued him from the lion and the bear would do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He said the LORD who rescued him from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear would rescue him from the hand of this Philistine (1 Samuel 17:37).
dailies.jordyn2: How can we pray about a hard thing without asking God to make us look big?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can tell him the truth, thank him that the battle is his, and ask him to help us trust him and take a faithful step. We do not need to sound brave. We need to depend on him, as David did.
dailies.passageText: 37 The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go, and the LORD be with you.” 47 All those gathered here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give all of you into our hands.”

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. Next, God used Esther’s courage to save her people.
dailies.verse: David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength.

dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. Then look ahead to Esther, whose courage God used to save her people.

dailies.jordyn2: The book of Ruth ended with David’s name, and this week David trusted the Lord. Next week God will use Esther’s courage to save her people. What should we carry from David into that story?

readings.text: 10 Then she instructed him to say to Mordecai, 11 “All the king’s officials and the people of the royal provinces know that for any man or woman who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned the king has but one law: that they be put to death unless the king extends the gold scepter to them and spares their lives. But thirty days have passed since I was called to go to the king.” 12 When Esther’s words were reported to Mordecai, 13 he sent back this answer: “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. 14 For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?” 15 Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: 16 “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.”

1 So the king and Haman went to Queen Esther’s banquet, 2 and as they were drinking wine on the second day, the king again asked, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be granted.” 3 Then Queen Esther answered, “If I have found favor with you, Your Majesty, and if it pleases you, grant me my life—this is my petition. And spare my people—this is my request. 4 For I and my people have been sold to be destroyed, killed and annihilated. If we had merely been sold as male and female slaves, I would have kept quiet, because no such distress would justify disturbing the king.” 5 King Xerxes asked Queen Esther, “Who is he? Where is he—the man who has dared to do such a thing?” 6 Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen.

story: Last week we learned that David trusted the Lord, not his own size or strength. Today we hear that God used Esther’s courage to save her people.

We do not leave today’s readings to tell the earlier verses as official text. In our words, Esther was queen, and her people were in great danger. Someone wanted to destroy them. We say that simply, and with care. It is not a scene to act out or to linger on.

Esther sent word to Mordecai. She said that anyone who went to the king in the inner court without being called could be put to death, unless the king held out the gold scepter and spared their life, and that thirty days had passed since she was called to go to the king. We hear the danger simply. Mordecai sent back this answer: “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?”

Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” We hear her words solemnly. This is not a game about dying. Esther chose to go, and she asked her people to fast with her.

Later, the king and Haman went to Queen Esther’s banquet. The king asked, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be granted.” Esther asked him to grant her life, and to spare her people. She told him that she and her people had been sold to be destroyed. We say that simply, and with care. The king asked, “Who is he? Where is he—the man who has dared to do such a thing?” Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen.
We do not leave today’s readings to tell the later verses as official text. In our words, God used Esther’s courage to save her people. She did not remain silent. She went, and she told the truth.
Next week we will hear that Daniel kept praying to God, and that God shut the lions’ mouths.
weeks.enochLine: God used Esther's courage to help her people!
enochActivities: Activity: Walk to a doorway, pause, then go through and say: I will be brave!
Activity: Tell one true thing to help someone, the way Esther told the truth.
elijahQuestions: In Esther 4:13–14, what did Mordecai tell Esther not to think, and what did he say about her royal position?
In Esther 4:16, what did Esther ask the Jews in Susa to do, and what did she say she would do?
In Esther 7:2–3, what did the king ask Esther, and what petition and request did she name?
In Esther 7:5–6, what did the king ask, and what did Esther say about Haman?
elijahAnswers: He said, “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:13–14).

She said, “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” (Esther 4:16).

The king asked, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be granted.” Esther asked him to grant her life—this was her petition—and to spare her people—this was her request (Esther 7:2–3).

The king asked, “Who is he? Where is he—the man who has dared to do such a thing?” Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen (Esther 7:5–6).
jordynQuestions: Mordecai said that if Esther remained silent, relief and deliverance for the Jews would arise from another place, and he asked, who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this? (Esther 4:14). What does this show about courage, and about remaining silent?

Esther said she would go to the king, even though it was against the law, and if I perish, I perish (Esther 4:16). At the banquet she asked the king to spare her life and her people, and she named Haman (Esther 7:3–6). How should we hear this courage without making a game of danger or of dying?
God used Esther’s courage to save her people. Next week we will hear that Daniel kept praying to God, and that God shut the lions’ mouths. What stays the same about God?
jordynAnswers: Courage is not loud talk. It is refusing to stay silent when people are in danger and you have a chance to speak. Mordecai did not say Esther was the only hope. Deliverance could arise from another place. But she had been placed where she was for such a time as this, and silence would still cost her. The brave thing was to go and tell the truth.

We tell the truth: it was dangerous to go, Esther fasted, she went, and she asked the king to spare her people. We say the danger simply, and with care. We do not act out perishing, or make a villain game out of Haman. We honor a solemn yes: she would go, and God used that courage to save her people.

God can be trusted, and he can save his people. He used Esther’s courage, and next week we will hear that Daniel kept praying, and that God shut the lions’ mouths. The same God is able to help, and he is worthy of trust and courage.
weeks.jordynApplication: God used Esther’s courage to save her people (Esther 4:10–16; 7:1–6). This week, when it would be easier to remain silent, tell the truth in a careful way that helps someone, and remember that God can use courage in such a time as this. Next week we will hear that Daniel kept praying to God, and that God shut the lions’ mouths.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week where she chose to speak up instead of remaining silent. If it is fitting, thank God together that he used Esther’s courage to save her people.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Mordecai said, “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?” Thank you that Esther said, “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” Thank you that she asked the king to spare her people, and that she told the truth about Haman. You used her courage to save her people. Help us not to remain silent when we should speak, and give us courage in such a time as this. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Mordecai told Esther not to remain silent, and he asked who knows but that she had come to her royal position for such a time as this.
dailies.verse: And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say with you: I will not stay silent!
dailies.elijah: What did Mordecai tell Esther not to think, and what did he say about relief and deliverance?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He said, “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. dailies.jordyn: Esther had sent word that going to the king uninvited could mean death, unless the king extended the gold scepter (Esther 4:11). How does Mordecai’s answer call her to courage without making the danger into a game?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He told the truth about the danger, and he also said that deliverance could arise from another place. He asked her to see her place as a time to act, not a place to hide. We hear the danger simply, and we practice courage by not remaining silent when someone needs help.
dailies.action: Read Esther 4:10–16 together. Then say, in your own words, that you will not remain silent when someone needs you to tell the truth.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Mordecai said, “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.enochActivity: Say with a grown-up: I will be brave!

dailies.elijahAnswer2: She said, “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. dailies.jordyn2: Esther chose to go even though it was against the law, and she said, if I perish, I perish (Esther 4:16). What kind of courage is this?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: It is a quiet, costly yes, not a show. She asked others to fast with her, and she would go to the king. We honor that solemn choice. We do not play at perishing. We can practice a smaller courage: telling the truth when silence would be easier.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Esther did not remain silent. She asked her people to gather and fast, and she got ready to go and tell the truth.
dailies.verse: Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me.
dailies.enoch: Walk to a doorway, pause, then go through and say: I will go and tell the truth!
dailies.elijah: What did Esther tell Mordecai to have the Jews in Susa do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: She said, “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” (Esther 4:16).
dailies.jordyn: This game is about getting ready to go and tell the truth, not about pretending to be in danger. How do we keep it kind and serious?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not act out going to a king to die, or make a game of fasting until it hurts. We practice a small pause, then a brave step, and we remember that Esther asked her people to gather and that she would go and speak.
dailies.action: Walk to a doorway, pause like someone getting ready, then go through and say, in your own words, that you will tell the truth. If you like, sit quietly for one short minute first, the way Esther asked her people to stop and fast, then stand and go. Do not pretend to perish.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Esther said, “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” Thank you that she would go, and that she asked her people to gather and fast. Help us get ready to tell the truth, and give us courage. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: “Go, gather together all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast as you do. When this is done, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” Today we practice getting ready and going, not a fight and not a death scene. A pause at the door can help us remember her courage.
dailies.enochActivity: Walk to a door, then go through and say: I will be brave!
dailies.elijah2: What did Esther say she and her attendants would do, and when would she go to the king?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: She said she and her attendants would fast as the Jews in Susa did. When this was done, she would go to the king, even though it was against the law. And if I perish, I perish (Esther 4:16).
dailies.jordyn2: Why is a doorway a better practice than acting out the palace law or the words if I perish, I perish?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The palace law was a real danger, and Esther’s words were solemn. We should not turn them into play. A doorway lets us practice pausing, then going to tell the truth, which is the courage we can actually use today.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: At the banquet, Esther asked the king to spare her life and her people, and she told the truth about Haman.
dailies.verse: Grant me my life—this is my petition. And spare my people—this is my request.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say with you: Spare my people!
dailies.elijah: What did the king ask Esther at the banquet, and what did she ask for?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The king asked, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be granted.” Esther asked him to grant her life—this was her petition—and to spare her people—this was her request (Esther 7:2–3).
