dailies.jordynAnswer: Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen (Esther 7:5–6). We tell that simply. We do not make a mocking game of Haman.
dailies.action: Read Esther 7:1–6 together. Then say, in your own words, that Esther asked the king to spare her people, and that she told the truth.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the king asked, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be granted.” Thank you that Esther asked him to grant her life and to spare her people, and that she said, “An adversary and enemy! dailies.teach: The king and Haman went to Queen Esther’s banquet. The king asked what she wanted. Esther asked him to grant her life and to spare her people, because they had been sold to be destroyed. We say that simply, and with care. The king asked who had dared to do such a thing. Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” Then Haman was terrified.
dailies.enochActivity: Say: Spare my people! I will tell the truth!
dailies.elijah2: What reason did Esther give for her petition, in Esther 7:3–4, and how should we hear those words?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: She asked the king to grant her life and to spare her people, and she said that she and her people had been sold to be destroyed, killed and annihilated. We say that simply, and with care. It is not a scene to act out (Esther 7:3–4).
dailies.jordyn2: Esther waited until the banquet to speak, and then she told the truth plainly. What can we learn about courage from the way she spoke?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Courage can be careful and clear at the same time. She honored the king, she asked for her life and her people, and she named the one who was harming them. We can tell the truth without shouting, and without making a game of someone’s fear.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Esther did not remain silent. God used her courage to save her people. Today we practice a careful, truthful word that helps someone.
dailies.verse: For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up think of one kind true word, then say it out loud!
dailies.elijah: What did Mordecai say would happen if Esther remained silent, and what question did he ask about her royal position?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He said, “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:13–14).
dailies.jordyn: Esther went to the king and asked him to spare her people (Esther 7:3). What is today’s challenge, and what is it not?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The challenge is to speak one careful true word that helps a person, when it would be easier to remain silent. It is not a dare, and it is not a game about danger or dying. It is ordinary courage: telling the truth in love.
dailies.action: Name one place where silence would be easier—a kindness left unsaid, a true word that would help a sibling, or a grown-up who needs to know something important. Then, with care, say that word, or ask a grown-up to help you say it. Do not use this as a chance to accuse someone harshly.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Esther did not remain silent, and that you used her courage to save her people. Help us tell the truth this week in a careful way that helps someone. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Mordecai warned Esther not to remain silent, and he asked who knows but that she had come to her royal position for such a time as this. At the banquet she asked the king to spare her people, and she named Haman. Today’s challenge is a real, careful word, not a play about the palace.
dailies.enochActivity: Say one kind true word to help someone!
dailies.elijah2: What did Esther say when the king asked who had dared to harm her people?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” (Esther 7:6).
dailies.jordyn2: How can we tell the truth about a wrong without turning it into a chance to mock or to show off?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can be clear and fair, as Esther was when she named the adversary. We do not pile on, or make a face, or tell the story to entertain. The point is to help people who are in danger or in need, and to trust that God can use courage like that.

dailies.jordynAnswer: We can thank God that she did not remain silent, and we can ask him for courage to speak when someone needs help. We pray solemnly, not as if danger were a game, and we remember that God used her courage to save her people.
dailies.action: Pray the family prayer slowly. When you hear, for such a time as this, pause and ask God to help you be brave and truthful today.

dailies.jordyn2: How can we pray about a hard conversation without pretending we are as famous or as endangered as Esther?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can tell God the real thing in front of us, thank him that he used Esther’s courage, and ask for a faithful word in our smaller place. God can use courage in ordinary rooms, not only in a palace.

dailies.jordynAnswer: God can be trusted, and he can save his people. He used Esther’s courage when silence would have been easier, and next week we will hear that Daniel kept praying, and that God shut the lions’ mouths. The same God is able to help.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: God used Esther's courage to save her people. Then look ahead to Daniel, who kept praying to God.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you used Esther’s courage to save her people. Thank you that she would not remain silent, and that she told the truth. Get our hearts ready to hear that Daniel kept praying to you, and that you shut the lions’ mouths. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we heard Mordecai call Esther not to remain silent, and we heard Esther gather her people to fast and go to the king. At the banquet she asked him to spare her people, and she named Haman. God used her courage to save her people. Next week we will hear that Daniel kept praying to God, and that God shut the lions’ mouths.
dailies.enochActivity: Wave a small hello toward tomorrow and say: Daniel kept praying!
dailies.elijah2: What did Mordecai say about such a time as this, and what did Esther say when she named the enemy?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Mordecai said, “Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?” Esther said, “An adversary and enemy! This vile Haman!” (Esther 4:13–14; 7:6).
dailies.jordyn2: Esther’s story is about courage in a dangerous time, and next week Daniel will keep praying when it is costly. What should we carry from Esther into that story?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should remember that God can use courage, and that his people do not have to remain silent. Esther went and told the truth. Daniel will keep praying. The same God can save his people, and he is worthy of trust.

readings.text: 10 Now when Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 11 Then these men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking God for help. 12 So they went to the king and spoke to him about his royal decree: “Did you not publish a decree that during the next thirty days anyone who prays to any god or human being except to you, Your Majesty, would be thrown into the lions’ den?” The king answered, “The decree stands—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” 13 Then they said to the king, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” 14 When the king heard this, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him. 15 Then the men went as a group to King Darius and said to him, “Remember, Your Majesty, that according to the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or edict that the king issues can be changed.”

16 So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” 17 A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that Daniel’s situation might not be changed. 18 Then the king returned to his palace and spent the night without eating and without any entertainment being brought to him. And he could not sleep.

19 At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the lions’ den. 20 When he came near the den, he called to Daniel in an anguished voice, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?” 21 Daniel answered, “May the king live forever! 22 My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” 23 The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den. And when Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

story: Last week we learned that God used Esther’s courage to save her people. Today we hear that Daniel kept praying to God, and that God shut the lions’ mouths.

We do not leave today’s reading to tell the earlier verses as official text. In our words, a law had been made that, for thirty days, people were not to pray to anyone except the king. We say that simply. Now when Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before.

Then these men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking God for help. They told the king about the decree, and the king answered, “The decree stands—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” Then they said to the king, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” When the king heard this, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him. But the men said, “Remember, Your Majesty, that according to the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or edict that the king issues can be changed.”

So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. We say that simply, and with care. It is not a scene to act out or to linger on. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” A stone was placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it. Then the king returned to his palace and spent the night without eating, and he could not sleep.

At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the lions’ den. He called to Daniel in an anguished voice, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?” Daniel answered, “May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den. And when Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
We do not leave today’s reading to tell the later verses as official text. What we need is already here: Daniel kept praying, and God shut the lions’ mouths. Daniel had trusted in his God.
Next week we will hear that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild.
weeks.enochLine: Daniel kept praying, and God shut the lions’ mouths!
enochActivities: Activity: Get down on your knees three times and say: Thank you, God!
Activity: Look toward a window and say a short thank-you prayer, the way Daniel kept praying.
elijahQuestions: In Daniel 6:10, what did Daniel do when he learned that the decree had been published?
In Daniel 6:13–14, what did the men tell the king about Daniel, and how did the king feel?
In Daniel 6:16, what did the king say to Daniel when he was thrown into the lions’ den?
In Daniel 6:20–23, what did the king ask, what did Daniel say God had done, and what was found when Daniel was lifted out?
elijahAnswers: He went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before (Daniel 6:10).

They said, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” When the king heard this, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him (Daniel 6:13–14).
The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” (Daniel 6:16).

The king asked, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?” Daniel answered, “May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” The king was overjoyed, Daniel was lifted from the den, and no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God (Daniel 6:20–23).
jordynQuestions: When Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he prayed three times a day, giving thanks, just as he had done before (Daniel 6:10). What does this show about praying when it becomes costly?

The king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” (Daniel 6:16), and later Daniel said that God sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions (Daniel 6:22). How should we tell the story of the den without making a game of fear or of harm?
Daniel kept praying to God, and God shut the lions’ mouths. Next week we will hear that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild. What stays the same about God?
jordynAnswers: Daniel did not wait to see if the danger would pass, and he did not hide the windows. He kept the same praying life he already had, and he gave thanks. Courage here looks like ordinary faithfulness that will not stop when a law makes it hard.

We tell the truth: Daniel was thrown into the den, the king could not sleep, and in the morning Daniel was unhurt because God had shut the lions’ mouths. We say that simply, and with care. We do not act out the den, or pretend to be lions. The point is that Daniel had trusted in his God, and that God can rescue the one who keeps praying.

God can be trusted, and he hears prayer. He used Esther’s courage last week, and this week he shut the lions’ mouths for Daniel, who kept praying. Next week we will hear that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild. The same God is able to help.
weeks.jordynApplication: Daniel kept praying to God, and God shut the lions’ mouths (Daniel 6:10–23). This week, keep a regular prayer—morning, midday, or evening—even when it would be easier to skip it, and trust God with the thing that feels too big. Next week we will hear that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she kept a regular prayer when it would have been easy to stop. If it is fitting, thank God together that Daniel kept praying, and that God shut the lions’ mouths.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Daniel got down on his knees three times a day and prayed, giving thanks, just as he had done before. Thank you that the king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” Thank you that Daniel said, “May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” You shut the lions’ mouths, and no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in you. Help us keep praying, and help us trust you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: When the decree was published, Daniel did not stop. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks, just as he had done before.
dailies.verse: Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up get on your knees and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah: What did Daniel do in his upstairs room when he learned that the decree had been published?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before (Daniel 6:10).
dailies.jordyn: The men found Daniel praying and asking God for help, and they said to the king, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” (Daniel 6:11–13). What does it mean that he still prayed three times a day?
dailies.jordynAnswer: It means he did not change his praying to stay safe. He kept the same habit of thanks and help, even after the decree was published. Faithfulness here is ordinary prayer that will not quit.
dailies.action: Read Daniel 6:10–15 together. Then get down on your knees once and thank God, the way Daniel kept giving thanks.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Daniel got down on his knees three times a day and prayed, giving thanks, just as he had done before. Help us keep praying, even when it would be easier to stop. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: In our words, a law had been made that people were not to pray to anyone except the king for thirty days. We do not leave today’s reading to tell those earlier verses as official text. When Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home, and three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks, just as he had done before. Men found him praying and told the king, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” The king was greatly distressed and tried to save him, but the men said the law could not be changed.
dailies.enochActivity: Get on your knees and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah2: What did the king answer about the decree, and what did he try to do for Daniel?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The king answered, “The decree stands—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” When he heard about Daniel, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him (Daniel 6:12, 14).
dailies.jordyn2: Daniel prayed with the windows opened toward Jerusalem, and he prayed just as he had done before (Daniel 6:10). Why does that matter when a new law makes prayer costly?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The windows were not a new show. This was his regular life with God. When the cost rose, he did not invent a secret, smaller faith. He kept the same thanks, in the same place, three times a day.
dailies.passageText: 10 Now when Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 11 Then these men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking God for help. 12 So they went to the king and spoke to him about his royal decree: “Did you not publish a decree that during the next thirty days anyone who prays to any god or human being except to you, Your Majesty, would be thrown into the lions’ den?” The king answered, “The decree stands—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” 13 Then they said to the king, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” 14 When the king heard this, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him. 15 Then the men went as a group to King Darius and said to him, “Remember, Your Majesty, that according to the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or edict that the king issues can be changed.”

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Daniel prayed three times a day. We can practice a small, regular thanks, not a game about lions.
dailies.verse: Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before.
dailies.enoch: Get down on your knees three times and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah: How many times a day did Daniel get down on his knees and pray, and what did he give?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before (Daniel 6:10).
dailies.jordyn: This game is about keeping a regular prayer, not about pretending to be in a den. How do we keep it kind and serious?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not roar, crawl, or act out being thrown to lions. We kneel three times, say thank you, and remember that Daniel kept praying even when it was hard. The practice is thanks, not fear.
dailies.action: Choose a window, or face one if you can. Kneel three times—morning, midday, and evening if the day allows, or three times in a row if that is simpler. Each time, say a short thank-you to God. Do not pretend to be a lion, and do not act out the den.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Daniel prayed three times a day, giving thanks, just as he had done before. Help us practice a regular thank-you, and help us not turn his danger into a game. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Three times a day Daniel got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. Men found him praying and asking God for help. Today we practice that regular thanks. We do not act out the den.
dailies.enochActivity: Kneel three times and say: Thank you, God!
dailies.elijah2: What were the men doing when they found Daniel, and what was Daniel doing?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: These men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking God for help (Daniel 6:11).
dailies.jordyn2: Why is kneeling to give thanks a better practice than acting out the lions’ den?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The den was a real danger, and we tell that simply later in the week, with care. What we can practice today is Daniel’s faithful habit: getting down on his knees, asking God for help, and giving thanks, just as he had done before.
dailies.passageText: 10 Now when Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 11 Then these men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking God for help.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den, and the king said that Daniel’s God, whom he served continually, might rescue him. We tell this simply, and with care.
dailies.verse: May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say with you: God can rescue!
dailies.elijah: What did the king say to Daniel when they threw him into the lions’ den?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” (Daniel 6:16).
dailies.jordyn: What happened after Daniel was thrown into the den, and how did the king spend the night (Daniel 6:17–18)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles. Then the king returned to his palace and spent the night without eating and without any entertainment being brought to him. And he could not sleep.
dailies.action: Read Daniel 6:16–18 together. Then say, in your own words, that Daniel served God continually, and that we tell the den simply, without acting it out.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” Thank you that Daniel served you continually. Help us trust you when something feels too big, and help us tell this story with care. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. We say that simply, and with care. The king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” A stone was placed over the mouth of the den and sealed. The king could not eat or sleep that night. We do not act this out. We remember that Daniel served God continually, and that the king hoped God would rescue him.
dailies.enochActivity: Say: God can rescue!
dailies.elijah2: What did the men remind the king just before this, and what order did the king then give?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The men said, “Remember, Your Majesty, that according to the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or edict that the king issues can be changed.” So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den (Daniel 6:15–16).
dailies.jordyn2: The king was greatly distressed and had tried until sundown to save Daniel (Daniel 6:14). How should we hear both the king’s effort and the throwing into the den?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can notice that the king cared, and that he still could not change the decree. We tell the den simply, not as an adventure game. The hope in the king’s own words is that Daniel’s God, whom he served continually, might rescue him.
dailies.passageText: 16 So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” 17 A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that Daniel’s situation might not be changed. 18 Then the king returned to his palace and spent the night without eating and without any entertainment being brought to him. And he could not sleep.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: At dawn the king hurried to the den. God had shut the lions’ mouths, and Daniel was unhurt because he had trusted in his God. Today we practice trust by keeping a prayer.
dailies.verse: My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up look toward morning and say: I will keep praying!
dailies.elijah: What did the king ask at the den, and what did Daniel say God had done?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The king asked, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?” Daniel answered, “May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” (Daniel 6:20–22).
dailies.jordyn: When Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God (Daniel 6:23). What is today’s challenge, and what is it not?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The challenge is to keep one regular prayer and to trust God with one hard thing, the way Daniel kept praying and trusted his God. It is not a dare, and it is not a game about lions or about being brave in a showy way.
dailies.action: Name one thing that feels too big this week. Tell God about it in a regular prayer—on your knees if you can, once or three times today. Then take one quiet faithful step. Do not act out the den, and do not test God by doing something unsafe.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Daniel said, “May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” Thank you that no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in you. Help us keep praying, and help us trust you with the thing that feels too big. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: At the first light of dawn, the king hurried to the lions’ den and called to Daniel in an anguished voice, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?” Daniel said that God had sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions. The king was overjoyed, Daniel was lifted out, and no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God. Today’s challenge is a real prayer of trust, not a play about danger.
dailies.enochActivity: Say: I trust you, God. I will keep praying!
dailies.elijah2: What did the king do at dawn, and what was found when Daniel was lifted out?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the lions’ den. The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out. When Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God (Daniel 6:19, 23).
dailies.jordyn2: Daniel said the lions had not hurt him, because he was found innocent in God’s sight, and he had not done wrong before the king (Daniel 6:22). How can that shape the way we trust God this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We trust God because he is the living God, not because we pretend there is no danger. Daniel had kept praying, and he had done no wrong. We can tell the truth, keep praying, and leave the rescue to God, without turning the story into a test we invent.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: We thank God that Daniel kept praying, and that God shut the lions’ mouths. We ask for the same trust.
dailies.verse: May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Thank you, God. Help us keep praying!
dailies.elijah: What did the king hope Daniel’s God would do, and what did Daniel later say God had done?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” Daniel later said, “May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” (Daniel 6:16, 21–22).
dailies.jordyn: No wound was found on Daniel, because he had trusted in his God (Daniel 6:23). How can that shape a family prayer?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can thank God that Daniel kept praying, and that God shut the lions’ mouths. We ask him to help us serve him continually, and to trust him with what feels too big. We pray solemnly, not as if the den were a game.
dailies.action: Pray the family prayer slowly. When you hear, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” pause and ask God to help you keep praying and to trust him.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Daniel prayed three times a day, giving thanks, just as he had done before. Thank you that the king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” Thank you that you sent your angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and that no wound was found on Daniel, because he had trusted in you. Help us keep praying, and help us trust you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we pray with Daniel’s faithful prayer in our ears. He got down on his knees three times a day and gave thanks, just as he had done before. The king said, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” God sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and Daniel was lifted out unhurt, because he had trusted in his God.
dailies.enochActivity: Fold your hands and say: Help us keep praying!
dailies.elijah2: What did Daniel give to God three times a day, and what had he trusted in at the end of the story?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. When he was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God (Daniel 6:10, 23).
dailies.jordyn2: How can we pray about a hard thing without turning Daniel’s rescue into a promise that every hard thing will end the same way tomorrow?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can thank God for what he did for Daniel, tell him the real thing in front of us, and ask for help to keep praying and to trust him. We leave the how and the when to God, and we remember that Daniel served him continually even before the rescue.

Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 16 So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” 22 My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” 23 The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den. And when Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

readings.text: 11 I went to Jerusalem, and after staying there three days 12 I set out during the night with a few others. I had not told anyone what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem. There were no mounts with me except the one I was riding on. 13 By night I went out through the Valley Gate toward the Jackal Well and the Dung Gate, examining the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire. 14 Then I moved on toward the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool, but there was not enough room for my mount to get through; 15 so I went up the valley by night, examining the wall. Finally, I turned back and reentered through the Valley Gate. 16 The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, because as yet I had said nothing to the Jews or the priests or nobles or officials or any others who would be doing the work.

17 Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” 18 I also told them about the gracious hand of my God on me and what the king had said to me. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work.

15 So the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days. 16 When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God.

story: Last week we learned that Daniel kept praying to God, and that God shut the lions’ mouths. Today we hear that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild.

We do not leave today’s readings to tell the earlier verses as official text. In our words, Nehemiah had come a long way, and God had opened a door for him to help Jerusalem. Then he went to Jerusalem, and after staying there three days he set out during the night with a few others. He had not told anyone what his God had put in his heart to do for Jerusalem.

By night he went out, examining the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire. We say the ruin simply, and with care. It is not a scene to linger on. He moved on toward the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool, but there was not enough room for his mount to get through, so he went up the valley by night, examining the wall, and then turned back. The officials did not know where he had gone or what he was doing, because as yet he had said nothing to the people who would be doing the work.

Then he said to them, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” He also told them about the gracious hand of his God on him and what the king had said to him. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work.

We do not leave today’s readings to tell the middle chapters as official text. In our words, the work took time, and there were people who did not want the wall built. We say that simply. Then the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days. When all their enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God. Nehemiah prayed and worked, and God helped his people rebuild.
Next week we will hear that God was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.
weeks.enochLine: Nehemiah prayed and worked, and God helped them rebuild!
enochActivities: Activity: Stack a few blocks or books, like starting a wall, and say: Let us start rebuilding!
Activity: Fold your hands to pray, then do one small helpful job.
elijahQuestions: In Nehemiah 2:11–12, when did Nehemiah set out, and what had he not told anyone?
In Nehemiah 2:13–15, what did Nehemiah examine by night, and what had happened to the walls and gates?
In Nehemiah 2:17–18, what did Nehemiah say to the people, what did he tell them about God, and what did they reply?
In Nehemiah 6:15–16, how long did the work take, and what did the surrounding nations realize?
elijahAnswers: He went to Jerusalem, and after staying there three days he set out during the night with a few others. He had not told anyone what his God had put in his heart to do for Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:11–12).

He examined the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire. He went up the valley by night, examining the wall, and then turned back and reentered through the Valley Gate (Nehemiah 2:13–15).

He said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” He also told them about the gracious hand of his God on him and what the king had said to him. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work (Nehemiah 2:17–18).

The wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days. When all their enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God (Nehemiah 6:15–16).
jordynQuestions: Nehemiah had not told anyone what his God had put in his heart to do for Jerusalem, and he examined the broken wall by night before he spoke (Nehemiah 2:12–16). What does this show about praying, looking carefully, and then working?

Nehemiah said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” He told them about the gracious hand of his God, and they said, “Let us start rebuilding.” Later the nations realized that this work had been done with the help of our God (Nehemiah 2:17–18; 6:16). How do prayer and work belong together in this story?

Nehemiah prayed and worked, and God helped his people rebuild. Next week we will hear that God was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid. What stays the same about God?
jordynAnswers: God had already put the work in Nehemiah’s heart. He looked carefully at the real trouble before he called others to build. Prayer is not a substitute for seeing what is broken, and seeing what is broken is not a substitute for trusting God. He waited to speak until he was ready to begin the good work.

They did not rebuild by talk only, and they did not rebuild as if God were absent. Nehemiah named the ruin honestly, invited the people to work, and pointed to the gracious hand of God. When the wall was finished in fifty-two days, even the enemies could tell that God had helped. Prayer and work belonged together from the start to the finish.

God can be trusted, and he helps his people. He heard Daniel’s prayer, he helped Nehemiah’s people rebuild, and next week we will hear that he is merciful even to people we would rather avoid. The same God is able to help, and he is kind.
weeks.jordynApplication: Nehemiah prayed and worked, and God helped his people rebuild (Nehemiah 2:11–18; 6:15–16). This week, pray about one broken or unfinished thing, then take one small faithful step to help rebuild it—a chore, a kindness, or a piece of work you have been putting off. Next week we will hear that God was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week what she prayed about and what small rebuilding step she took. If it is fitting, thank God together that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Nehemiah said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” Thank you that the people said, “Let us start rebuilding.” Thank you that he told them about the gracious hand of his God, and that the wall was completed in fifty-two days, with the help of our God. You helped your people rebuild. Help us pray and work. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.elijahAnswer: After staying in Jerusalem three days, he set out during the night with a few others. He had not told anyone what his God had put in his heart to do for Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:11–12).
dailies.jordyn: What did Nehemiah examine by night, and what had happened to the walls and gates (Nehemiah 2:13–15)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He examined the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire. We say that simply. He went up the valley by night, examining the wall, and then turned back and reentered through the Valley Gate.

dailies.teach: Nehemiah went to Jerusalem, stayed three days, and then set out at night with a few others. God had put something in his heart to do for Jerusalem, and he had not told anyone yet. By night he examined the broken walls and the gates destroyed by fire. We say the ruin simply. The officials did not yet know where he had gone or what he was doing.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Nehemiah looked at the broken wall, then the people said they would start rebuilding. We can practice looking, then beginning a small good work.
dailies.verse: Let us start rebuilding.
dailies.enoch: Stack a few blocks or books, like starting a wall, and say: Let us start rebuilding!
dailies.elijah: What did the people reply when Nehemiah told them about the gracious hand of God and what the king had said?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work (Nehemiah 2:18).
dailies.jordyn: This game is about starting a good work, not about fighting enemies or playing in ruins. How do we keep it kind and useful?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not pretend to smash walls or act out a battle. We look at a small mess or a stack of blocks, then begin to build or tidy. The practice is starting the good work, the way they said, “Let us start rebuilding.”
dailies.action: Walk once around a table or a room, looking carefully like Nehemiah examining the wall. Then stack a few books or blocks, or tidy one small thing, and say, “Let us start rebuilding.” Do not knock things down on purpose.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the people said, “Let us start rebuilding.” Thank you that they began this good work. Help us look carefully, then start the work you put in our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Nehemiah told the people the trouble they were in, and he told them about the gracious hand of his God. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work. Today we practice looking, then starting, not a fight and not a ruin game.
dailies.enochActivity: Stack a small wall of blocks and say: Let us start rebuilding!
dailies.elijah2: What trouble did Nehemiah name, and what did he invite the people to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” (Nehemiah 2:17).
dailies.jordyn2: Why is stacking or tidying a better practice than acting out burned gates or enemies?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The ruin was real, and we tell it simply, with care. Enemies come later in the week, and even then we do not make a mocking game of them. What we can practice today is the people’s yes: starting a good work with God’s help.

dailies.elijah: What did Nehemiah say about the trouble they were in, and what did he invite the people to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” (Nehemiah 2:17).
dailies.jordyn: What did Nehemiah also tell them, and how did they answer (Nehemiah 2:18)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He also told them about the gracious hand of his God on him and what the king had said to him. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work.
dailies.action: Read Nehemiah 2:17–18 together. Then say, in your own words, that God had been gracious, and that it is time to start a good work.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Nehemiah said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” Thank you that he told them about the gracious hand of his God, and that they said, “Let us start rebuilding.” Help us begin the good work you give us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After examining the wall, Nehemiah spoke. He said, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” He did not hide the ruin, and he did not hide God’s help. He told them about the gracious hand of his God on him and what the king had said to him. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work.
dailies.enochActivity: Say: Come, let us rebuild! God will help us!
dailies.elijah2: Nehemiah told them about the gracious hand of his God and about the king. Why do both of those belong in the same speech?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: God had already been at work, and the king’s words were part of that help. Nehemiah wanted the people to start rebuilding because of the gracious hand of God, not because they had to pretend the trouble was small (Nehemiah 2:18).
dailies.jordyn2: The people began this good work after they heard both the trouble and God’s gracious hand. What should we remember when a job looks too big?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should tell the truth about what is broken, remember that God’s hand can be gracious, and then start. The first yes is not finishing the wall. It is beginning the good work with him.

dailies.enochActivity: Pray, then do one small helpful job!
dailies.elijah2: What happened when all their enemies heard that the wall was completed?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God (Nehemiah 6:16).
dailies.jordyn2: How should we hear the enemies’ fear, and how should that shape our work this week?

dailies.jordyn2: How can we pray about a long job without pretending we can finish it in a day, the way the wall was finished in fifty-two days?

dailies.jordyn: We have seen that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild. Next week we will hear that God was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid. What stays the same about God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God can be trusted, and he helps his people. He heard Daniel’s prayer, he helped Jerusalem rebuild, and next week we will hear that he is merciful even to people we would rather avoid. The same God is able to help, and he is kind.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Nehemiah prayed and worked, and God helped his people rebuild. Then look ahead to Nineveh, and to God’s mercy.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that you helped your people rebuild. Thank you for the gracious hand of God, and that the wall was finished with your help. Get our hearts ready to hear that you were merciful to Nineveh, and that you want us to love people we would rather avoid. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we heard Nehemiah examine the broken wall by night, name the trouble, and tell the people about the gracious hand of his God. They said, “Let us start rebuilding.” The wall was completed in fifty-two days, with the help of our God. Next week we will hear that God was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.
dailies.enochActivity: Wave a small hello toward tomorrow and say: God was merciful!
dailies.elijah2: What had God put in Nehemiah’s heart, and what did the nations realize at the end?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: God had put in his heart something to do for Jerusalem. The nations realized that this work had been done with the help of our God (Nehemiah 2:12; 6:16).
dailies.jordyn2: Daniel kept praying, Nehemiah prayed and worked, and next week God will show mercy to Nineveh. What should we carry from this wall into that story?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We should remember that God helps his people, and that his help can be seen in prayer and in work. He is also merciful. The same God who helped them rebuild can teach us to love people we would rather avoid.
dailies.passageText: 12 I set out during the night with a few others. I had not told anyone what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem. There were no mounts with me except the one I was riding on. 17 Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.” 18 I also told them about the gracious hand of my God on me and what the king had said to me. They replied, “Let us start rebuilding.” So they began this good work. 15 So the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days. 16 When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God.

readings.text: 1 The word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai: 2 “Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.” 3 But Jonah ran away from the LORD and headed for Tarshish. He went down to Joppa, where he found a ship bound for that port. After paying the fare, he went aboard and sailed for Tarshish to flee from the LORD. 4 Then the LORD sent a great wind on the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship threatened to break up. 5 All the sailors were afraid and each cried out to his own god. And they threw the cargo into the sea to lighten the ship. But Jonah had gone below deck, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep. 6 The captain went to him and said, “How can you sleep? Get up and call on your god! Maybe he will take notice of us so that we will not perish.” 7 Then the sailors said to each other, “Come, let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity.” They cast lots and the lot fell on Jonah. 8 So they asked him, “Tell us, who is responsible for making all this trouble for us? What kind of work do you do? Where do you come from? What is your country? From what people are you?” 9 He answered, “I am a Hebrew and I worship the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.” 10 This terrified them and they asked, “What have you done?” (They knew he was running away from the LORD, because he had already told them so.) 11 The sea was getting rougher and rougher. So they asked him, “What should we do to you to make the sea calm down for us?” 12 “Pick me up and throw me into the sea,” he replied, “and it will become calm. I know that it is my fault that this great storm has come upon you.” 13 Instead, the men did their best to row back to land. But they could not, for the sea grew even wilder than before. 14 Then they cried out to the LORD, “Please, LORD, do not let us die for taking this man’s life. Do not hold us accountable for killing an innocent man, for you, LORD, have done as you pleased.” 15 Then they took Jonah and threw him overboard, and the raging sea grew calm. 16 At this the men greatly feared the LORD, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to him. 17 Now the LORD provided a huge fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

1 Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: 2 “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” 3 Jonah obeyed the word of the LORD and went to Nineveh. Now Nineveh was a very large city; it took three days to go through it. 4 Jonah began by going a day’s journey into the city, proclaiming, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.” 5 The Ninevites believed God. A fast was proclaimed, and all of them, from the greatest to the least, put on sackcloth. 6 When Jonah’s warning reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, took off his royal robes, covered himself with sackcloth and sat down in the dust. 7 This is the proclamation he issued in Nineveh: “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Do not let people or animals, herds or flocks, taste anything; do not let them eat or drink. 8 But let people and animals be covered with sackcloth. Let everyone call urgently on God. Let them give up their evil ways and their violence. 9 Who knows? God may yet relent and with compassion turn from his fierce anger so that we will not perish.” 10 When God saw what they did and how they turned from their evil ways, he relented and did not bring on them the destruction he had threatened.

1 But to Jonah this seemed very wrong, and he became angry. 2 He prayed to the LORD, “Isn’t this what I said, LORD, when I was still at home? That is what I tried to forestall by fleeing to Tarshish. I knew that you are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity. 3 Now, LORD, take away my life, for it is better for me to die than to live.” 4 But the LORD replied, “Is it right for you to be angry?” 5 Jonah had gone out and sat down at a place east of the city. There he made himself a shelter, sat in its shade and waited to see what would happen to the city. 6 Then the LORD God provided a leafy plant and made it grow up over Jonah to give shade for his head to ease his discomfort, and Jonah was very happy about the plant. 7 But at dawn the next day God provided a worm, which chewed the plant so that it withered. 8 When the sun rose, God provided a scorching east wind, and the sun blazed on Jonah’s head so that he grew faint. He wanted to die, and said, “It would be better for me to die than to live.” 9 But God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the plant?” “It is,” he said. “And I’m so angry I wish I were dead.” 10 But the LORD said, “You have been concerned about this plant, though you did not tend it or make it grow. It sprang up overnight and died overnight. 11 And should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left—and also many animals?”

story: Last week we learned that Nehemiah prayed and worked, and that God helped his people rebuild. Today we hear that God was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.

The word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai: “Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.” But Jonah ran away from the LORD and headed for Tarshish. Then the LORD sent a great wind on the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship threatened to break up. We say the storm simply, and with care. It is not a scene to act out. The sailors were afraid. They asked Jonah what they should do, and he said, “Pick me up and throw me into the sea,” “and it will become calm. I know that it is my fault that this great storm has come upon you.” They took Jonah and threw him overboard, and the raging sea grew calm. Now the LORD provided a huge fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. We say that simply too. It is not a game about being eaten.
We do not leave today’s readings to tell Jonah 2 as official text. In our words, Jonah prayed in the fish, and the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.

Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” Jonah obeyed the word of the LORD and went to Nineveh. He began by going a day’s journey into the city, proclaiming, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.” The Ninevites believed God. A fast was proclaimed, and all of them, from the greatest to the least, put on sackcloth. When Jonah’s warning reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, took off his royal robes, covered himself with sackcloth and sat down in the dust. He issued this proclamation: “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Do not let people or animals, herds or flocks, taste anything; do not let them eat or drink. But let people and animals be covered with sackcloth. Let everyone call urgently on God. Let them give up their evil ways and their violence. Who knows? God may yet relent and with compassion turn from his fierce anger so that we will not perish.” When God saw what they did and how they turned from their evil ways, he relented and did not bring on them the destruction he had threatened.

But to Jonah this seemed very wrong, and he became angry. He prayed, “Isn’t this what I said, LORD, when I was still at home? That is what I tried to forestall by fleeing to Tarshish. I knew that you are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity. Now, LORD, take away my life, for it is better for me to die than to live.” The LORD replied, “Is it right for you to be angry?” The LORD God provided a leafy plant to shade Jonah, and Jonah was very happy about the plant. Then God provided a worm, which chewed the plant so that it withered, and a scorching east wind. Jonah said it would be better for him to die than to live. God said, “Is it right for you to be angry about the plant?” Jonah said, “It is,” “And I’m so angry I wish I were dead.” We hear his anger and his wish simply, not as a joke and not as a game. Then the LORD said, “You have been concerned about this plant, though you did not tend it or make it grow. It sprang up overnight and died overnight. And should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left—and also many animals?” God was merciful to Nineveh, and he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.
Next week we will hear that Jesus will make a new heaven and a new earth, and that God will live with his people forever.
weeks.enochLine: God was merciful to Nineveh, and he wants us to love people too!
enochActivities: Activity: Walk one way, then turn around and walk the other way, like Jonah finally going to Nineveh.
Activity: Name one person to be kind to, and say: God is merciful!
elijahQuestions: In Jonah 1:1–3, what did the LORD tell Jonah to do, and what did Jonah do instead?
In Jonah 1:15–17, what happened when they threw Jonah overboard, and what did the LORD provide?
In Jonah 3:1–10, what did Jonah proclaim, what did the people of Nineveh do, and what did God do?
In Jonah 4:1–11, why was Jonah angry, and what did the LORD say about Nineveh?
elijahAnswers: The LORD said, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.” But Jonah ran away from the LORD and headed for Tarshish (Jonah 1:1–3).

They took Jonah and threw him overboard, and the raging sea grew calm. The LORD provided a huge fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights (Jonah 1:15–17).

Jonah proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.” The Ninevites believed God, and they turned from their evil ways. When God saw what they did, he relented and did not bring on them the destruction he had threatened (Jonah 3:4–10).

To Jonah this seemed very wrong, and he became angry, because he knew that the LORD is a gracious and compassionate God. The LORD said, “You have been concerned about this plant, though you did not tend it or make it grow. It sprang up overnight and died overnight. And should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left—and also many animals?” (Jonah 4:1–11).
jordynQuestions: Jonah ran away from the LORD when he was sent to Nineveh, and later he became angry when God relented (Jonah 1:3; 4:1–3). What does this show about Jonah’s heart, and about the people he would rather avoid?

The LORD said, “You have been concerned about this plant, though you did not tend it or make it grow. It sprang up overnight and died overnight. And should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left—and also many animals?” How is God’s concern for Nineveh different from Jonah’s concern for the plant?

God was merciful to Nineveh, and he wants us to love people we would rather avoid. Next week we will hear that Jesus will make a new heaven and a new earth, and that God will live with his people forever. What stays the same about God?
jordynAnswers: Jonah knew that the LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity. That is why he fled, and that is why he was angry when Nineveh was spared. His heart was hard toward people he would rather avoid, even while he told the truth about God’s mercy.

Jonah was concerned about a plant he did not tend or make grow, which sprang up overnight and died overnight. God had concern for a great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left—and also many animals. God’s mercy is larger than Jonah’s comfort, and larger than our wish to stay away from people we do not like.

God can be trusted, and he is merciful. He helped his people rebuild, he was merciful to Nineveh, and next week we will hear that Jesus will make all things new, and that God will live with his people forever. The same God is kind, and he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.
weeks.jordynApplication: God was merciful to Nineveh, and he wants us to love people we would rather avoid (Jonah 1:1–17; 3:1–10; 4:1–11). This week, pray for one person who is hard for you to like or to go toward, then take one small kind step toward them—a word, a help, or a welcome. Next week we will hear that Jesus will make a new heaven and a new earth, and that God will live with his people forever.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whom she prayed for and what kind step she took. If it is fitting, thank God together that he was merciful to Nineveh, and that he wants us to love people we would rather avoid.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you said, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.” Thank you that when Jonah ran, you still sent him, and that Nineveh believed you and turned from their evil ways. Thank you that you said, “You have been concerned about this plant, though you did not tend it or make it grow. It sprang up overnight and died overnight. And should I not have concern for the great city of Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left—and also many animals?” You were merciful to Nineveh. Help us love people we would rather avoid. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: The LORD sent Jonah to Nineveh, but Jonah ran the other way. Even then, the LORD did not let him go.
dailies.verse: Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up walk one way, then turn around, and say: God still wants us to go!
dailies.elijah: What did the LORD tell Jonah to do, and what did Jonah do instead?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The LORD said, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.” But Jonah ran away from the LORD and headed for Tarshish (Jonah 1:1–3).
dailies.jordyn: When the sailors asked Jonah who he was, what did he answer (Jonah 1:9)? What happened after they threw him overboard (Jonah 1:15–17)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He answered, “I am a Hebrew and I worship the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.” They took Jonah and threw him overboard, and the raging sea grew calm. dailies.action: Read Jonah 1:1–17 together. Then thank God that even when Jonah ran, the LORD still made the sea and the dry land, and still had a word for Nineveh.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you said, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before me.” Thank you that Jonah said, “I am a Hebrew and I worship the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.” When we want to run the other way, help us trust you and go. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Jonah said, “Pick me up and throw me into the sea,” “and it will become calm. dailies.elijah2: What did the sailors cry out to the LORD before they threw Jonah overboard?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They cried out, “Please, LORD, do not let us die for taking this man’s life. Do not hold us accountable for killing an innocent man, for you, LORD, have done as you pleased.” Then they threw him overboard, and the raging sea grew calm (Jonah 1:14–15).
dailies.jordyn2: Jonah said he worshiped the LORD, who made the sea and the dry land, even while he was running away. What does that show us?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Telling the truth about God is not the same as obeying him. Jonah knew who God was, and he still fled from the LORD. God still had mercy enough to stop him, and still had a word for a city Jonah did not want to love.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Jonah ran one way, then God sent him again, and he went to Nineveh. Today we practice turning around and going toward someone, not acting out a storm or a fish.
dailies.verse: Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.
dailies.enoch: Walk one way, then turn around and walk the other way, and say: I will go!
dailies.elijah: When the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time, what did the LORD say, and what did Jonah do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The LORD said, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” Jonah obeyed the word of the LORD and went to Nineveh (Jonah 3:1–3).
dailies.jordyn: This game is about turning around and going, not about a storm, a fish, or being thrown. How do we keep it kind and useful?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not pretend to drown, to swallow anyone, or to throw anyone. We walk one way, then turn and walk toward a person or a room, the way Jonah finally went to Nineveh. The practice is going toward people, not acting out danger.
dailies.action: Stand at one side of a room. Walk a few steps as if you are going the wrong way. Stop, turn around, and walk to the other side, as if you are going to Nineveh. Say, I will go. Do not throw anything, and do not play a fish game.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you said a second time, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” Thank you that Jonah obeyed and went. Help us turn around when we would rather run, and help us go toward people you love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: We do not leave today’s reading to tell Jonah 2 as official text. In our words, Jonah prayed in the fish, and the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land. Then the word of the LORD came a second time: “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” Jonah obeyed and went to Nineveh. Today we practice turning around and going, not a storm and not a fish.
dailies.enochActivity: Turn around, walk the other way, and say: I will go!
dailies.elijah2: Jonah ran toward Tarshish the first time. What was different the second time the word of the LORD came?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The second time the LORD said, “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” And Jonah obeyed the word of the LORD and went to Nineveh. Now Nineveh was a very large city; it took three days to go through it (Jonah 3:1–3).
dailies.jordyn2: Why is turning and walking a better practice than acting out the storm or the fish?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The storm and the fish were real, and we tell them simply, with care. They are not a game. What we can practice is the second obedience: turning around and going to people God wants to have mercy on.
dailies.passageText: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: 2 “Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message I give you.” 3 Jonah obeyed the word of the LORD and went to Nineveh. Now Nineveh was a very large city; it took three days to go through it.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Jonah proclaimed the LORD’s warning, Nineveh believed God and turned, and God relented. He was merciful to the city Jonah had avoided.
dailies.verse: Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up say: The people of Nineveh believed God!
dailies.elijah: What did Jonah proclaim in Nineveh, and what did the Ninevites do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.” The Ninevites believed God. A fast was proclaimed, and all of them, from the greatest to the least, put on sackcloth (Jonah 3:4–5).
dailies.jordyn: What did the king do, and what did God do when he saw that they turned from their evil ways (Jonah 3:6–10)?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The king rose from his throne, took off his royal robes, covered himself with sackcloth and sat down in the dust. He issued a proclamation that everyone should call urgently on God and give up their evil ways and their violence. When God saw what they did and how they turned from their evil ways, he relented and did not bring on them the destruction he had threatened.
dailies.action: Read Jonah 3:1–10 together. Then say, in your own words, that God was merciful when Nineveh turned.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jonah proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.” Thank you that the Ninevites believed you, and that when they turned from their evil ways, you relented. You were merciful to Nineveh. Help us believe that you are merciful still. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The word of the LORD came a second time, and Jonah went to Nineveh, proclaiming, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown.” The Ninevites believed God. We say their evil ways and their violence simply, as the text names them, without making a show of them. The king sat down in the dust and called the city to turn. When God saw what they did and how they turned from their evil ways, he relented and did not bring on them the destruction he had threatened.
dailies.enochActivity: Say: The people believed God, and God was merciful!
dailies.elijah2: What was the king’s proclamation in Nineveh?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He issued this proclamation: “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Do not let people or animals, herds or flocks, taste anything; do not let them eat or drink. But let people and animals be covered with sackcloth. Let everyone call urgently on God. Let them give up their evil ways and their violence. Who knows? God may yet relent and with compassion turn from his fierce anger so that we will not perish.” (Jonah 3:7–9).
dailies.jordyn2: God saw what they did and how they turned, and he relented. What should we remember about mercy when people turn?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God’s mercy is not reluctant in the way Jonah was reluctant. When Nineveh believed God and turned from their evil ways, he did not bring the destruction he had threatened. He is a God who relents from sending calamity, and he wants us to love the people he has mercy on.
